sources.title: How to raise a seed round in 2026: investor funnel, qualifying VCs, moats vs AI labs
sources.originalTitle: How to Raise a Seed Round in 2026: Ask Jason | E2294
sources.summary: Jason Calacanis answers community questions on fundraising mechanics, how startup costs collapsed, and differentiating from frontier AI labs. Treat fundraising as a full-time sales funnel, judge investors by behavior rather than words, and build community, multiplayer and human services around what LLMs won't ship.

principles.text: Judge investors by what they actually invest in, not what they say in meetings.
principles.quote: You have to divorce what people say in social settings especially investors from their behavior.

principles.text: Seed fundraising is a numbers game: about 150 targets, 50 meetings, 15 second meetings, two term sheets.
principles.quote: you need to contact 150 seed funds, get 50 meetings with seed funds to get 202 meetings to get two to give you a term sheet.

principles.text: Run fundraising as a qualified sales funnel and make it a full-time job for one co-founder.
principles.quote: You have to look at fundraising as a full-time job. You have to collect investors and build deep, meaningful relationships with them over time.

principles.text: If too early for later-stage investors, use accelerators for a first check and customers, then return.
principles.quote: get your 125k, your 25k check, your 250k check, get your first five customers and then you can go back to them and they might be a greater later stage.

principles.text: Differentiate from AI labs with features, community, multiplayer and human services the model interface won't add.
principles.quote: there's always going to be a feature set that the interface of the large language model is not going to add because of clutter and confusion.

principles.text: Hardware is now a moat and investors have reversed their stance; fund it via investors or Kickstarter pre-sales.
principles.quote: hardware is is the only one of the only moes left.

sources.title: Jason Calacanis: from Brooklyn grit to Silicon Alley Reporter, Weblogs Inc and All-In
sources.originalTitle: Jason Calacanis on Brooklyn Grit, Big Asks, The Magic of Thinking Big, and More
sources.summary: Jason tells how a Brooklyn kid with no money built Silicon Alley Reporter from a photocopied zine, lost it in the dotcom bust, then rebuilt with Weblogs Inc and sold to AOL for $30M. He also covers moderating All-In, loyalty in friendships, and defining success as enthusiasm rather than net worth.

principles.text: Get to a new medium first; early movers collect disproportionate credit and value.
principles.quote: I was always very interested in mediums right because if you get to a medium first you can exploit it

principles.text: Ask for things, even outrageous ones; people often say yes.
principles.quote: when I ask people things that many times people will do what I ask them to do

principles.text: Use rejection as fuel to prove it was no fluke, and start building the very next day.
principles.quote: I am going to prove I can do this again I am going to show everybody that this was not a fluke

principles.text: After a crash, call around the ecosystem to see what builders are tinkering with and spot the next wave.
principles.quote: I started calling people up I started calling people out what are you working on what's happening

principles.text: Model unit economics in a spreadsheet, then scale the content business and someone will buy it.
principles.quote: all we have to do with this business is scale it and then somebody will buy it

principles.text: Judge success by whether you can't wait to get out of bed, and design your life around that.
principles.quote: the right score card is did you wake up and couldn't get couldn't wait to get out of bed

sources.title: Jason Calacanis on podcasting, angel investing and founder-first investing (ACQ Sessions)
sources.originalTitle: ACQ Sessions: Jason Calacanis
sources.summary: A casual conversation where Jason describes how he built All-In's audience and character arcs, raised his fund publicly, and screens startups for world-class design and product velocity. He also shares how a pricing nudge helped Calm's early business model and why he prefers meritocratic, hands-on early-stage investing.

principles.text: Screen early startups for world-class design: best or top-10 in the category, not a template.
principles.quote: world-class design to me is if you were to look at all the companies in the space this one would have the best design or this would be one of the top 10

principles.text: Judge product velocity by asking what changed since the last meeting; look at the changelog and roadmap.
principles.quote: we met with this company in June it's now July what's changed about the product and they're like we don't know I'm like okay well let's find out where's their changelog where's their roadmap

principles.text: Price subscriptions against the real value of the alternative, not against one-off app prices.
principles.quote: I said Alex and Michael how much does it cost to go to a meditation class

principles.text: Raise a fund in public: tell people you're raising and run webinars instead of waiting for institutions.
principles.quote: literally I did two webinars couple hundred people came

principles.text: As a podcast host, act on behalf of the audience: pause jargon and ask for explanations to find the audience's edges.
principles.quote: I'm asking that question on behalf of the audience

principles.text: Anyone can learn and build now; nobody cares where you went to school, only your product, traction and team.
principles.quote: nobody cares where you went to school nobody cares where you live anymore nobody cares where you live they care about what you've built and your traction

sources.title: Jason Calacanis on angel investing, founder traits, and building a syndicate
sources.originalTitle: 433 TIP. The Art and Science of Investing in Startups w/ Jason Calacanis
sources.summary: Jason explains how he picks founders (broken, driven, with something to prove), why startups are war and sports, and how radical delegation and a syndicate let him invest at scale. He also covers product-market fit, compounding, riding winners, and deal terms.

principles.text: Product-market fit is fixed by improving the product, not the packaging.
principles.quote: instead of making the burger better, they do everything but the burger. So, they change the furniture in the restaurant. They changed the name of the store

principles.text: Make ten things 10% better rather than one thing twice as good.
principles.quote: it's very hard to make one feature of your product twice as good, but it's very easy to make 10 of your features 10% better.

principles.text: Look at the upside case first; red flags are a roadmap of what to fix, not a reason to pass.
principles.quote: I say make a list of all the things that could go wrong. And then on the other side of your journal, list the things, you know, but what if it goes right, but what if it works?

principles.text: Radically delegate and spend time only on the highest-leverage activities.
principles.quote: I am ruthless about delegation. Uh and I get more ruthless.

principles.text: Ride your winners and avoid selling too early; the last doublings are the most valuable.
principles.quote: if you get $10 million in an exit and you sell your Facebook shares for 10 million bucks, if you had held them, you would have had another 10x.

principles.text: Standard clean deal terms keep the cap table aligned; funky terms scare off later investors.
principles.quote: We don't do funky stuff like that because it's against our best interest in the long term

sources.title: Jason Calacanis on angel investing, startup intensity, loyalty and capitalism
sources.originalTitle: Jason Calacanis: Startups, Angel Investing, Capitalism, and Friendship | Lex Fridman Podcast #161
sources.summary: Jason Calacanis explains how he picks early bets (imagine the world if it works), why a well-built product plus delighted customers matters most, and why venture money is jet fuel not for everyone. He argues startups are an Olympic-level pursuit, that learning new skills is the key edge, and that loyalty and gratitude compound.

principles.text: Evaluate an idea by asking what happens if it works, not what could go wrong.
principles.quote: the way to do really well as an angel investor or just in technology or in life is to not say what could go wrong but to say what could go right

principles.text: Outlandish ideas nobody believes in often produce the biggest returns.
principles.quote: in almost all cases the crazy outlandish ideas that nobody believes in are the ones that have the greatest returns

principles.text: The best startups create a new market rather than just taking share from incumbents.
principles.quote: the best startups induce a market to exist

principles.text: The meta-skill is learning new skills fast; know enough that nobody can snow you when you hire.
principles.quote: the skill you need to refine is the ability to learn new skills

principles.text: Back a well-built product and delighted customers; engagement is the tell.
principles.quote: you can tell the delighted customer by just the amount of time they use it that's called engagement just a fancy word for how much they use it

principles.text: Venture capital is jet fuel; take it only if you want to go big and fast, otherwise grow off revenue.
principles.quote: it's jet fuel you only want to take that money if you really want to build something big and you want to build it fast

sources.title: Raising capital and surviving a downturn: Jason Calacanis on runway, cuts, and investor pitches
sources.originalTitle: A Super Angel's Views on Raising In Challenging Times w/ Jason Calacanis
sources.summary: Recorded in the early 2020 COVID crisis, Jason Calacanis gives a wartime playbook: be honest about the business, get to 18 months of runway, cut fast, and take services revenue to survive. He also covers pitching investors in a down market, valuation resets, cheap pivot tests and remote demos.

principles.text: Aim for 18 months of runway in a downturn; with six months of cash you will probably die unless you act.
principles.quote: you're gonna need eighteen months of cash that's the bottom line if you have six months of cash you're probably gonna die if you don't do anything

principles.text: Make the cuts and extend runway before you pitch; investors back founders who have already landed the plane.
principles.quote: after you've done all the necessary work of making the cuts extending the runway and driving revenue as best as you can that's a good time to go talk to investors

principles.text: In a crisis revenue is revenue: take services or consulting work from customers to survive, even at lower margin.
principles.quote: revenue is revenue if you can get revenue in the door through services yeah it's not the same margin but you got to eat

principles.text: Expect valuations to roughly halve in a down market, and don't be precious about price or round size.
principles.quote: I would say half of what the current market rate is and for YC companies maybe a third

principles.text: Don't spin your numbers; show raw weekly or monthly revenue and be candid about what works and what doesn't.
principles.quote: don't spin it's it's really a wasted thing if you spin this stuff we find out anyway and then you look like you're you know playing games

principles.text: Test a pivot with the laziest, cheapest experiment: a landing page that takes a credit card before you build anything.
principles.quote: that's how you do proper pivoting is what's the least amount of work what's the smallest test the most efficient test I can do the laziest way to get an answer to my question

sources.title: Jason Calacanis on angel investing rules: revenue first, small checks, bet only where you have an edge
sources.originalTitle: How To Pick Startup Winners With Jason Calacanis
sources.summary: Jason Calacanis explains how he picks startups and manages risk: start with revenue-generating companies and the smallest checks, judge product and customers over founder charisma, and only bet where you hold an edge. He also treats his public-market "J-trades" as paid education and uses a revenue, price-to-sales, growth and cash checklist.

principles.text: For your first 20 angel investments, back only companies with a product in market and revenue.
principles.quote: যেমন, আমি লোকেদের বলি শুধুমাত্র সেইসব কোম্পানিতে বিনিয়োগ করতে যাদের পণ্য বাজারে আছে এবং আপনার প্রথম ২০ টি বিনিয়োগের জন্য আয় আছে।

principles.text: While you are learning, invest the smallest check you can; even a single slot is fine.
principles.quote: এবং তারপর আপনি সর্বনিম্ন যে পরিমাণ অর্থ বিনিয়োগ করতে পারেন, তা-ই করুন।

principles.text: Only bet money in areas where you have an edge; treat other bets as paid education.
principles.quote: আমি কেবল সেইসব বিষয়েই টাকা বাজি ধরতে চাই যেখানে আমার সুবিধা আছে।

principles.text: Judge startups by product and customers; founder charisma can be faked, a great product and happy customers cannot.
principles.quote: কিন্তু আপনি একটি দুর্দান্ত পণ্যের ভান করতে পারবেন না । আপনি সন্তুষ্ট গ্রাহকদের ভান করতে পারবেন না ।

principles.text: In a long bull market, make sure you have a path to profitability and cash in the bank, and raise at the top.
principles.quote: শুধু নিশ্চিত করো যে তোমার লাভজনক হওয়ার একটা পথ আছে, অ্যাকাউন্টে কিছু ভালো পরিমাণ নগদ টাকা আছে এবং তুমি বাজারের সর্বোচ্চ দামে অর্থ সংগ্রহ করছো।

principles.text: To vet a beaten-down public company, check revenue, price-to-sales and user growth, then cash and burn.
principles.quote: আমি রাজস্ব দেখব, তারপর মূল্য-বিক্রয় অনুপাত দেখব এবং তারপর ব্যবহারকারীর বৃদ্ধি দেখব

sources.title: How Jason Calacanis built a media career from zines to All-In: skills, ranking, and podcast consistency
sources.originalTitle: EP 39: All-In’s Jason Calacanis Joins, Breaking Into Media, Tech in Journalism and Kanye
sources.summary: Jason recounts going from Brooklyn night-school kid to zine publisher, blog-network founder (Weblogs Inc, sold to AOL) and podcaster. Key lessons: self-teach the skills a product needs, use media to gain influence, hold consistency across 100 episodes, and let a podcast feed an investing business. Much of the Kanye/Elon chatter comes from the host, not Jason.

principles.text: Learn the skills your product needs; 60-70% proficiency is enough to know who to hire for the other 20-30%.
principles.quote: I believe you can get to 60 or 70 Proficiency in any uh discipline if you just put your mind to it that doesn't mean you're gonna become great at it but you only really need 60 70 percent to be able to figure out who has the 80 or 90 that you could hire

sources.title: Jason Calacanis on angel investing: venture as jet fuel, portfolio math, and founder grit
sources.originalTitle: Jason Calacanis | How Does Angel Investing Work? | Modern Wisdom 154
sources.summary: Jason explains how venture investing works: it's rocket fuel for outlier companies, most fail, and winners are unpredictable, so you place many bets and support every founder. He also covers leadership under chaos, knowing your superpower, and why podcasts are displacing journalism.

principles.text: Venture capital is rocket fuel for outlier companies; it doesn't suit normal small businesses.
principles.quote: venture capital is like jet fuel it's 40 or rocket fuel you wouldn't put rocket fuel like on a Vespa would not work out well

principles.text: Venture returns are a power law: most bets go to zero, and a rare winner returns 30x or more.
principles.quote: six are going to zero the seventh and eighth will return half the amount of money you put into them the ninth will return two or three times

principles.text: Nobody can pick winners in advance, so place many bets and treat every portfolio founder as a winner.
principles.quote: you just don't know which ones are gonna win so you just basically treat everybody who's in your portfolio amazing you try to just be as supportive as possible

principles.text: Define the goal, the plan, and who executes it; leaders stay calm and block out non-essentials in chaos.
principles.quote: what's the goal here what's the plan and who's going to execute the plan

principles.text: Founder success comes from self-possession and persistence, not a particular archetype; fill skill gaps with team members.
principles.quote: the founders that succeed most often are the ones who are self possessed and don't give up

principles.text: Know your superpower and lean into it; Jason's is talking, so he runs a podcast and invests in founders.
principles.quote: it's very important for you to understand what your skillset is what your personality is what you enjoy and then lean into that

sources.title: Jason Calacanis on angel investing: constraint, traction over pitch, and swinging for outliers
sources.originalTitle: Pomp Podcast #320: Jason Calacanis - The World’s Most Successful Angel Investor?
sources.summary: Jason Calacanis talks with Anthony Pompliano about ICO-era fundraising, why too much early capital hurts startups, and how he evaluates founders today. He stresses constraint, real customer traction, smart investors over high valuations, and a power-law portfolio approach.

principles.text: Too much early capital distances a team from the customer and breeds entitlement; constraint forces focus.
principles.quote: it distances the core team from reality so much and reality is the customer that they start arguing over things like chairs or the receptionist's desk or where the office is located

principles.text: Raising money just to start building signals you need permission; cheap tools mean builders should just ship.
principles.quote: you've basically signaled to the market that you are a permission asker you're somebody who needs permission or validation in order to build

principles.text: Pitch tropes are now easy to fake, so traction is what matters; talk to customers.
principles.quote: the secret weapon is to just talk to the customers right you talk to the customers they is very hard to fake customers

principles.text: Pick investors for intelligence and involvement, not the highest valuation; a few points of dilution are worth smart backers.
principles.quote: you want the smartest people on your teams and the incremental 20% on valuation when your company does have trouble

principles.text: Build an angel portfolio for outliers: a few winners should make up nearly all returns, so swing for the fences.
principles.quote: I'm swinging for the fences and I want the top two or three deals to be the absolute 90 percent of the portfolio we're not playing for singles and doubles

principles.text: On a platform you depend on, play nice and pay its fee; it can reward you with promotion.
principles.quote: pay the Vig to Apple if you play nice with Apple and you let them make money from it they can invest in the App Store and then they might promote you

sources.title: Jason Calacanis on angel investing, Founder University and media: bet on "what if it works"
sources.originalTitle: Inside All-In: Investing Lessons from Elon, Trump, Travis K | Jason Calacanis
sources.summary: Jason explains how he invests (high-volume small checks, "what if it works"), how Launch and Founder University filter thousands of applicants, and how he approaches new media formats and interviewing. He also covers the Uber/Robinhood bets, Elon's work ethic, the Twitter overstaffing lesson and AI-driven job displacement.

principles.text: Judge new bets by asking 'what if it works?' instead of sizing the TAM; manifest the market.
principles.quote: I just said to myself, what if it works? Which is what I always say to myself. What if it works?

principles.text: Treat new media formats as a sandbox: assume they'll work, play early, and don't dwell on failures.
principles.quote: I've always looked at like new mediums coming out as like a playground, and I just assume they're going to work, and if they don't work, who cares?

principles.text: Early-stage investing is a volume game: many small checks across lots of surface area, since most seed companies go to zero.
principles.quote: You have to have a lot of bets and you don't know which one's going to hit.

principles.text: Founders should expect rejection as a numbers game: talk to hundreds of investors, since you only need a few yeses.
principles.quote: You don't need a hundred out of a hundred people to invest in your company. You need three out of a hundred, two out of a hundred

principles.text: Great interviews come from listening: the next best question is embedded in the previous answer, not on your list.
principles.quote: the next best question is embedded in the previous answer.

principles.text: Reduce rejection friction by repeating back a founder's vision before deciding; it raised satisfaction scores markedly.
principles.quote: can I repeat back your vision to you so I make sure I didn't miss anything and once we started doing that the ratings got much better

sources.title: Scaling your startup, Team: hiring generalists, outsourcing, firing and equity
sources.originalTitle: E930 Scaling Your Startup E4 "Team": hiring, outsourcing, HR, structure, comp, firing, tough choices
sources.summary: Jason Calacanis and the Launch team walk through building a startup team: who to hire first, in-house versus outsourced work, hiring outreach, org structure, firing, and compensation. Jason's main points: keep engineering in-house, hire missionaries, explain the why behind goals, fire kindly but firmly, and let candidates choose cash or equity.

principles.text: Early hires wear many hats; specialization emerges as the company grows into departments.
principles.quote: it goes from having one person do five jobs to five people do five jobs to five people doing one job and that's called a department

principles.text: Keep developers in-house; dev shops don't build company knowledge and slow your pace.
principles.quote: when you hire those dev shops you don't accrue the knowledge into the company and then you can't move as fast because you're waiting on some dev shop that has four different customers

principles.text: Run the team at about 80% capacity to avoid burnout and leave room for special projects.
principles.quote: one way to make your organization grow is to say I'm going to keep everybody at 80 percent which is what I like to do here

principles.text: Write personal job posts and hire missionaries, not mercenaries.
principles.quote: you really want missionaries not mercenaries

principles.text: Explain the reason behind each goal; startup employees want to know why.
principles.quote: I think that's really the heart the hardest thing about being a manager today is that you're dealing with and a start-up people who want to know why

principles.text: Offer candidates a choice between more cash or more equity.
principles.quote: I'll offer um $80,000 plus one percent of the company or ninety thousand dollars and fifty basis points or a hundred thousand dollars and twenty basis points and let them pick which one they want

sources.title: How to raise a round right: VC-scale, metrics and fundraising process (Scaling Your Startup E1)
sources.originalTitle: E919 Scaling Your Startup E1 "Funding Your Company": How to raise a round right
sources.summary: Jason Calacanis, with Launch's Jason Demant and Ashley Whitehurst, walks through whether to fundraise at all, angels vs VCs vs syndicates, diligence pitfalls, and the metrics investors want. He frames VC money as jet fuel for rare, venture-scale businesses, and fundraising as a full-time sales funnel.

principles.text: VC and angel money only fits businesses that can return 20-100x; lifestyle outcomes don't qualify.
principles.quote: يسعى أصحاب رؤوس الأموال المخاطرة إلى مضاعفة استثماراتهم 20 أو 30 أو 40 أو 50 مرة. أما المستثمرون الملائكيون، فنسعى إلى مضاعفة استثماراتهم 100 مرة.

principles.text: Venture capital is jet fuel, not coal: take it only if you're ready for unnatural, rocket-speed growth.
principles.quote: أعتقد أنه من المهم أن يفهم الناس أن هذا أشبه بوقود الطائرات. إنه ليس فحمًا.

principles.text: Bootstrapping to get a product to market before raising is a legitimate, clear path to success.
principles.quote: إذا استطعت إيجاد طريقة للتمويل الذاتي لإيصال المنتج إلى السوق ثم جمع التمويل، فهذا طريق واضح آخر للنجاح.

principles.text: Churn compounds against you: at 20% monthly churn you must replace your whole user base every five months.
principles.quote: إذا كان 20%من مستخدميك يتسربون ، فهذا يعني أنه عليك استبدال قاعدة المستخدمين بالكامل أو أكثر كل 5 أشهر، أليس كذلك؟

principles.text: For consumer apps, pre-revenue Series A bar is roughly 10M monthly actives; seed is about 10-20% of that.
principles.quote: سمعت أن 10 ملايين مستخدم شهريًا هو المعيار الجديد.

principles.text: Raise enough for about 18 months and have plan B and C, so you don't have to fundraise repeatedly.
principles.quote: لماذا لا تجمع ما يكفي لمدة 18 شهرًا، وتضع خطة محكمة للوصول إلى تلك المراحل

sources.title: Jason Calacanis #AskJason: low-cost marketing, protecting ideas, focus, and knowing when to quit
sources.originalTitle: E883 #AskJason-Running out of $, marketing, protecting IP, transparency, traction, non-tech founders
sources.summary: Jason answers Reddit/Quora founder questions with his CMO. He covers low-cost offline marketing (meetups, street teams, podcasts), why unique ideas matter less than execution, keeping early momentum by studying feature usage data, and testing willingness to pay before burning five years on a startup.

principles.text: Beat paid-ad costs with real-world exposure: meetups, street teams and freebies that also yield product feedback.
principles.quote: real-world exposure to products is a great hack and you can very simply compare it to the cost of your online acquisitions

principles.text: Don't broadcast your idea before executing; people who do the work win credibility over people who talk.
principles.quote: you want to be in the bucket of people who do the work not the stalkers

principles.text: You don't need a unique idea; win on unique strategic, tactical and execution decisions plus timing.
principles.quote: you do not have to have a unique idea what you need to have is unique strategic tactical and execution ideas

principles.text: Keep momentum by plotting features by usage frequency and share of users, then focus ~90% of attention on the top ones.
principles.quote: you should put 90 percent of your attention towards whatever those number one and number two features are

principles.text: Stay focused on your core group and compound small daily gains instead of chasing side projects.
principles.quote: turn those 300 people into 303 or 307 and if you're doing that every day and you're adding you know one percent a day

principles.text: If a product hasn't worked in five years, force users to pay or engage to find out if there's a business.
principles.quote: if it hasn't worked in five years it's likely that it's not gonna work out

sources.title: Jason Calacanis on metrics, B2B lead gen, raising vs bootstrapping, and relentless focus
sources.originalTitle: E891 #AskJason Call-in: metrics, customer acquisition, qualified leads, investor $, relentless focus
sources.summary: In this #AskJason call-in, Jason advises founders on which metrics investors care about, how to win enterprise customers bottom-up, and whether to raise venture money. His biggest lesson from 2018: after early traction, narrow focus and scale what works rather than adding new products.

principles.text: Investors want growth plus acquisition channels; solid retention and persona work lets them skip to 'is it growing?'
principles.quote: you're checking off all the boxes and that you're just getting to the meat and potatoes of it which is is this growing or not

principles.text: Assume you can build the product; the question now is whether you can grow it. Be a growth founder.
principles.quote: we assume that you're going to be able to build a great product we assume you're gonna have all the measurement tools let's just get to you know let's just get to the cut to the chase can you grow it

principles.text: Present a numbered list of growth experiments, then triple down on the winners.
principles.quote: here are the 7 experiments we're running this quarter next quarter we're going to run these seven experiments and then we're gonna take the learning from those 14 experiments whichever three do the best we're gonna triple down on them

principles.text: Sell first to the frontline user with a short sales cycle; their feedback and word of mouth beat slow top-down deals.
principles.quote: I prefer you to go after the short sale cycle and the more modest reward not just because it's an easier sale but because of the feedback you're gonna get so you can refine the product

principles.text: Land-and-expand: win users one account at a time on a corporate card and let consensus build upward, as Slack, Yammer and Asana did.
principles.quote: they did not try to go in and win the top-level CTO they said let's win you know this group of developers over here let's win the group of salespeople over here and let them sign up one account at a time

principles.text: Venture money is a fast track: investors demand hypergrowth, and it adds investor management to your workload.
principles.quote: investors do not want slow growth they do not want methodical growth even if they say that they want things to break out they're looking for their uber their Airbnb their Google their Facebook their Instagram

sources.title: Jason Calacanis on virality, learning skills fast, and angel investing for founders
sources.originalTitle: How the best products build virality - Jason Calacanis (Angel Investor) | Startup Playbook Ep086
sources.summary: Jason explains why a product customers won't shut up about is the core growth engine, with marketing built on top of it. He also covers resourcefulness (RTFM, reaching 60-70% of any skill in weeks), selling early vs. taking secondary, and how new angels should deploy capital.

principles.text: Virality comes from a product customers can't stop talking about; build everything else around that.
principles.quote: the great products people can't wait to tell their friends about them so it all starts and ends with having a great product

principles.text: Use Net Promoter Score to test for virality; 9-10 scores signal advocates, 7-8 means you'd better have margins or monopolies.
principles.quote: the highest NPS score products are the ones that tend to be like these kind of products that people won't shut up about and they tell their friends about

principles.text: Study your few superfans to find your beachhead; early on, you need learning, not all the answers.
principles.quote: there's one or two people give us a nine or ten and we're studying them to figure out why they love it so much

principles.text: Profitable products can fund marketing; spend a small slice of profit on channels that may not provably work.
principles.quote: if you have a product that makes money and it's profitable and is great you can then spend money marketing it

principles.text: Marketing tactics decay (like infographics), but referral credits that make people feel good giving to friends last.
principles.quote: you have to understand that marketing channels burn out some of them are timeless some of them are have a half-life

principles.text: Basic competence in most skills takes weeks, so skip excuses and learn it yourself before outsourcing.
principles.quote: getting to the base level of skill as an audio engineer in other words understanding 60 or 70 percent of what the best audio engineer knows might take a hundred hours or 50 hours

sources.title: How to run a fundraising process: Jason Calacanis' investor funnel, pitch rules and follow-up playbook
sources.originalTitle: How to fundraise for your startup with VC Investor Jason Calacanis - LIVE!
sources.summary: Jason walks through items 81-90 of his startup checklist: pitch rules, building a curated list of about 150 investors, a short cold email with a Loom, nailing the first meeting, following up, backdoor-referencing investors, and SEC basics. He treats fundraising as a sales funnel, a numbers game where careful targeting and practice matter most.

principles.text: Curate a targeted list of ~150 investors, matched by firm, partner, and stage, then follow up two or three times.
principles.quote: you want to make a qualified list of targets we suggest 150 in the launch accelerator 150 people you email them you follow up with them two or three times

principles.text: Treat fundraising as a sales funnel: many targets narrow to only a few term sheets.
principles.quote: 150 targets really carefully selected to get but one two three four term sheets

principles.text: Make the cold email a short trailer, not the whole movie, with a quick demo or Loom to earn the meeting.
principles.quote: the trailer is not the entire movie the trailer is to get you to buy a ticket to the movie that's what this email is

principles.text: Every custom Loom is another rep; send many, learn from replies, and lead with your strongest asset.
principles.quote: every time you do one of these looms it's another rep it's you getting another swing at bat

principles.text: Practice on lower-priority investors first, then pitch your dream investors in weeks two or three.
principles.quote: start with the people you're not really concerned with winning them as a business and then you know the people you really want to win as investors and partners you can put in week two or three

principles.text: Answer investor questions concisely, like ping pong, and end every meeting with clear next steps.
principles.quote: you answer the question in as much time as they took to ask the question that's ideal

sources.title: Jason Calacanis on angel investing: small bets, performance over pitch, pre-emptive follow-ons
sources.originalTitle: Renowned Angel Investor, Jason Calacanis, Everything You Wanted to Know About Investing in Startups!
sources.summary: Jason explains how he approaches early-stage investing: make many small bets, judge founders on performance and customer love rather than charisma, and pre-emptively fund winners to raise ownership. He also argues family offices should avoid passed-over seed deals or hire a dedicated investor, and covers remote work economics and consumerized enterprise software.

principles.text: Judge founders on performance and customer love, not charisma; talk to their customers.
principles.quote: the number one thing you should do that you are not doing and you're not doing it let's be honest is to talk to customers of that product

principles.text: Entry valuation matters: lower prices let you take more shots on goal for the same capital and ownership.
principles.quote: be valuation conscious it actually matters your entry point

principles.text: Preemptively fund your own breakout winners to raise ownership instead of waiting for them to go to market.
principles.quote: we're preemptively funding our own winners then we move from you know a six percent ownership percentage to a twelve to twenty percent ownership percentage

principles.text: Early-stage investing is a power-law game: most bets go to zero, so make many bets and double down on the breakouts.
principles.quote: it takes to win is being able to have proprietary deal flow make a lot of bets identify which ones are breaking out and then 10x seeing down on them

principles.text: Have a real edge. Family offices seeing deals only after top VCs passed are getting the leftover hands; prefer later-stage companies with revenue or back proven fund managers.
principles.quote: make sure that this company has not been passed on by everybody else because then you're just trying to split the arrow

principles.text: Be relentlessly helpful to everyone; that is how access to great deals like Uber happened.
principles.quote: if you just are a person who's helpful and you're helpful to everybody you meet like many people in Silicon Valley where to me and I probably wasn't the easiest person to be helpful to at times you're gonna have a great career

sources.title: Jason Calacanis: How to angel invest by betting on founders, starting small, and being relentlessly helpful
sources.originalTitle: Ep. 241 - Jason Calacanis: How to Invest: The Guidebook from an Angel Investor Who Turned $100K i...
sources.summary: Jason Calacanis explains why he moved from "I only invest in myself" to angel investing, and walks through the playbook in his book Angel. Bet on the founder rather than the idea, start with small checks across many deals, and be psychotically helpful. Insist on monthly updates, and wait for a launched product before writing a check.

principles.text: Judge the founder, not the idea. Your own read on whether an idea works is limited, so double down on whether the person will succeed.
principles.quote: that really is the secret to being a great investor it's just removing your ability to know if this Pro idea is going to work and doubling down on your ability to know if the person is going to succeed

principles.text: Don't dwell on why a startup will fail. List the one or two reasons it could work and weigh those.
principles.quote: when I look at startups now I don't look at all the reasons of why it will fail I'll write them down sometimes uh and then I usually rip that page up and then I just list the one or two reasons of why it will work

principles.text: Start with many small checks but act as if each were big. You gain experience, a network and a reputation as helpful.
principles.quote: your first 10 investment should just be $1,000 into you know a random number of syndicates on Angel list or on seed invest but act as if you put in 10,000 or 100,000

principles.text: Wait until a startup has launched with a few real customers before investing. This filters out most failures.
principles.quote: if you invest in only launch products you've already eliminated 97% of the failures

principles.text: Get monthly updates from founders, including ones you passed on. Silence from a portfolio company usually signals failure.
principles.quote: if you're not getting those updates it's a 99% chance the company's going out of business

principles.text: Great founders have a maniacal, unnecessary attention to detail and craftsmanship, even if they are annoying to deal with.
principles.quote: that maniacal sense of detail that most people don't see that's what greatness is about is an intention to detail that's unnecessary right and the great Founders all have that

sources.title: Scaling your startup: sales hiring, compensation and process, from Jason Calacanis and Launch
sources.originalTitle: E933 Scaling Your Startup E5 "Sales" Hiring, compensation, prospecting, upselling, process, tools
sources.summary: Episode 5 of the Launch scaling series covers early sales. Founders run the first calls themselves, then hire a line account executive instead of a senior VP. Pay is roughly half base and half commission, paid when cash arrives. Other topics include outsourced SDRs, email sequences, BANT, and upselling.

principles.text: Founders should run the first sales calls themselves. A senior sales hire too early is set up to fail.
principles.quote: founders should be on those first sales calls they should do them themselves and it's very dangerous to hire somebody to senior

principles.text: Pair the founder with a line account executive and push for ~10 calls a week to learn objections and who buys.
principles.quote: just try to get ten phone calls under your belt every week and after five six seven you know weeks of that you're gonna be a really good shape to understanding what the objections are

principles.text: Treat first-year sales pay as half market research, half selling, since early deals are slow and inefficient.
principles.quote: I like to really think about their compensation half research and half actual selling

principles.text: Pay commission only when money comes in, so cancellations and refunds claw back and incentives stay honest.
principles.quote: I like people to get paid when the money comes in the door

principles.text: A rep who wants little variable pay is a bad sign. Aim for about 50/50 base and commission.
principles.quote: A red flag is somebody who wants less than a third of their compensation to come from commissions

principles.text: Great sales funds the fixes for everything else, so invest in the sales process early.
principles.quote: sell solves everything if you have great sales and you're selling boy every other problem seems to get solved because you have resources to go solve them

sources.title: VC Roundtable: second-time founders, founder-led sales and performance-based equity splits
sources.originalTitle: VC Roundtable: Recruiting Secrets, Second-Time Founders & Product-Market Fit Myths | E2143
sources.summary: Jason hosts Doug Leone and Gili Raanan on Wiz, hiring, product-market fit and VC cycles. Most of the substance comes from the guests; Jason mainly asks questions and adds a few reactions about repeat founders, founder-led selling and tying equity to performance.

principles.text: Back second- and third-time founders who still have the energy; you simply take their calls.
principles.quote: المؤسسون للمرة الثانية أو الثالثة، إذا كانوا لا يزالون يملكون الطاقة، نعم، عليك ببساطة أن ترد عليهم، أليس كذلك؟

principles.text: Founders make the best early salespeople because their honesty and belief in why they built it transfers to the buyer.
principles.quote: هناك صدقٌ وانتقالٌ للحماس عندما يشرح المؤسسون في الغرفة سبب ابتكارهم لشيء ما، لدرجة أنك تشعر بالحماس ينتقل عبر الطاولة

principles.text: Tie startup equity to performance and contribution, not an even split of what everyone feels they deserve.
principles.quote: لأن أساس تأسيس الشركة ، يا دوغ، هو الأداء، وماذا سنحصل عليه إذا حققنا أداءً جيدًا، بدلًا من أن يحصل كل فرد على ما يستحقه؟

sources.title: Angel: How Jason Calacanis invests in startups and bets on founders over ideas
sources.originalTitle: Angel: How to Invest in Technology Startups | Jason Calacanis | Talks at Google
sources.summary: Jason Calacanis explains his angel investing approach from his book "Angel": bet on founders rather than ideas, invest in the "Goldilocks zone" before Series A, and build networks through syndicates and monthly updates. He also shares advice for founders on engagement over investor-hacking and where false-start technologies may now work.

principles.text: Bet on the founder, not the idea: passion, skill, and not giving up matter more than whether the idea seems good.
principles.quote: I don't need to know if your idea is going to succeed. I just need to know if you're going to succeed.

principles.text: Invest in the Goldilocks zone: after the product launches but before VCs arrive with sharp elbows.
principles.quote: pre-series A, pre-venture capitalists wanted to join the board, but post the product being launched into the market

principles.text: Ask what could go right, not what could go wrong; long lists of failure reasons are cheap and the success list is short.
principles.quote: you have to ask yourself, not what could go wrong, but what could go right.

principles.text: Founders should spend energy on customer engagement, not hacking investors; then tell that story in meetings.
principles.quote: why not spend those 90 cycles trying to triple the engagement of your current customer base

principles.text: Send monthly updates with key metrics to build trust and credibility; investors may watch for three months before investing.
principles.quote: put me on your monthly update for three months. I'll read your monthly updates for three months before I invest

principles.text: Build an investor network via syndicates, small real-money bets, and mail-merging co-investors for deal flow.
principles.quote: email your co-investor and say, we're co-investors in this. That makes you like family members.

sources.title: Venture roundtable: post-ZIRP survival, secondaries, and why AI-first teams beat adding headcount
sources.originalTitle: The End of the ZIRP Era, and why recruiting is SO PAINFUL | E2164
sources.summary: Jason hosts a VC roundtable on secondaries, backlogged unicorns, and the shift from growth-at-all-costs to profitability. His own contributions: scaling a portfolio via buckets and pods, selling some shares along the way, and a closing point that automating a job function beats the pain of recruiting.

principles.text: Smart founders solve problems with automation instead of adding headcount; recruiting is slow and often wrong.
principles.quote: Smart founders are starting to realize I don't need to solve every problem by adding a body that once you realize the best way to solve a problem is automation, not recruiting people. Recruiting people is painful.

sources.title: How Jason Calacanis turned a conference into the Launch Fund and syndicate
sources.originalTitle: How Jason Calacanis turned a conference into a VC fund: Angel S6 E7 | E1393
sources.summary: Jason is interviewed about raising Launch Fund One from his conference, his friends and a big list. He covers pairing the fund with an AngelList syndicate, charging fees, ownership concentration and scaling a team. His mistakes and fixes are as useful as the wins.

principles.text: Say yes to opportunities and take leaps of faith; a few payoffs outweigh the many that go nowhere.
principles.quote: the times in my life where i just said yes to something and took that leap of faith you know good things happened and there's a long list of things i said yes to like probably three or four a year that resulted in nothing

principles.text: Pair a fund with a syndicate: the fund gets every deal first, and the syndicate multiplies capital and investor advocates.
principles.quote: the first rule of the road is the fund gets a hundred percent of deals so there's no syndication of a deal that the fund's not in period full stop

principles.text: Syndicate investors act as advocates: a founder gets a crowd who reply to asks for intros, hires and help.
principles.quote: they're voting with their dollars to support you so when you send them an update and you're like i need a cfo or i need an introduction to disney or does anybody have an experience with a patent attorney that's affordable

principles.text: Charge fees that fund real support staff; waiving management fees was a mistake and hurt the fund and its LPs.
principles.quote: there's nobody who's investing in a venture fund who's not used to paying two and a half percent in fees

principles.text: Double down on winners and aim for 5 to 15 percent ownership with a board seat, rather than 50 basis points.
principles.quote: you have to double down on your winners so the big criticism i got when i started talking to the big lps the top funds in the world was oh wow it's great that you found these companies but you're an idiot for not continuing to invest in them

principles.text: Avoid cynical partners, and delegate the work you hate or are weak at to empower your team.
principles.quote: picking partners if you pick one who's really cynical and dark things tend to trend to a dark place

sources.title: Jason Calacanis on disrupting conferences, product focus, and when to take the exit
sources.originalTitle: From The Vault Jason Calacanis - Startup Grind
sources.summary: A 2011 Startup Grind fireside where Jason explains how he undercut pay-to-pitch conferences, why resilience and product focus matter most, and when to ignore advice. He also argues founders should take big exit offers and ignore the press, drawing on his own $20M mistake.

principles.text: Resilience and resourcefulness are the top entrepreneur traits, and he hires on them.
principles.quote: Perseverance, resilience, and resourcefulness are the most important traits of an entrepreneur.

principles.text: Change the rules when you can't win the game as it stands; fight the fight you can win.
principles.quote: fight the fight you can win and if you can't win, just change the rules of the game.

principles.text: Pick ideas most people don't yet get. If everyone likes it, it's already tried or too small.
principles.quote: if the majority of people understand the idea and think it’s a good idea I have absolutely no interest in doing it because it means by default that everyone has that idea

principles.text: Success comes from focusing on the product; test it by asking whether people get repeated value.
principles.quote: At the end of the day it’s all about product. All of my success in life has come when I've focused on the product and made something that people connected with

principles.text: To beat an incumbent in search or similar categories, you must be 2-3x better, not 10-20% better.
principles.quote: you have to make something 2-3 times better, I'm convinced, in order for people to switch. The mental cost of switch is high, people think it’s low.

principles.text: Take a disproportionate exit offer; passing on big money often means ending with nothing.
principles.quote: If they offer you $100 million, take the money for God's sake!

sources.title: OpenClaw & the Great Hiring Hiatus: why Jason Calacanis paused hiring for AI agents
sources.originalTitle: OpenClaw & The Great Hiring Hiatus - by jason@calacanis.com
sources.summary: Jason Calacanis says his 20-person firm moved about 20% of its tasks to OpenClaw agents ("replicants") in 20 days and expects not to hire another human for a year or two. He argues agents that act, not just advise, and improve through skills and memory are cheaper and faster than adding headcount.

principles.text: Agents that execute tasks beat LLMs that only research and summarize.
principles.quote: once you authenticate it with your online services, it actually “does things” as opposed to “tells you things.”

principles.text: Using an executing agent means accepting responsibility for its mistakes.
principles.quote: When you install OpenClaw, you assume that responsibility.

principles.text: Offload repetitive work to agents in small steps and measure how much you have moved.
principles.quote: we’ve offloaded about 20% of our tasks to OpenClaw in 20 days, and it’s getting better every day because of “skills” and memory.

principles.text: Have agents research best practices on a schedule and fold them into their own skills so they keep improving.
principles.quote: our Producer Replicant conducts a deep research project every Saturday at noon, finding people discussing how to make better thumbnails

principles.text: Setting up agents is faster and cheaper than hiring, so pause human hiring and treat a new hire as a luxury.
principles.quote: Adding a human to our team will be a luxury spend for now.

principles.text: Automating chores frees people for higher-value human work, which helps team buy-in.
principles.quote: Every time we tell a replicant to take over repetitive chores, we get to spend more time with other humans

sources.title: How Jason Calacanis invests: process, Goldilocks window, and buying in down markets
sources.originalTitle: Smart Humans Jason Calacanis Transcript - Vincent
sources.summary: Jason Calacanis explains his angel investing playbook: invest in a Goldilocks stage window, build ownership via pro rata and super pro rata, and sell some on the way up. He argues down markets are the best time to invest and hire, and that startups come down to team, product velocity and customers.

principles.text: Down markets are the best time to invest: less competition, more time for diligence, and only committed people remain.
principles.quote: fortunes are made in the down market, they're collected in the up market. So the best time to be investing is in a down market.

principles.text: Invest in a Goldilocks window: product launched, early revenue, reasonable valuation multiple, room to buy about 5%.
principles.quote: Okay, you've got your product launched, you're at 250k in revenue, 20k a month, 30k a month, last month, I times it by 12, we come to a reasonable valuation multiple on that. And we get to buy 5%.

principles.text: Build ownership by milestones: start small, then add at pro rata or super pro rata as the company breaks out, aiming for about 15%.
principles.quote: you don't need to buy all the shares in the seed round. You just need to be a great partner to the founder.

principles.text: Take some money off the table on the way up to lock in a win and gain downside protection.
principles.quote: it really is important to have some downside production and lock in a win. And a lot of people don't do that.

principles.text: Companies are about team, product and customers. Watch product velocity, release cadence and growth signals, not distractions like TAM or competitors.
principles.quote: Companies are really about three things, the team that builds a product and the customers who consume that product.

principles.text: Process is what you control. Write down why you said yes or no, review decisions, and keep refining the process obsessively.
principles.quote: if you want to get good at something, you better be a fucking maniac, because you're competing against people who are fucking maniacs like me.

sources.title: Angel investing for small startups: add a zero, take more risk, own your audience
sources.originalTitle: How to find an angel investor for small startups w/ Jason Calacanis
sources.summary: Jason explains how profitable "dude businesses" doing about $1M a year can raise angel money to scale, what angels expect, and why founders should take more risk and run cheap experiments. He also covers why he moved Inside.com from apps to email and why podcast networks struggle.

principles.text: Own a direct relationship with your audience; use platforms only for customers, and collect emails everywhere.
principles.quote: I think use any of these other platforms if it gets you customers, but own a direct deep relationship.

principles.text: Taking angel money is a starter pistol: investors expect a return, so deploy it intelligently on growth.
principles.quote: in fact that’s the starter pistol as we talked about earlier. That just means okay, now you’ve deployed it, and those people want you to return.

principles.text: Most founders under-risk. A failed startup makes you more credible, not dead, so take more risk.
principles.quote: if you’re climbing the startup mountain and you fall, it gives you more credibility, and you just get to start over at the bottom of the mountain again.

principles.text: Treat experiments as probes: find the cheapest, quickest way to get a signal, then follow revenue, engagement and open rates.
principles.quote: what’s the least costly and quickest way to get the signal to understand if this is gonna work or not? That’s your goal.

principles.text: Pitch angels in a few sentences: what you do, a revenue chart, and a demo link. Skip the life story.
principles.quote: “I have a business called blank. We make money by doing blank for blank. Here’s a revenue chart, quarterly, monthly, week, whatever, and here’s a link to our product demo.”

principles.text: Send investors a monthly update with metrics. The discipline of writing it plus a clear plan makes companies more successful.
principles.quote: If you have a plan to be successful and you execute the plan, you will be more successful.

sources.title: Jason Calacanis's VC training program and LAUNCH Festival: hiring and founder-access playbook
sources.originalTitle: Jason Calacanis on Startups | jason@calacanis.com | Substack
sources.summary: A Substack index page of Jason Calacanis's recent posts. The substantive content is his pitch for a zero-tuition VC training program (hiring for work ethic over pedigree) and his rationale for reviving LAUNCH Festival to give founders affordable access. The rest is event and podcast promotion.

principles.text: Hire for learning speed, executive function, focus and curiosity rather than fancy degrees.
principles.quote: Be a learning machine  2. Have high executive function  3. Be extremely focused and curious  4. Be able to work 12 hours a day for our founders

principles.text: Credentials matter little; hunger counts. Favor people with a chip on their shoulder.
principles.quote: we don't care about how fancy your degree is, we love folks from UT Austin, and we love folks with a chip on their shoulders.

principles.text: Be highly selective and move people up in stages, earning each promotion.
principles.quote: We accept < 1% of applicants

principles.text: You can beat most competitors simply by outworking them, since most are lazy.
principles.quote: 80% of VCs are lazy AF, and you can beat them by simply showing up for work and doing 10-12 hours a day and checking your email on the weekends.

principles.text: Build the thing you couldn't afford when you were coming up, so more people can get access.
principles.quote: I couldn’t afford that, and I said that if I ever made it, I would create an event just for founders.

principles.text: Podcasts compound learning and relationships: use them to learn, network and share.
principles.quote: Podcasts are my way of committing to lifelong learning, networking with driven people, and sharing with like-minded folks.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Calacanis answers community questions on fundraising mechanics, how startup costs collapsed, and differentiating from frontier AI labs. Treat fundraising as a full-time sales funnel, judge investors by behavior rather than words, and build community, multiplayer and human services around what LLMs won't ship.

chunks.heading: Fundraising: why "too early" really means "wrong investor for your stage"
chunks.text:
- Jason says to judge an investor by behavior, not words: "the best way to judge a person is to look at their previous behavior."
- Check what stage they have actually invested in. A family office that writes $30M private-equity checks for friends' deals will not write a $125K-$250K seed check, however nice the meeting felt.
- Investors say nice things in social settings to everyone, so he tells founders to "divorce the nice things they're saying from the reality of what they do."
- If an investor says you're "too early," go to the programs built for that stage first: Y Combinator, Techstars, Antler, a16z, Pear (summer program), Sequoia Arc, and his own Launch Accelerator.
- Take the $25K, $125K or $250K check there, get your first five customers, then return to the bigger investors.
- His own programs target year zero: Founder University runs six cohorts a year across three geographies (Riyadh, Tokyo, US), wants two or three founders, and does not require incorporation or customers.
- The accelerator investment wants you incorporated.

chunks.heading: The 2026 seed funnel: contact 150 funds to get two term sheets
chunks.text:
- His numbers for a seed round today: contact 150 seed funds, get about 50 meetings, convert about 15 (10% of the list) into second meetings, and get two term sheets.
- Judge only second meetings. People are not obligated to take one, so a second meeting is a real signal.
- Stories of founders who "instantly get funded" without trying are memorable because they are not the norm.
- Treat it as a sales funnel and qualify each investor:
  - Do they invest at your stage?
  - Are they actively investing, or in maintenance mode between funds?
  - What check size do they write?
  - Do they lead or follow?
  - Do they take cold email, or only intros?
- Fundraising is a full-time job. With three co-founders, one handles product, one sales, and one corporate development, which "is another fancy way of saying raising money."
- Build deep relationships with investors over time.
- Same lesson as job hunting or content creation: you fill out 100 applications for one job.

chunks.heading: Finding the investors who fit your company
chunks.text:
- Investors differ in thesis and process. Jason knows a True Ventures investor in his 60s who only takes meetings via another VC or a portfolio founder.
- Jason's Launch (launch.co/apply) meets about 10% of applicants. Some weeks bring 200 to 500 applications, and they meet about 25 a week (it used to be 140, which was too many).
- Per year that is 3,000-5,000 meetings and about 100 investments, from 10,000-20,000 applications.
- Firms have sector preferences. They don't do biotech, and they have been looking at military tech.
- Research method: use a Crunchbase account, follow firms on social media, and build a list of about 150 firms that invest at your stage in similar companies.
- Pitch the pattern match. Example: he did Thumbtack (marketplace) and Robinhood and Wealthfront (fintech), so a fintech marketplace pitch fits him.
- If an investor only takes intros, meet their founders first. To reach 10 target firms, email about 50 founders, get about 20 meetings, and hope to reach 3-4 firms through them.
- Launch has a tool called Whisper Network where founders search and request introductions. Even with it, "you're hunting, you're pecking."
- Creative visibility works too. One founder put "AI B2B startup raising pre-seed, product is live, come say hi" on his laptop in a San Francisco cafe, and several investors came up to him.
- Jason's view is that the Bay Area's culture of helping people without expecting short-term returns is why being physically there matters.

chunks.heading: How the cost of starting a company collapsed, and what it changes for investors
chunks.text:
- The biggest shift versus 10 years ago is the capital and time needed to reach product-market fit.
- Web 1.0 era (1990s):
  - A seed round was about $3M, with 20-30 people.
  - Reaching market took about 12 months.
  - Spending went on a PR firm (about $10K/month for 18 months, roughly $180K), an office at about $25K/month, a $250K letter of credit, about $100K of legal, and HR, accounting and legal hires (about $250K).
  - He totals this at roughly $3M before launch.
- Cloud era: about $300K, three people eating ramen at home, a startup standing up in under 6 months.
- Today: about $30K for servers, often with free credits. Founders vibe-code a product, get a first customer, and then apply to YC, Techstars, Antler or Launch Accelerator.
- A typical applicant now says they "vibe coded a product, got to 100K in revenue" and then applied.
- Idea to first customer (a light form of product-market fit) is now weeks or a weekend.
- His example is the bounties program (twistartups.com bounties): the real-time fact-checker bounty drew 15 submissions, about three really good ones, in under 30 days. A second $5,000 bounty was for "annotated."
- He wants to hire winning bounty founders and incubate the product as a real startup.

chunks.heading: Building a moat against OpenAI, Anthropic and other frontier labs
chunks.text:
- The big LLM interface will always leave out features, because of "clutter and confusion."
- His example is Rome, a travel startup that built an interface on top of a model. It returned money to investors after ChatGPT absorbed the basic function, but its approach points to the real moat.
- Build features and community around the model output that the labs won't:
  - Multiplayer mode: a group researching a Tokyo trip together, seeing each other's picks, voting, and adding to a shared agenda.
  - A virtual travel agency: an AI-assisted human planner paid by the hour.
  - Ground support: matching travelers with a local guide, such as a food guide who skips the tourist-trap lines.
- His summary: they "are just going to give you your basic output," so own the community, marketplace and human service layered on top.
- His example of AI plus a human service layer: AI planning that ends in someone on the ground who gets you in line, translates, and arranges a back-kitchen ramen visit.
- Tax is another vertical he names where this pattern applies.

chunks.heading: Hardware is back as a moat
chunks.text:
- Investors flipped on hardware: it used to be "hardware is hard, I don't want any part of it," and now it is "one of the only moats left."
- Hardware gives lock-in and raises the fidelity and usefulness of the product. His examples: Plaud, and Whoop.
- His own hardware investments: Terra Cafe and Cafe X (both still going; he says Cafe X is doing well), plus a Butterfly (a Dropcam/Ring competitor) and an early smoke detector that failed. Most fail and a few succeed.
- For a bootstrapped hardware founder nearing profitability, he says to raise money from investors who are comfortable with the capital needs.
- Work backward from the many existing hardware investors.
- Kickstarter and viral ads are still viable for the first thousand customers paying far above eventual retail, since early adopters "just want to be the first to have it."

chunks.heading: Robotics business model idea: price per hour, lease to consumers
chunks.text:
- Sell robots like labor: if Amazon pays about $27/hour (about $35 fully loaded with insurance and workers' comp) to sort packages, a robot maker like Optimus or Figure could offer a robot at about $4/hour with on-site maintenance.
- At about 8,000 hours a year, that is roughly $32K a year per robot.
- His guess is that commoditized robots will ultimately cost "a dollar or $2 an hour."
- For consumers, he would abstract it like a car lease: about $299/month for 500 hours, with overage at a dollar an hour.
- He likens security robots to guards who earn about $20/hour: the robot never sleeps and records 360 degrees.

chunks.heading: Training and credentialing: associate program and a possible Founder University degree
chunks.text:
- His firm is hiring six associates-in-training in June for the venture side: researcher, then analyst, then associate, over about three years, with pay in the $60K-$90K range.
- He hires about two to three times as many as needed because one or two will opt out or be let go, and about one-third become stars.
- His framing: "instead of paying for a degree in venture capital, we pay you."
- Plan: two professional-training sessions a week (Monday morning, Friday end of week) with the rest of the week spent in a business unit. His goal is to make it good enough to charge about $50,000 for a two-year version.
- Benchmark: Kauffman Fellows charges about $80,000 for two years, which he calls overpriced and elitist; he thinks he could run a better one with 10 people at $50K each ($500K) and two full-time staff.
- He believes his version would be better because fellows go to Saudi Arabia and Tokyo and interview companies.
- Legal constraint: he can give a certificate or diploma but not a degree in the US without a partner university, though UK universities may allow a UK-accredited degree.
- Ideas: a two-year Founder University that combines the founder and venture tracks (major one, minor the other).
- He would add media skills (newsletter, social, podcast), because many brilliant founders and investors are "dead air" on a podcast.

chunks.heading: Personal wealth and who Jason criticizes
chunks.text:
- He puts "F-you money" at exactly $10M: at 5% that is $500K a year, or $400-500K after tax, enough to "just exist."
- His criticism is of behavior, not personal feuds. On Mark Zuckerberg, he says every time he had a chance to do the right thing, he "picked his own self-interest."
- His examples are teenage girls and Instagram, user privacy, and how partners and founders were treated in Meta's partner program.
- He also cites blatantly copying others' ideas, and optimizing platforms to keep people online.
- He says it is not personal; he hasn't spoken with Zuckerberg in person in a decade.
- On Sam Altman, he says he does not like what he did to Elon Musk, whom he calls a friend.
- He notes both men are among the most successful in business history and that self-interested, burn-bridges decisions can be "a quick path to extraordinary success."
- On the media, he distrusts press pieces and viral clips. He says that when he reports news, a low-double-digit percentage of the time it is not exactly accurate, so he adds "allegedly" and disclaimers, and thinks before reacting.
- He declined a New Yorker request to comment on Altman, with no business interest and a policy of not talking to the press.
- He also says he regrets how harshly he reacted to a military-tech founder who was fired, calling it kicking a man when he was down.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason tells how a Brooklyn kid with no money built Silicon Alley Reporter from a photocopied zine, lost it in the dotcom bust, then rebuilt with Weblogs Inc and sold to AOL for $30M. He also covers moderating All-In, loyalty in friendships, and defining success as enthusiasm rather than net worth.

chunks.heading: Starting a business with no money, and the "ask" that unlocks it
chunks.text:
- Jason grew up in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn. His dad's bar was padlocked by the feds and the tax authority in 1988 when Jason was 18. He calls it one of the great traumas of his life.
- He went to college at night over five years, paying his own way by fixing laser printers and building local networks before the internet.
- He started Silicon Alley Reporter as a photocopied zine. He had no money to print it, and the overnight manager at the print shop let him pay $100 on a $1,750 bill.
- Jason's takeaway: "when I ask people things that many times people will do what I ask them to do." He learned early that you can ask for outrageous things and sometimes get them.
- He photocopied about 1,000 copies of the zine, then handed 200 out at an internet party at Roseland. By the end of the night, everyone at the party was reading it.
- The next morning he made postcards offering a subscription: 10 issues for $90. He had seen Esther Dyson charge $1,000 for her newsletter, so he picked a price far below hers.
- Within two or three months, subscription envelopes of $90 each were piling up at his office share. He quit his jobs.
- He frames the experience as a sliding-door moment: a nobody became important in about 60 days.

chunks.heading: Get to a new medium first
chunks.text:
- Jason says he has always been fascinated by new mediums: "if you get to a medium first you can exploit it." That covers zines, the early web, blogging and podcasting.
- His reasoning: the people who tinker with a platform early get disproportionate credit and attention. The platform's value then rises around them, like buying a loft in an unfashionable neighborhood before everyone else arrives.
- Silicon Alley Reporter worked because he covered the internet when browsers couldn't show graphics. He says the timing "was so insane."
- When the dot-com bust hit, he tinkered. He called people to learn what was happening and watched who was building things: Flickr, Delicious, Wi-Fi, early blogs.
- He wanted a read on the landscape after the crash, because everyone had quit and gone to find jobs.

chunks.heading: Rage after the bust, and Weblogs Inc.
chunks.text:
- By 1999 the magazine ran about 300 pages, with almost 100 people working for him. He was making about $7-8 million a year from the magazine and a couple of million from events, and he turned down a $20 million offer because the business was his identity.
- The bust wiped out the business. He sold the remains to Dow Jones with a roughly $500-600K employment contract. Dow Jones then fired him and handed him a check for $500,000.
- He says the emotion in that moment was a "hulk-like rage." He felt he had to prove it wasn't a fluke, got an office the next day, and started whiteboarding ideas.
- His early ideas included Mercury Club, a $100-a-month delivery service for rich New Yorkers using Vespas and an 800 number.
- His next business came from two observations. An employee, Rafat Ali, was moonlighting on a blog (paidContent.org), and his event producer, Shani, was making far more from a blog than he had paid her.
- He concluded blogs were "faster, better, cheaper," and decided to build business blogs at scale.
- Weblogs Inc. details:
  - Co-founded with Brian Alvey (technology).
  - 87 blogs in 18 months, about 450 bloggers, 200 of them active.
  - Bloggers were paid per post: $2-3 at first, then $5, then $10, and the economics were modeled in a spreadsheet.
  - Peter Rojas was the missing piece; he insisted on distinct, branded blog names.
  - Mark Cuban invested $300,000 for about 20%, and Jason says he gave Cuban $6 million back.
  - AOL bought the company for $30 million.
- His conclusion: "once you're lucky twice you're good." The sale proved the first success wasn't a fluke.

chunks.heading: Events and community as a business
chunks.text:
- Jason says he loves hosting events because "if you host the party those people get to meet new people create some relationship or moment that then changes their life forever."
- His event "Open the Kimono" (OTK) is still remembered by attendees as a peak experience years later. It included a wine-making competition, and the winning wine was bottled for attendees.
- He says events are far more tiring than podcasting for introverts, and that he is highly extroverted (86 and 100 on two tests).
- For a hosted event, he suggests a format where the host interviews someone on stage, recovers backstage, and then takes audience questions.
- He frames the purpose as manifesting a community in a physical space and creating shared memories.

chunks.heading: All-In: how a podcast with partners works
chunks.text:
- All-In started as a spinoff of poker games during Covid. The four hosts are Jason, Chamath Palihapitiya, David Sacks and David Friedberg.
- He modeled the format on the McLaughlin Group: opinionated, interrupting, full-contact discussion.
- Chamath proposed it first as a two-person show, and Jason suggested the name "All In" because of poker.
- Jason acts as the producer and moderator. His routine:
  - A shared Google Doc "docket" each week, built with his producer Nick, filled with links and bullet points. The group chats on Signal.
  - He feeds each host topics suited to them: science for Friedberg, politics and law for Sacks, markets and startups for Chamath.
  - He compares his role to a point guard: set up each partner to score.
- His moderation techniques:
  - Give private notes after episodes. He tells a partner, for example, that they made four strong points and should make one or two, then ask what another host thinks.
  - Use a circling finger to signal "wrap it up."
  - Say "okay" to break in on monologues, a habit he picked up from Sam Harris.
  - Drop a joke when a debate overheats; he cites Bill Maher doing this well.
  - Explain that when he challenges a partner, he's helping clarify their position rather than disagreeing.
- He says the show works because viewers like seeing friendship and unguarded conversation.

chunks.heading: All-In: conflict, ads and the Venture fund
chunks.text:
- Jason says all four hosts were opinionated people who'd never had a boss, so the show repeatedly came close to breaking up over the event, spinoffs and advertising.
- The group chose to stay together because the audience loved the show.
- His partners refuse to run ads. Jason says that leaves roughly $25 million in advertising on the table (about $6-7 million a year, and he'd get a quarter).
- Instead he used the show's reach to raise his next venture fund:
  - He used a 506(c) designation, which lets a fund solicit publicly.
  - He mentioned on the podcast that he was raising a fund and asked people to email him.
  - About a thousand emails came in, and five webinars produced $44 million in commitments. His prior fund was also $44 million.
  - He describes the return as having to deploy the money and earn about 25% of the profit, and notes every LP meeting begins with a request for a selfie.
- His rule for the show: the partners should root for each other, and a hard debate (he cites Ukraine arguments with Sacks) shouldn't damage the relationship.

chunks.heading: Money, success and friendship
chunks.text:
- Jason says that past a certain point, wealth stops changing daily life. He points to a night with billionaire friends: the same restaurant, the same ski trips.
- His real scoreboard: "did you wake up and couldn't wait to get out of bed."
- He says he drives a Model Y rather than the Plaid and prefers a New York strip to wagyu.
- He says people treated him very differently after he became a millionaire: "like all of a sudden I got like 30 more IQ points and I was two feet taller."
- He argues for loyalty. His dad taught him and his brothers to always have each other's back.
- He says his two best life moves are "have great friends and build cool stuff."
- On friendships, he says as you become more successful your world gets smaller, and a trusted inner circle matters most.
- He describes a friend's loss, and the deaths of two poker friends, as the point where he started to reassess what matters.
- He is writing a book about money and wealth. His theme is what happens when you "catch the car."
- He advises:
  - Take chances: "what if it actually works out."
  - Be kind, and have productive disagreements with a big open heart.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A casual conversation where Jason describes how he built All-In's audience and character arcs, raised his fund publicly, and screens startups for world-class design and product velocity. He also shares how a pricing nudge helped Calm's early business model and why he prefers meritocratic, hands-on early-stage investing.

chunks.heading: Jason's path: from Brooklyn printer repair to media, then angel investing
chunks.text:
- Jason's dad lost his bar to the feds over unpaid taxes after the 1987 crash, about six weeks before Jason started college. He told Jason to take care of his mom and said he might go to jail.
- Jason worked days fixing laser printers and took 16 credits a semester at Brooklyn College, six to nine PM four nights a week. He called himself an underperformer in academics.
- His early hustles were cracking and copying software to sell for $10, and selling hot VHS tapes.
- He published zines, starting with Cyber Surfer, about dial-up services and CD-ROMs.
- He then built Silicon Alley Reporter and Digital Coast Reporter in LA: two magazines, two conferences and two email newsletters.
- He grew that business to $10 million in revenue "off my credit cards" with 75 to 100 staff at age 27. He taught himself ad sales and magazine operations.
- Fred Wilson and Jerry Colonna at Flatiron paid him $1,000 plus sushi to read business plans. He wrote about GeoCities and told them to invest. Flatiron made a fortune on it, and he chose to keep the magazine over a VC career.
- Weblogs Inc was sold to AOL for $30 million. Mark Cuban put in $300K for roughly 10%.
- When the money landed, Jason cried. He said his family would never have to worry about money again, because he had spent his life worried about it after his dad lost the business.

chunks.heading: How All In started and why it works
chunks.text:
**Origin**
- Chamath and Jason knew each other from the AOL era. Jason kept inviting Chamath onto his podcast. Chamath said yes only after he left Facebook.
- They played cards together, traded notes, and became close. Chamath later called after an interview and asked to do a podcast with just the two of them.
- Jason suggested the name "All In", a poker name, and they added Sacks and Friedberg. They had a poker game that had been referenced on air for years.
