- Jason expected it to last 10 to 20 episodes. The pandemic made people want information and perspective, and it took off.

**His read on why it works**
- Real friendship and rapport around a poker table, and the willingness to disagree on air.
- Sacks and Jason fight on the show, and Jason says the fights are real and unscripted. He says the world wants the hosts to be enemies, and he likes the "best of enemies" dynamic of Gore Vidal and William F. Buckley.
- Jason says he deliberately cast characters. He called Friedberg the "Sultan of Science" and gave Sacks his red meat in politics. He plays the point guard who shapes the conversation.
- He studied the McLaughlin Group to learn moderation and interjection. He later realized Sacks is a relentless debater, so he now works to keep it a conversation rather than a debate.
- He plays audience proxy: "Can you unpack that?" He asks what an acronym means on behalf of listeners, even when he knows it.
- Listeners get an information edge from people who see 20 or more founder meetings a week, plus the "billionaire porn" appeal and likeable characters.

**Format craft**
- He wants podcasts that are "candy and vegetables" at once: personality and entertainment alongside real depth.
- Guests need to be intelligible. He lets them go deep but makes sure they "take the stairs" rather than jump straight into brain surgery.
- He says Howard Stern is the playbook: build characters, brand them, and do live events. Jason says he is starting a reality show in the Gordon Ramsay vein, helping founders.
- He says All In deliberately did not monetize. His partners agreed to keep the show pure rather than sell it to a network, though the second-order value of deals and brand is huge.
- The All In Summit made a small profit on a couple million dollars and was the number one tech event of the year, by his account. He plans to run it again, either as All In or under a new brand if the others vote no.

chunks.heading: Working hours, team, and how he runs the Angel business
chunks.text:
- Jason says he works harder now than ever, and with more energy than in his 20s. He says he finds meaning in the work after the death of his friend Tony Shea.
- He says he gets "great joy" from the daily show and from entertaining an audience, and he treats it like going to the gym.
- He dislikes legal, HR, accounting, operations and tax work. He does not enjoy negotiating term sheets either.
- To handle that, he brought in Mike Savino, his first boss from his 20s, as president to run the company. Jason does the podcast, founder meetings and LP fundraising.
- The team is about 22 people, 10 on media and 12 on investments. The investment team does about 60 first meetings a week, heading toward 100 total meetings a week across 10 to 12 people.
- He moved investment team meetings to two sessions a week, Tuesday and Thursday 2 to 4 PM, rather than one long Monday meeting.
- He tells every hire he works 60 to 70 hours a week and says "keep up". He looks for a solid 50 to 60 hours from them.
- Most staff stay two to four years and then leave to start their own funds. Jason is fine with that.
- He says the Angel Syndicate is the largest in the world. He has deployed about $185 million as an angel and now deploys about $50 million a year. The syndicate has roughly 11,000 angels.
- He says he does not aspire to be a billionaire. If he did, he says he would raise a late-stage fund. What he wants is to be happy and to do what he loves each day:
  - the podcast
  - skiing
  - time with his kids
  - meeting early founders
- His investing ambition is to be on the "Mount Rushmore" of angels and to be in the conversation among all investors.

chunks.heading: Raising Fund IV in public (Rule 506(c)) and democratizing venture
chunks.text:
- Jason's funds grew quickly:
  - Fund I was $10 million, raised from friends including Bill Gurley, Dave Goldberg, Tony Shea, Sacks and Chamath. It took about five years to deploy.
  - Fund II was $11 million and took about two years to deploy.
  - Fund III was $44 million and took about two and a half years to deploy.
- Raising time dropped each time. Fund I took six months to a year, Fund II three to six months, and Fund III three months. He expects Fund IV to raise in the first ten days what earlier funds took months to raise.
- For Fund IV he used a 506(c). That lets him publicly say he is raising, and he runs webinars for prospective LPs. He tweeted about it and about 1,000 people signed up.
- The limits he cites are 250 accredited investors for up to $10 million, and 2,000 for larger sizes, which are QPs. He cites a $5 million investable-assets test for QPs.
- He believes accreditation will eventually become a test you can pass by taking a course, rather than purely an income or net worth test.
- He says the hardest part of raising was the grind. He cites Magna VC (see Jason's interview with him), who took "50 meetings a week" to build a fund, and he thinks anyone willing to do that can do it.
- His thesis is: "now is the time to democratize venture capital." Accredited investors who have never been in a venture fund should at least consider the asset class. He warns that it is high risk and high reward, and he says he is in about 20 venture funds himself.
- The institutional view he reports is that big endowments say they rarely add funds and that a solo GP is a hard sell. One of them told him to put one more fund on the board and come back. He decided to see which QPs come out of the woodwork rather than chase institutions.
- Alternatives he considered:
  - invest only his own money in each deal and Syndicate it, with deal-by-deal carry and no LPs, audits or admin
  - raise a fund and be accountable to LPs
- He chose a fund because of what he finds meaningful. He especially wants an endowment like Memorial Sloan Kettering or a cancer foundation, since both his parents are cancer survivors.
- He says Sequoia's annual founder dinner showed what foundations did with the returns, which made the work feel more serious.

chunks.heading: Angel investing: Uber, Calm, and his pattern-matching checklist
chunks.text:
**Early angel path**
- He became a Sequoia scout and learned about Syndicates and SPVs from Naval Ravikant at AngelList.
- His first Syndicate deal was Calm.
- He was an early angel in Uber, with Travis Kalanick at Dogpatch Labs. He had worked with Dogpatch Labs through Open Angel Forum.

**Calm**
- He invested $378K for about 6% at a $4 million valuation, before the company raised again at a roughly $250 million valuation. That meant no dilution in between.
- He says Alex and Michael later told him they were about to shut down. They had pitched about 40 investors who all said no. They debated whether to burn his money, and took it because he insisted.
- Pricing advice he gave them: they planned to sell the app at $10 a year. He asked what a meditation class costs; he says it was a $20 suggested donation per class. He asked how often someone should practice, and the answer was daily or weekly. He said that implied around $80 a month, and asked about $10 a month. They went with a monthly price around that idea (he recalls it landing at about $60 a year) and he says it became "a money printing machine."
- He tells the story as proof that pricing and product-market fit are often a few questions apart.

**His investing checklist (teaching founders and his team)**
- He is training his team to score companies against "nine" criteria and an "anti-list" of things that kill companies. He gave only two:
  - World-class design. Meaning the best, or one of the top 10, in the category. He cites Calm vs. Headspace and Robinhood vs. E-Trade. A website-builder template with stock photos does not count as world class; that is "serviceable."
  - Product velocity. Ask what changed since a June meeting by July. He looks for a changelog or roadmap, and cites Superhuman's constant shipping. He says a founder like Travis would take a call and walk you through what they are debating that Sunday.
- He says his team must tell him how many of the criteria a company hits, and how many red flags it has.
- He is trying to avoid meetings with companies he will not invest in. He basically does not take a pitch unless he intends to invest, so his team front-loads the work.
- He says he has never made a pre-product-market-fit investment now worth over a billion except Calm.
- He runs Founder University: a 12-week course where founders pay $700 and get it back if they finish. About 90 percent finish, roughly 200 people have gone through, and he invests $25K in some of them. He uses it to filter talkers from walkers.
- He rejects the idea that you must have gone to Stanford. He says maybe five percent of his founders did. He says nobody cares where you went to school or live; they care about product, metrics, team and growth rate, which he calls "as beautiful of a meritocracy as I've ever seen."

chunks.heading: Public markets, Adobe-Figma, and valuation logic
chunks.text:
- Jason says he is buying equities and trading publicly (he mentions Adobe, TSMC, Twilio and Shopify as names he likes, with a "not investment advice" caveat). He says it balances his understanding of public versus private success.
- He argues Adobe buying Figma was the right move even at a huge premium. Adobe was unlikely to rebuild Figma without a full rewrite. Buying it removes the risk that Figma builds Photoshop, and puts Figma into Adobe's distribution channel.
- He reasons that the market's drop on the news was a discount on a good decision.
- Valuation logic: a company with strong network effects inside an organization deserves a meaningful revenue multiple, like a castle with a bigger moat. Figma extends to non-designers, and everyone from BD to the CFO to legal comes in.
- His Weblogs Inc lesson: AOL paid $30 million against about $200K in cumulative revenue. People thought that was crazy because they did not realize AOL's distribution drove huge ad revenue to the blogs.
- He says an acquisition that looks absurd can look like a bargain five years later. He cites WhatsApp, YouTube and Instagram: "leave it alone, don't screw it up."
- He gives a rough take on All In's value: a top-40 podcast is worth at least $50 million on its own, and possibly $50 to $100 million. He points out that one extra Uber-type deal would add more.

chunks.heading: Views on capitalism, wealth, and learning to build
chunks.text:
- Jason says the world is unfair but that in America it has never been more fair. He says anyone can learn almost anything for free:
  - YouTube
  - MIT OpenCourseWare
  - Google's free career courses
  - founder-built channels
- He says term sheets used to be secret. Now there are many videos on how to negotiate one.
- He argues people create jobs and are rewarded for it. He supports capitalism and criticizes attacks on founders.
- His example: Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren attacked Bezos, and Amazon then paid about $22 an hour, with benefits and college. He says the free market delivered what the politicians could not pass.
- He criticizes San Francisco politics and a supervisor who celebrated taxing founders. He points out that one Slack exit generated about a billion in taxes for the state.
- He thinks California will be damaged for a decade or two.
- He describes himself as an independent and moderate, a fiscal conservative and social liberal, and says he is writing a book about wealth and money.
- He wants to be on a venture Hall of Fame list. His own picks for impact include Don Valentine, Arthur Rock, Paul Graham, Doug Leone and Mike Moritz, YC, Ron Conway and Bezos.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason explains how he picks founders (broken, driven, with something to prove), why startups are war and sports, and how radical delegation and a syndicate let him invest at scale. He also covers product-market fit, compounding, riding winners, and deal terms.

chunks.heading: Early-stage angel investing: take the bet, don't hunt for red flags
chunks.text:
- Jason rejects "negative art" screening, where one red flag means pass. His method: list everything that could go wrong, then on the other side list "but what if it works?" If it works, he rips up the red-flag side, because those flags were only a map of what to fix or avoid.
- His driving analogy: there are a million ways to die on the way to the Warriors game, but you focus on staying in your lane. Race drivers are told "don't look at the wall, look at the road."
- He distrusts consensus: "If there's consensus on the idea, it probably should exist already." He introduced Uber to about 25 people and 3 invested. Ninety percent passing doesn't make an idea good, but it can mean an outlier idea with outlier results.
- He never underestimates a founder because early Steve Jobs pitches were raw too: "everybody who starts in this business is awkward and has weird ideas and is unrefined."
- He claims the human brain is pessimistic by default, because scared people lived longer, so investors must correct for that bias.
- Hit rates: he asks successful angels how many investments it takes to hit a 25x, 50x or 100x outlier. The usual answer is 20 to 50. His own record is roughly one unicorn per 50 investments, and earlier in his career closer to one per 25. He has made over 300 investments (about 30-40 a year).
- He teaches this in Angel University, a 3-4 hour course taught with Mike Zavino. Proceeds go to charity (about $150-175K donated), and he charges so attendees have skin in the game. Each class adds 300-500 members to his syndicate.

chunks.heading: Syndicates: structure, economics and why they work for angels and founders
chunks.text:
- A syndicate is a group of people investing in an LLC that invests in a company, with a lead (Jason). His started on AngelList for the first 30 deals, then moved to thesyndicate.com.
- Starting one is cheap: Ashure Fund Management (which Jason invested in, and which was AngelList's back end) sets up a syndicate's legal documents for about $15K.
- Scale: 68 deals closed in 2021 for $51M, the largest syndicate in the world, with about 9,500 members adding a couple hundred a month (about 1,000 when his book came out, with a goal of 10,000). He does about two deals a week.
- Minimum is $4K per deal and the average member puts in about $7K. His average deal allocation is about $750K, often oversubscribed ($1.5-2M of interest), so he trims members' requests.
- Why members join: finding deal flow alone means years of building a brand and roughly 25-50 meetings to find one qualified company, and direct checks usually start around $50K. A syndicate lets you do twelve $4K checks instead of one $50K check, choosing which deals and how much, unlike a fund where you get a year-end statement and learn the result a decade later.
- Quality varies: there are no rules for syndicates, and some leads do no diligence. His does diligence, checks legal documents, and hosts a webinar with the founder.
- Founder benefit: one line on the cap table instead of many angels, plus 100-200 syndicate members who can give feedback, introductions and help finding employees.
- He leaves tiny syndicate deal-term debates to a team and standard terms (see below).

chunks.heading: Deal terms: keep the cap table clean and everyone aligned on share price
chunks.text:
- Jason's firm takes preferred shares, not common, and won't waive pro rata rights, because "we have LPs" and need pro rata to run a successful fund. Founders have asked for common about 10 times and the answer has always been no.
- He avoids funky structures. East Coast VCs sometimes add odd terms, and the next serious investor sees it and may be scared away.
- His principle: the share price is the aligning device. A founder with 40%, a seed investor with 7%, a Series A at 15%, a Series B at 10%, employees at 15%: everyone sees price go from $1 to $4 to $12 and wins together.
- How preferred works: it converts one-to-one to common at IPO or acquisition. Before exit, its protective provisions stop founders from taking the money and shutting down. Example: $5M invested and a $3M sale means investors get paid first (60% whole).
- Examples of structure he warns about: a $1B valuation with a 2x participating preferred (sell at $500M, the $100M investor takes $200M, or 40% of proceeds); or a distressed $500K bridge with a 4x liquidation preference on a $5M company.
- Down rounds mean selling more shares to raise less, which can start a "debt spiral" or "death spiral" if the cocktail is too complicated to unwind. Funky terms don't doom a company but cause pain later.

chunks.heading: Radical delegation: spend time only on the highest-leverage behaviors
chunks.text:
- With 300+ investments, he says you must "be ruthless about delegation," and "go fast alone, go far together."
- Example: he used to meet every accelerator applicant (hundreds per cohort, then the last 50 and follow-ups). Now his team applies his rubrics and heuristics to the check of about $100K, and he watches a pitch video or reads coverage only.
- Deal structure and legal debates are delegated using a standard-deal rule set. His team may vary terms about 10%, and tells founders what they can approve and gives his mobile number if they want to escalate.
- The two things he keeps: hanging out with founders he's invested in and meeting new elite founders, and his podcast, which helps him meet startups and promote portfolio companies. "You got to look at the highest leverage behaviors and then get rid of everything else."
- Benefit of the podcast as deal flow: it also builds the brand that feeds the syndicate.

chunks.heading: Picking founders: the broken, driven Jedi, and why leadership is a later skill
chunks.text:
- He looks for a founder with "something to prove," a chip on the shoulder, and an energy level he says is easy to discern. "If you show me a balanced person, I will show you a moderate outcome in startup land." He cites Jobs and Travis Kalanick; he thinks a founder working 70-80 hours a week needs this drive.
- Founders often start as great individual contributors (writing code, marketing, selling). Success later demands leadership: "What got you here will not get you there." The brutal standards founders hold themselves to cannot be unleashed on their team. He tells them to inspire people, ask good questions, "make them feel 12 feet tall," demand excellence and empower them.
- His Michael Jordan reference: Jordan's savage standards won titles but left him miserable and estranged from Scottie Pippen. The team-builder analogies: Draymond Green as the glue for Steph and Klay; one superstar scoring 40 can still lose.
- On experience: young founders (Zuckerberg, Gates, Jobs, Larry and Sergey) show audacity and a drive to prove something, but serial founders have a much higher success rate and higher aggregate returns. They avoid unforced errors, like a veteran who knows how to set a pick, because games are won by a few points. Nobody has studied whether young hits stick with a company for decades, so he notes both can be true.
- He tells serial investors to look at the anti-portfolio and forecast critically, and to keep asking whether success was causation or correlation.
- Founders survive on resilience: "The great ones are like, 'Yeah, I lost a limb… I'll go on the next mission.'" After more than a decade of an up market, he sees soft, entitled founders. He tells them there's "no timeout" when they have ammunition left.
- Crucible moments make founders: Uber and Robinhood both had hard stretches that battle-tested their founders, and he argues a founder who survives is stronger, not flawed.

chunks.heading: Startup failure modes: burger quality, runway shame and crisis behavior
chunks.text:
- Product-market fit means consumers love the product. His burger metaphor: founders change the furniture, name of the store and everything but the burger. "Make another burger and make it 10% better and do that 10 times." Do it seven times and compounding makes it better.
- Product velocity needs strong, focused product people. Focus beats creativity: he says Zuckerberg copied features and won through focus, speed and simplicity.
- Failure often comes from shame and silence. Young founders hide it until two weeks of runway remain. He wants to hear everything early, being "the safe space" for a founder crying in the shower before brunch.
- In a crisis, never concede while you have capital left. Options he's seen work: ask staff to defer salary with a signed promise of repayment plus interest, cut pay in half, or move to minimum wage for two months.
- Market cycles: he lived through 1987, 1994-95, the dotcom bust and 2008. In the shakeout after 13 years of up markets, easy rounds based on a good deck or network end, and investors now want performance. Rounds 'sell the promise' first, then performance.
- Founders at 500K revenue with four months of runway who quit because "I'm not enjoying it" show the wrong mindset. He tells them to keep fighting.

chunks.heading: Compounding, the Rule of 72 and many small product gains
chunks.text:
- He teaches the Rule of 72 in his accelerator: divide 72 by the growth rate to get the periods to double. At 10% a month you double in 7.2 months (not 10), and at 10% a week in 7.2 weeks. Many founders don't see compounding.
- He says making one feature twice as good is very hard, but making 10 features 10% better is easy, and users feel it. His burger example: bun, cook, cheese, plate, box, sauce, order process, speed.
- He tells founders to think in decades: Elon's electric cars and SpaceX are in their second decade, and "how long can you suffer through a neverending series of challenges" is the lesson of success.
- On Uber's economics, he used simple math: if they lost about 50 cents a ride across billions of rides, raising price by $1.50 could produce $2B more, and even if 10% of rides vanished the result was $1.8B. He saw the lever as obvious once the competitive dogfight eased.
- Superhuman example: Rahul Vohra asked how to beat free Gmail. Jason's math: if Superhuman saves 10 minutes a day, that's about 60 hours a year, worth $60,000 at $1,000 an hour, so $360 a year is about 0.6% of the value. He invested $500K in the seed round, having earlier backed Reportive (a tripling when LinkedIn bought it), after Rahul promised Jason would be his first call. Jason says he also invests in people who return his call.

chunks.heading: Holding winners and building a founder network
chunks.text:
- He advises riding winners and taking some chips off the table as you go. Selling Uber early at about $5B would have missed another 12-20x. He sold some Uber and kept some, and has not sold any Robinhood (once $30-40, then about $10) or Square, which he says he will never sell, citing Jack Dorsey.
- His reasoning for holding Uber: the on-demand super app (rides, food, experiences, trucking/logistics). He thinks Uber, Airbnb and DoorDash are takeout candidates for Walmart, Amazon, Google, Apple or Facebook.
- Capital allocator advice: start small. His wife could invest 1-5% of net worth, learn from losses and then concentrate on winners.
- Billionaire paths: allocate capital, found a company or be among the top 50-100 investors in an outlier. He says wealth past $10-20M doesn't change much, and he'd choose 40 ski days over 10 more investments.
- Friendships: be a loyal friend and give relentless support, even public "air cover" (defending Travis and Robinhood on CNBC). His friend Fritz taught him to call friends when alone. He urges people to double down on relationships as their circles shrink with success.
- Founder University: a 12-week course for $700 refunded if you finish. About 90%+ complete, versus about 6% for typical online courses, because of skin in the game. Concept: 100 graduated first, 200 are in the current cohort.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Calacanis explains how he picks early bets (imagine the world if it works), why a well-built product plus delighted customers matters most, and why venture money is jet fuel not for everyone. He argues startups are an Olympic-level pursuit, that learning new skills is the key edge, and that loyalty and gratitude compound.

chunks.heading: Investing philosophy: ask what could go right
chunks.text:
- Jason says the way to do well as an angel investor, in tech or in life, is "to not say what could go wrong but to say what could go right," then imagine the world if it works.
- He invested in Robinhood at a dive bar (Antonio's Nuthouse, Palo Alto) after founder Vlad Tenev pitched him. The idea: get millennials to trade stocks, free, at a time when the dot-com crash and 2008 had killed retail investing.
- His reaction: a group with no interest in saving, and a free business model. He said "I'm in because in almost all cases the crazy outlandish ideas that nobody believes in are the ones that have the greatest returns."
- Uber: he introduced it to about 25 investors and only 3 said yes (about 12%).
- Examples of ideas that sound like they can't work: Wikipedia (no one paid, yet it became the largest encyclopedia), Airbnb (staying in a stranger's home), Robinhood.
- Best startups "induce a market to exist." Uber competed with car ownership, not taxis. Airbnb made people take trips (e.g. 3 weeks in Kyoto) they would not otherwise take.

chunks.heading: What to look for when angel investing: product, customers, engagement
chunks.text:
- Jason teaches angel investing (book "Angel", the course Angel University six times a year, and a syndicate with about 6,500 members, the largest in the world).
- He says two things cannot be faked: a product built really well (craftsmanship, "transcendent": Calm, Robinhood, Uber, Tesla, Amazon) and delighted customers. A great team usually builds a good product and iterates to delight users.
- Engagement is the tell: "just a fancy word for how much they use it."
- Snapchat example: far fewer users than rivals, but the top third opened the app every hour, with streaks. Clubhouse was funded on hours of use per month.
- Calm was the syndicate's first deal: $378K at a $5M company, about 6-7% ownership. Now worth about $2B; the syndicate still owns about 5%. He invested after Sam Harris explained meditation and UCLA's mindfulness researchers confirmed it was real.
- Calm grew from $10K/month to millions per month over four years, raising only a $250M round in between. He has seen that capital efficiency only 3-4 times.
- He prefers to be the first, second or third check: "I want to meet them on day zero." He turned down mega-fund offers to write $150M checks, saying that is "like being an atm."

chunks.heading: Venture capital math and whether to raise
chunks.text:
- Venture money is "jet fuel": only about 1 in 1,000 US startups gets funded. It makes sense only if you want to build something big and fast.
- Jason's own portfolio: 7 of 10 startups he invests in go to zero.
- Fund math: a $300M fund with 30 names at $10M each needs one or two to return 30x-60x. The goal is about 3x cash on cash in 10 years (about 25% annualized); he says the stock market only doubles money in that period.
- VCs are betting on 30 names and need 2-3 to hit, so they push founders to go 100x, not grow 50% a year. Growing 10% on your own revenue is the "bicycle"; VC money is a rocket that can explode.
- The J-curve: bad news comes first (failures die fast), winners take 4-6 years, and it takes about a decade to know if an investor is good. Early on "you feel like an idiot."
- Bootstrapping on customer revenue requires extreme product-market fit and a good price with a healthy margin. Hardware is nearly impossible this way, so it is mostly software.
- Young VCs can be nervous and get in the way of founders.

chunks.heading: Distribution and growth in the modern era
chunks.text:
- Market size was underestimated: first 10-20M broadband homes, then 60M, then billions of phones with an app store and a credit card in them.
- Companies now reach global scale in 2-4 years, not decades. Clubhouse went from private beta to the number one app in Germany and Japan in about six months.
- Social networks follow a pattern: about 20 players ever win a category, and 80% is owned by the top 2-3, but the leaders change (Friendster, MySpace, Facebook, Snapchat).
- Jason argues Instagram should not have sold to Facebook ($500M valuation after a Sequoia round); standalone it would be worth about $500B, and Facebook would have been in decline without Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Silicon Valley's playbook for a decade or two is removing friction. Uber removed tipping and the payment step; Amazon had one-click; Clubhouse is one click to listen and two to speak. Unintended consequences follow: Facebook's easy add-to-group feature ended up outing gay students who had joined a choir group.
- Feeds changed from reverse chronological to ranking by likes and comments, which drove outrage-driven engagement. His fix idea: let users bring their own algorithm.
- Amazon Prime: the business was getting people to subscribe (about $13/month or $120/year), not shipping products. He credits Bezos's "two-day shipping" goal as an audacious target that rallied the team.

chunks.heading: Founders, leadership and the "Olympic" nature of startups
chunks.text:
- Jason says building a startup is like an Olympic sport or Navy SEAL effort: "seven days a week, 12 hours a day," with no work-life balance. If you want a normal job, do not join a startup or an ambitious company.
- He compares it to people not blaming Michael Phelps for ice baths. The mismatch is people conflating a regular job with an extreme pursuit. Those who sign up to work for Musk or Bezos should know what they are choosing.
- Leaders set the standard. Elon is "indefatigable"; Bezos debated; Jobs was a design genius. A leader's time ends when they can no longer set the standard, and then they should pass the baton (as Bezos did at 57).
- Founders need a purpose: "when you dread going to work that day and you don't feel like solving that problem anymore, that's the tell." People who start only because they want to make money tend to quit around month 9 or 10.
- Common founder traits: charisma (storytelling that gets people, investors and press on the journey), and often hardship or immigrant parents.
- First-principles/"day one" thinking: pause and ask how you would solve it fresh. Elon asks the basic questions engineers dislike. Balance it with pragmatism, goals and dates so you don't over-engineer and never ship.
- Closing quote: "The number one reason a startup shuts down is not running out of money. The number one reason a startup fails is that the founder gives up."

chunks.heading: Skills, execution and mindset advice
chunks.text:
- Ideas get zero credit: "it's all about execution." People saying they need a technical co-founder with no skill of their own ("I have an idea") are not credible.
- His career advice: learn to learn new skills. Replace roughly 400 hours of TV (e.g. Game of Thrones plus Breaking Bad) with learning design, UX, development or sales.
- He gets to about 50% of the knowledge in a field (design, writing, sales, development) so "people can't snow you" when he hires. Knowing enough to call out bad work is the unlock.
- Use deliberate practice: he improved at chess by reviewing losses on chess.com instead of just playing more. Tim Ferriss picked up basketball form by studying him closely for a couple of hours.
- Every course from MIT, Harvard and Stanford is free online. He rejects the idea that poor Americans cannot access it, citing smartphone and internet penetration.
- Competition improves things: chess.com at about $100/year, Elon forcing every automaker to go electric, Michael Jordan's "I took that personally."

chunks.heading: Loyalty, crisis handling and the Tesla story
chunks.text:
- Jason says investors have three choices when a portfolio company is under fire: fight for the team, go silent, or throw them under the bus. He is "ride or die" and asks the founder first whether to defend them publicly. He did this for Uber and, in the GameStop episode, for Robinhood.
- His view of the Robinhood crisis: it was a liquidity and collateral demand (clearinghouses asking for billions), not a conspiracy with hedge funds. Robinhood raised about $3.5B in a week or so. He says communication is the top issue: put all bad news out immediately, though legal limits can keep founders quiet.
- With Chamath, a competing investor/CEO angle (SoFi), the fight got heated on the All-In podcast. They resolved it privately by acknowledging love and loyalty, and he judges people by intent ("nuance and intent have been totally lost").
- Tesla story (Elon has told it publicly): around the 2008 financial crisis, Tesla had about two weeks of cash. Elon showed him the unreleased Model S clay model. Jason told him "if you make that car you'll change the god damn world," and sent two $50,000 checks to pay for a reservation. He was reservation number 73 and Elon gave him a Roadster; the checks cleared months later.
- Jason's closing advice on gratitude: "Nobody gets there alone." Write thank-you letters; gratitude amplifies joy.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Recorded in the early 2020 COVID crisis, Jason Calacanis gives a wartime playbook: be honest about the business, get to 18 months of runway, cut fast, and take services revenue to survive. He also covers pitching investors in a down market, valuation resets, cheap pivot tests and remote demos.

chunks.heading: Surviving a downturn: the first moves Jason demands of founders
chunks.text:
- Jason says to be brutally honest about the state of the business, get the data, build a plan, communicate it to the team, then execute. "Standard leadership stuff", and people respect transparent leaders.
- Without revenue and with a short runway, he says the company will likely die unless it acts. He puts the target at 18 months of cash. Six months of cash is a likely death.
- He uses a foxhole image: "we've got like six bullets each", so the plan can't be walking through the front door.
- Cutting costs is not optional. When a founder said they didn't want to run the company if they had to lay off two out of three people, Jason's reply was that they never should have started a company. His analogy is the pilot who lands the plane in the Hudson: "You don't have a choice."
- A founder's job in a crisis is to save as many jobs as possible by saving the business, so jobs can be brought back later.
- Take any available government money, such as PPP loans. In his words, if you don't apply "you're insane" because it is "essentially a grant".
- He advises weighing the employee tradeoff openly: with a million in the bank and a million a month burn, either everyone takes a pay cut or you cut people. His move is to survey the team on the maximum pay cut they could take, possibly traded for extra options, then decide.
- Furlough rather than agonize. "You can always hire people back, but you can't always save the company."
- He warns against "white knight syndrome". If an investor "is getting the term sheet together", set a deadline (he suggests Wednesday) and make the cuts if it doesn't arrive.

chunks.heading: Services revenue and survival tactics when revenue is thin
chunks.text:
- Revenue is revenue. If a SaaS company can bring in consulting revenue, he says to take it.
- For a company with customers that have money, the move is to offer custom software or outsourced development, such as building the features a big customer asked for. His illustrative figure was a project of about $300,000 for the year.
- Normally he would reject a services business on margin terms, but in a crisis he says "you've got to eat".
- For R&D-heavy and hard-tech companies (med tech, biotech) that may run out of cash before revenue, he suggests consulting to potential customers, for example offering to run a customer's lab while the startup works on its own idea.
- Do not be "too precious". Survive at all costs.
- If the founder thinks of it as four to six weeks of cash rather than four to six months, the behavior changes. Do that mental exercise.

chunks.heading: Raising capital in a downturn
chunks.text:
- Sequence matters. Make the cuts, extend the runway and drive revenue first, then talk to investors. Investors sort founders into people who want to win. Going in saying "I need a million for six months" with two payrolls in the bank gets "I'm not catching that falling knife".
- Show seriousness: you have cut, you took a 50% pay cut, co-founders took 60% and 10%. This reads as fundable and serious.
- Know your investor type. Angels investing from a balance sheet that just fell 30-40% will pause. Syndicates should be expected to take about twice as long to close and fill for about half the amount, possibly at half the valuation.
- Funds with dry powder get conservative and will double down on existing winners and thin the herd. He triages his own 100+ active portfolio companies first and says that will take him three to six months, so new investments will be "few and far between".
- Don't be precious about size or valuation. A founder who planned a $20M raise may end up raising $1M at $5M post. He says that may be the reality "and that's okay".
- Treat raising as sales: you are selling equity. If you can convince a sophisticated investor, you can sell customers and hire. He ranks the difficulty: investors are hardest, customers medium to hard or easy depending on price, and employees were hard but will become easy in a downturn.
- Trial close at the end of a pitch. He cited a founder who closed his laptop and asked the investor what he would need to see to write a check; the investor named milestones, and the founder returned later and got funded. A related close: ask "when should I come back to you, at what milestone?" and push for a benchmark.
- Prefer a fast no over a long maybe, and cross investors off if they are not a fit.

chunks.heading: What investors want to see now
chunks.text:
- The era of growth at all costs is over for now. Investors want sustainable growth, cohorts of users who really use the product, and unit economics that work.
- He describes a pilot's checklist: look at airspeed and altitude, then go down the checklist. For a startup that means, for example, spending $6,000 to acquire a customer via Facebook and Instagram ads, then looking at what churn those customers show. Artificial growth gets discounted.
- If half your customers are at risk of churning and don't show true product-market fit, consider raising prices to push them out and focus on the top half.
- The pitch should be unvarnished: here is the reality, what is working and what isn't, the challenges and how you'll overcome them, and why you will come out the winner. "Figure it out later" won't fly.
- Don't spin or hide early numbers. Show weekly or monthly revenue and metrics rather than a quarterly view that hides bad months. Investors expect early numbers to be unpredictable, and he says the point is to help founders make them predictable. They will find out anyway. "Here's what we figured out, here's what we need help with" is attractive to people who like to solve problems.
- He recommends emailing him a revenue chart by week or month, plus a PDF deck, with no links to unknown files.

chunks.heading: Valuations and deal terms
chunks.text:
- Jason predicts that seed valuations roughly halve. He remembers investing in Uber, Thumbtack and other eventual unicorns at about $4-5M valuations when they had products in market, and thinks we go back to that.
- His rule of thumb: half of the previous market rate. YC companies might drop by about a third, for example from $10-14M caps. Accelerator companies at roughly $6-10M caps might go to roughly $4-7M.
- Series B and breakout companies may take about a 30% haircut.
- Don't benchmark against anomalies (Zoom, Slack, Box, or Tom Cruise's pay). Breakouts are unusual. Uber looked like a money-losing business but in its early days the Lincoln Town Car service was printing money with near-zero CAC through over-the-shoulder virality.
- Founders who optimized for valuation are now telling him they over-optimized. He criticizes six-month notes with bumped caps (moving a cap from eight to twelve to raise another $600K for six months) and says raise a proper round with 18 months of runway. He calls the downside "risk of ruin".
- On safes and notes: he says the safe was almost a way to "troll investors" when it has no expiration date or cap. He recommends an expiration date, which forces everyone to sit down, re-evaluate and agree to extend, convert or return money. A note that never converts is bad for both sides, especially if the company breaks out. He cited TopTal as a case where investors were hurt because no equity round was ever done.

chunks.heading: How Jason picks investments and what Launch looks for
chunks.text:
- He is sector agnostic. His biggest hits defined sectors that had no names yet: Robinhood and Wealthfront defined fintech, Uber and Airbnb defined the on-demand economy. His own Calm investment looked silly (people wrote about him losing money on a meditation app) until it worked, so he avoids trend-chasing.
- He looks for founders with resilience and leadership, who are self-possessed, confident, and will fight for their opinion. His test is to ask a question like "why consumer and not enterprise?" and see whether they defend their view. He says he is not trying to change their mind. He credits Uber's decision to be full-stack consumer as a decision where an investor pushing an enterprise-software model would have been wrong.
- His line: tactics matter less than what customers think and what the team sees in the results. The people on the front line have insight he won't.
- Launch's "Goldilocks zone" is about $250K a month in revenue, or a consumer product growing about 5% week over week. If a company has a competitive Series A going, it doesn't need Launch; if it has only an idea and no launched product, Launch is not that helpful. Launch helps with the bridge to a roughly $1M to $5M round. Its real contribution, he says, is "anointing": the Launch name signals a real company.
- Check size in the discussion: a $100K check, wired quickly once a company joins the accelerator.
- Launch plan at the time: more cohorts run virtually, with the goal of 100 companies a year at seven per cohort, around twelve cohorts a year.
- A prototype with no customers is not fundable for him. Free users are "freeloaders, not customers", so charge. He wants a couple of paying customers first, though he'll talk earlier.
- Jason notes that Travis Kalanick demoed Uber at his Open Angel Forum, where people watched a car pull up. His lesson: back people who take action, and outsiders who are authentic.

chunks.heading: Staying in touch with investors and cold outreach
chunks.text:
- It is always a good time to contact investors if the business is good. Build a list of people who said no and send a short monthly update.
- Format: very short and tight. Lead with a chart of the true metric, then new customers, new hires, a press link, product screenshots or a video, a customer testimonial. "Less text, more visual, more data." Nobody cares about long narratives.
- Cold email example structure: acknowledge they are busy, mention something specific from a podcast or post of theirs, give one-line traction (for example 1,600 customers growing 20% a month, with a chart), offer to update, and state when the next monthly update will be sent.
- Add context: follow them on Twitter and connect on LinkedIn with a personalized note. Play the long game.

chunks.heading: Pivot versus persevere, and testing cheaply
chunks.text:
- Persevere or pivot is a judgement call from the heart, the data and customers. Twitter meandered and then caught fire; Angry Birds came after dozens of tries. He worries about founders who pivot too often and also about those "banging on a door with their head" when it's a brick wall.
- He wants founders who stay for the mission, not mercenaries asking about exit. He still holds his Uber stake and thinks it is a trillion-dollar company.
- To pivot well, run the laziest, smallest test. Example: a landing page for an iMessage-based virtual admin for executives at $50 an hour or $500 a month. Advertise to 10,000 LinkedIn CEOs, take a credit card with charging to start June 1, and measure conversion and CAC before hiring anyone. Do not hire a team to pretend to be the product before you know demand.

chunks.heading: Market outlook, pitch decks and practical tips
chunks.text:
- Do not time the market. It is never a bad time to start a great company. After 9/11 and 2008, Jason says the world mostly went back to normal with small tweaks (the TSA, then PreCheck and Clear as the "antibody"), so expect remote work and food delivery to accelerate rather than a wholly new category.
- He expects a "Yolo" rebound in travel, cruises, events and hotels, and likes competing in sectors that are getting crushed right now.
- Silicon Valley: roughly 80% of Launch companies are from outside the Valley. He sees Launch as an Ellis Island: sort the winners, anoint them, introduce them, and send them back to a low-cost location. Being close to capital helps in a crisis. He thinks commuting is a dumb cost, and that remote work will reduce pressure to take the company bus.
- Pitch deck: don't plaster it with COVID. Focus on customers, metrics, acquisition and stickiness. Include COVID only if it is relevant (his example is off-grid travel).
- Zoom pitching: use wired Ethernet (turn Wi-Fi off, buy the $10 dongle), a real microphone, good lighting and a quiet room. Set up a separate "presenter" user account on your computer with no notifications, no Spotify, and a clean desktop.
- If the business benefits from the crisis (online education, entertainment, telepresence), raise, invest in people, product and customer acquisition. Customer acquisition costs on Facebook and Google are probably down.
- On apps: the golden era isn't over. Consumer subscription changed things. A company can reach scale with about 15 to 30 people (he cited Calm and Instagram as small-team examples, and Fitbod among his own), but iOS developers are expensive.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Calacanis explains how he picks startups and manages risk: start with revenue-generating companies and the smallest checks, judge product and customers over founder charisma, and only bet where you hold an edge. He also treats his public-market "J-trades" as paid education and uses a revenue, price-to-sales, growth and cash checklist.

chunks.heading: Angel investing: start small, start with revenue, learn by doing
chunks.text:
- Jason's rule for a first-time angel: make your first 20 investments only in companies that already have a product in market and generate revenue. If someone pitches a pre-revenue company, "don't do it. Wait."
- Invest the minimum check you can. If the minimum is $5,000, ask whether you can do one or two slots instead of a full check.
- On his syndicate, a $1M allocation is split into roughly 250 slots of about $4,000. People ask to take a single slot and he says yes. He has had investors who wanted to put in $500 and he says yes if there is room.
- He encourages newcomers to take their time and learn how it works rather than rush in.
- He compares it to learning poker: you can learn just as well at a thousandth of the cost, so don't learn at a $25,000 buy-in table.
- He requires people in his syndicate to take his Angel University course (about $300, with the money donated to charity) and read his book (about $10-20). The fee is meant to stop people from burning seats.
- His first investment for a new syndicate member is typically $4-5K, which he calls effectively a small charitable donation as the cost of learning.

chunks.heading: How Jason evaluates startups: product and customers over charisma
chunks.text:
- He bets on team, product and customers. Early on he looked at the product and the customer base more than the founder's personality.
- On charisma: "You can't fake a great product. You can't fake happy customers." He argues charismatic founders can be coached to fake charisma, so he discounts it, and says it will get easier to fake still.
- Examples of how he judged early bets:
  - Uber: he had known Travis for a while, the product was a done deal and customers were very happy.
  - Calm: he met Alex, the valuation was $4.5M, revenue was only about $10,000, and no one else would invest. He liked the product, and believed meditation could be huge. People thought the bet was foolish.
- Jason says he "wrote the million-dollar homepage" comment in jest about the Calm founder's homepage; the point is the product was excellent despite thin revenue.
- His investing team has 10-11 people. They take about 70 meetings a week, 50-60 of them first meetings, and invest in about two companies a week, usually one follow-on and one new. They have gone from 10-20 thousand pitches and thousands of meetings down to about 50 companies.
- He keeps questioning his own investments and uses writing (his book, deal memos, public trades) as a way to hold himself accountable.

chunks.heading: Deal memos and risk framing
chunks.text:
- Jason writes a deal memo for each syndicate deal. He syndicates a $500,000 allocation across several hundred angels on his platform, now over 10,000 investors.
- His syndicate runs with over 11,000 accredited investors and more than 260 deals. He has invested in about 350 companies.
- He is deliberately candid in memos: founders can lie, take the money to Vegas, defraud a vendor or be incompetent. So "invest as little as you can."
- He uses the word "bet" on purpose so readers understand it is a bet, and he states how he is placing his own bet.
- He only lets accredited investors in, to follow the rules, even though non-accredited people would be 25 times more potential participants. Average check is now about $6-7K, up from $3-4K.
- On accreditation, he thinks it should work like a driver's license or a PADI scuba certification: read a book, take a test, spend 10 hours and $100-200. He doesn't think net worth should be the test, and finds it absurd that a non-accredited person can buy a leveraged-mortgage ETN through a brokerage but not invest in a friend's startup.
- He runs Angel University free for people who want help getting accredited.

chunks.heading: Cycles, downturns and preparing for a bust
chunks.text:
- Jason says he warned in December 2018 that a long bull market was ending. His advice was to make sure you have a path to profitability, hold a healthy amount of cash in the account, and raise money at the top of the market. He admits his timing was off by a year or 18 months and takes little credit: "It's a pretty basic piece of advice."
- He calls the pull-back a stress test of everything: stocks, NFTs, crypto, real estate. He expects countless lawsuits, citing the dot-com era when litigation ran for years.
- On valuations, he points to companies valued at $100M with 4,000 users and no revenue, then $1B, then $4B, which did not make sense. He credits Clubhouse for taking a reset to about $250M and then executing.
- On large LPs: pension funds and endowments are sophisticated, diversified across cycles, and can handle losses in some funds. He worries less about them than about unfair outcomes for consumers, which will drive the most litigation.

chunks.heading: Crypto and Web3: what he thinks works and what doesn't
chunks.text:
- Jason bought Bitcoin at about $2-3, then again at $100-200, and has made seven figures. He lost the early coins because he didn't have the keys and the site was hacked. He says it is not that he doesn't understand crypto.
- He says Bitcoin could go to zero (hack, ban, denial-of-service style attack, black swan) and that all technology is eventually replaced by something better. He was attacked for saying so.
- He calls 99% of ICOs and crypto projects things that never became anything reasonable, and says a significant portion were scams, incompetence or both. In startups, by contrast, you get paid after proving something.
- On retail losses: he suspects some VCs structured token deals (foundations in places like Panama, legal spend about 100 times normal) so they could exit positions before product-market fit. He frames this as speculation, not something he can prove. He notes that it was the retail buyers who ended up holding the tokens.
- He expects district attorneys, who want higher office or to keep their seats, to go after crypto fraud, and says the "this is not financial advice, do your own research" disclaimer will draw regulator attention.
- What he finds promising:
  - NFTs tied to real rights, such as club memberships (Soho House, a golf club) where a smart contract sets resale rules, e.g. return of the original investment plus a split of profits with the club.
  - DAOs for shared ownership, like a Tuscan farm held through an LLC with weekly use shares, or a scholarship fund where members vote on applications.
  - Gaming and prediction markets, such as online poker or an oil-price bet settled through an oracle, with no intermediary.
  - Free-to-mint NFTs, e.g. The 100 Thieves minting for about 700,000 people to celebrate a championship, as a way to avoid the need to sell.
- What he is skeptical about:
  - Blockchain as a database: slow and always behind modern tech.
  - Fully decentralized companies and DAO governance: "when things go badly... you need a general who can make decisions quickly."
  - Decentralized versions of eBay, PayPal, Stripe or Airbnb: he thinks most customers prefer a trusted central brand and want refunds when hacked.
- Pricing point: to compete, a crypto payment product should be about 10 times cheaper than the best existing deal. If Stripe is about 3%, aim for about 30 basis points. Gas fees are "ridiculous."
- He says Web3's real believers got drowned out by people there to flip assets, like the dot-com era, and hopes the crash pushes out 70-80% of players so those who can ship products remain.

chunks.heading: Jason's "J-trading" public-market experiment and edge
chunks.text:
- Jason has historically held index funds (Vanguard, Wealthfront) plus real estate, a barbell with high-variance startup investing. He recommends most people use Wealthfront-style auto-invest: he got his whole family on it at $500-1000 per month.
- He set aside a few million dollars to trade public stocks, announcing trades on This Week in Startups with the hashtag #Jtrading. The plan is about 20 positions and about $1-2M, hold for 10 years, then publish the results and pick his best seven ideas.
- Trades he mentioned: Stitch Fix (he bought about 5,000 shares because he knew and trusted Bill Gurley, who bought a million shares), Disney (he thinks a bundle of Disney, Hulu and ESPN+ could reach 1 billion subscribers), and Amazon.
- His screen for a beaten-down stock: revenue, price-to-sales, user growth, cash on the balance sheet, and whether it is losing money. Example discussion on Snap: about $4.5B revenue, about $16B market cap, about $5B cash, so roughly 2-2.5x sales net of cash, with a possible acquirer such as Microsoft or Google. He called Evan Spiegel a product genius.
- BuzzFeed: he calls journalism a bad business with no viral growth path, thin cash and quarterly losses, so a falling knife. He would own Snap or Peloton before BuzzFeed.
- His edge principle: "I only want to bet money where I have an edge." He has an edge in private markets and poker, none in crypto, and is trying to build one in public markets. If he wanted a crypto edge, he'd stop other investing, start a crypto startup and hire 10 crypto developers and architects. He frames the trading money as his MBA tuition.
- Poker lesson: two small changes (tighter ranges out of position, folding weak suited hands under the gun) took him from losing three of four home games to winning most.

chunks.heading: Building a media business with friends (All-In) and starting new shows
chunks.text:
- Jason says working with friends is great, but All-In is a special case: four alpha personalities, "like Game of Thrones."
- The show began when Chamath asked him to do a podcast; they added the two Davids. Jason focused on being a good moderator: challenging people, interrupting, forcing them to explain terms.
- The show grew to regularly rank in the top 30 podcasts. He says they got offers but none large enough to change their lives. About $5M a year in revenue, which he produces, and he says he created the name and format and does most of the work.
- Tension arose over the All-In Summit. Jason says the event could have made millions but they gave away half the tickets and spent heavily on a $600 gift bag. He asked for 2 extra equity points (31 for him, 23 each for the others, as CEO) to run a bigger media company, and said his 20-person team was pulled off investing work to produce the event.
- The four had different goals (Sacks wanted just the weekly podcast, Chamath and Jason had ambition, Friedberg had worries). They settled on 25% each and just the weekly podcast, no more events.
- They agreed on three things: they love doing it together, listeners love it, and they believe they are doing something that matters. He calls the third the key.
- His moderating approach on politics: steer toward first principles (fiscal conservatism, government staying out of personal lives, guns) rather than tribal fights about Trump, Biden or DeSantis.
- He is launching two more podcasts in September: Founder University (weekly, a 15-minute lesson on scaling a business, taught to his three portfolio companies already) and a roundtable with guests who can't join All-In because the All-In crew appears weekly, with Jason again as point guard.
- His method for building skill: pick a new skill and aim to reach roughly the top 10% (70th to 90th percentile). Moderating has led to TV deal inquiries.

chunks.heading: Staying motivated and spending money on experience
chunks.text:
- Jason says he always wanted to be a millionaire and stop worrying about money, but he is not driven by needing more; he plays for fun and love of the game.
- After two friends died young (Dave Goldberg and Tony Hsieh), he reassessed what he actually enjoys. A friend pointed out that nearly everything he did was for others.
- Changes: he bought a ski house and skied 40 days in a year (more than the prior decade), bought a roughly $9,000 Specialized e-bike, and spends summers with his kids around Tahoe, keeping his calendar clear.
- His view: life is a collection of "best experiences" you laugh about with friends, so he tries to create more of them with his kids, wife, friends and business partners.
- He is learning to spend money on things that raise his happiness, which goes against his Irish Catholic Brooklyn upbringing. He has his chief of staff test-drive bikes and find an instructor.
- He has a 12-year-old and six-year-old twins, and tells people to enjoy every moment.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason recounts going from Brooklyn night-school kid to zine publisher, blog-network founder (Weblogs Inc, sold to AOL) and podcaster. Key lessons: self-teach the skills a product needs, use media to gain influence, hold consistency across 100 episodes, and let a podcast feed an investing business. Much of the Kanye/Elon chatter comes from the host, not Jason.

chunks.heading: Early media career and the zine playbook
chunks.text:
- Jason grew up in Brooklyn. His dad owned a bar and lost it in the 1987 market crash. He went to Fordham at night and fixed Laser Printers during the day.
- On the subway he became obsessed with magazines and asked how people got on the cover, what an editor-in-chief and a publisher do.
- He started two zines at 22 and 24. The first was Cyber Surfer (five issues, about online services before the web browser). The second was Silicon Alley Reporter, which began as a 16-page photocopied newsletter.
- Silicon Alley Reporter grew to a 300-page glossy mailed to 100,000 people, with $12M a year in revenue and 100 employees. He built it "all on my credit cards."
- He was on the cover of the New York Times, appeared on Charlie Rose and got a New Yorker feature.
- He ran an early event called Ready Set Pitch in 1996. Seven companies pitched Microsoft and AOL at Josh Harris's loft (sudo.com, an early online radio network).
- He had a choice between joining Fred Wilson and Jerry Colonna's Acme Ventures (he read business plans for them, including Beverly Hills Internet, which became GeoCities) and keeping his magazine. He chose the magazine.
- After the .com bust he sold the company to Dow Jones for two years of salary.

chunks.heading: Learning skills fast and using media as a power lever
chunks.text:
- He taught himself PageMaker, writing and photography.
- Principle: "a big part of being an entrepreneur is being fearless about adding skills." Break down what skills a product takes, such as writing, selling ads, taking pictures, layout and distribution.
- You can get to 60-70% proficiency in almost any discipline by putting your mind to it. That is enough to figure out who has the 80-90% you can hire.
- Media made him powerful quickly. He went from outsider to having Harvard and HBS founders lobbying to get into his magazine.
- He created the Silicon Alley 100 ranking deliberately. He put Esther Dyson at #1 over DoubleClick (the company with the most funding), justifying it because she "was here before them and she set the stage." The point was to provoke debate.
- His takeaway: lists are meaningless and exist to tweak people. When founders ask for help getting on "30 under 30" lists, his answer is "it's meaningless, get back to work."
- Media-plus-investing is now a common playbook, and he describes himself as an entrepreneur who learned to be a journalist and then started angel investing.

chunks.heading: Weblogs Inc and the Engadget exit
chunks.text:
- After the bust he watched his former employees make about $10K a month each from blogs (Jenny Jordan on Boing Boing, Rafat Ali on paidContent). That made him realize blogs were a business.
- Around 2003 he started Weblogs Inc to build business-to-business blogs, with the idea of doing "like 100 of these" across niches. He used subdomains (wifi.weblogsinc.com, apple.weblogsinc.com), influenced by About.com.
- Nick Denton attacked the idea publicly, saying Jason would ruin blogs by commercializing them.
- To compete with Gawker he tried to hire talent. A friend told him he had targeted the wrong blog, because most of Gawker's money came from Gizmodo.
- He took Peter Rojas out to dinner and offered double pay, a MacBook Air and equity. Rojas had been promised equity at Gawker and never got it. Together they built Engadget, which grew to about 10x the size of Gizmodo.
- Mark Cuban was his only investor. He sold to AOL (Ted Leonsis and Jim Bankoff) about 18 months after starting, for roughly $30M, in 2006. Rojas, Jason and his partner each made millions.
- Bankoff later took the playbook and built Vox Media and The Verge.
- It was his first big win and his "second act" after Silicon Alley Reporter.

chunks.heading: Podcasting: This Week in Startups
chunks.text:
- Podcasting took off in 2007-2008 once RSS enclosures could be downloaded into iTunes. He was in that RSS crowd (Dave Winer, Ev Williams) and recorded his famous question to Steve Jobs about open podcast RSS feeds.
- He started with "Calacanis Cast" for about 30 episodes, then renamed it This Week in Startups after appearing on Leo Laporte's This Week in Tech.
- First guest was Brian Alvey (2010). It was weekly, then twice, then three times, then four days a week. His rule to his team: sell out the ads three to six months ahead and he'll add an episode. He eventually reached six days a week and hired Molly Wood in January 2023.
- Early setup: Skype calls plus a roughly $20,000 TriCaster video switcher.
- He did it for personal enjoyment first. He grew up on Charlie Rose and Howard Stern and thought daily radio was the most fun job possible.
- The show feeds his business. You can buy ads on TWiST but not on All-In. People meet him for investing and start with talk about the podcast.

chunks.heading: How the podcast changed his fundraising and deal flow
chunks.text:
- He raised his fourth fund (a 506(c) public raise). He mentioned it on All-In and TWiST, did a couple of webinars, and got about $44M in interest.
- After five hours of webinars, with no road show and no pitching existing LPs, he had $40M in commits. The last fund was $44M.
- Deal flow has shifted from fighting to get into deals to oversubscribed deals fighting to get him in "because they perceive some value in it." He cites that as the real difference once a podcast has a few years behind it.
- Two founders offered him an allocation in an oversubscribed round if he could get them two All-In Summit tickets. He gave up two of his 15 tickets.
- His advice on consistency: do 100 episodes and it becomes "second nature," like basketball or poker.
- He sees the platform as one of the great paradoxes of his career. A non-commercial, shared-with-three-other-people project is among his biggest successes.

chunks.heading: Running All-In: format, moderation and the besties' rules
chunks.text:
- All-In was never supposed to get this big. It reached roughly #26-27 on the overall charts. His selfie requests in San Francisco went from a few to 10-20 a day.
- The four besties agreed on rules of the road: just do the podcast every week, no Summits, meetups or brand extensions early on. Aim for 50 episodes a year and 100 every two years, with a high-quality show.
- He bases the format on The McLaughlin Group: heated but friendly argument among smart people. "Just enough heat makes it interesting"; too much takes away from the experience.
- His role as moderator: "let's play like the Warriors, let's pass the ball." He gets each bestie their touches, built a science corner for Friedberg, who zoned out during politics, and let Sacks have politics.
- His techniques: a finger twirl "wrap it up" signal, passing to another person, asking questions to clarify positions for the audience, and moving between altitudes (explaining acronyms, then going into the weeds).
- He lets disagreement play out. He and David Sacks disagree on a lot but are close friends, and their families vacation together. His message is that people can disagree and still be friends and make progress.
- On expertise: the group claims expertise in capital allocation, startup formation, technology and markets (over 100 combined years). On politics and social issues they are like much of the audience, and everyone should discuss hard issues.
- He cut his X replies to followed accounts only for a while after brigading from MAGA and crypto fans who misread his clarifying questions.
- Lesson: he has caught "lightning in a bottle" about half a dozen times, but 20 other projects didn't hit.

chunks.heading: Tech and the press, and platform responsibility
chunks.text:
- Early on, tech press was collegial because tech was niche. Now coverage is cynical, and one company's mistake gets 100 stories while 99 good companies get none.
- He argues there's a long-standing grudge because tech gutted media's business. AOL, Google and Facebook took ads, eBay and Craigslist took classifieds, and Apple intermediated subscriptions.
- He thinks podcasts and Substack are a rebalancing, with podcasts giving more nuanced, accurate coverage than many traditional outlets.
- He defended Away founder Steph Korey. He sees the "work hard at Christmas" message as a normal CEO rally cry that was unfairly spun, and thinks anonymous sourcing is overused.
- On Palmer Luckey: he said it was an unforced error for a CEO to fund anonymous extreme trolling, with collateral damage to employees and families. Several game studios dropped Oculus development. He later hosted Luckey on the All-In stage, asked why he was fired, and apologized for the harshness.
- On platforming harmful people, he argues it's a mistake to give a megaphone to someone going through a manic episode (Kanye West). At a large audience scale, even 0.001% of listeners is thousands of people.

chunks.heading: Personal operating principles
chunks.text:
- Stay normal. In Silicon Valley some people get rich or famous "and they stop acting normal."
- Be fearless about adding skills, and don't be afraid to be an outsider (night school, no Stanford).
- Embrace being public and extroverted. He scores 96-100 extroverted on Myers-Briggs and enjoys the micro-celebrity.
- Combine roles. His edge comes from being an entrepreneur, a journalist and an investor at once.
- His goal now: squeeze everything out of "this amazing orange that fell in my lap."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason explains how venture investing works: it's rocket fuel for outlier companies, most fail, and winners are unpredictable, so you place many bets and support every founder. He also covers leadership under chaos, knowing your superpower, and why podcasts are displacing journalism.

chunks.heading: Venture capital as rocket fuel: who angel and VC money is for
chunks.text:
- Jason separates ordinary businesses (design agency, PR shop, pizzeria, dry cleaner, consulting firm) from venture-scale ones. Ordinary businesses are great, can employ people and give the owner independence, and need little money. His example: you can start a consulting firm for $0 with a free website and an email to a thousand people.
- Venture capital is "jet fuel" or "rocket fuel". You wouldn't put it in a Vespa. It is for outlier companies that can grow at a velocity others find unrealistic and reach hundreds of millions or a billion people (Uber, Robinhood, Cal.com style bets).
- Those companies are more complex, have a lower chance of success, and mostly fail hard. If they succeed, they can "change the fabric of society" (Google, Facebook, Uber, Airbnb). He calls it an Olympic-caliber sport.
- Founders of ginger beer, tea or "noble purpose" companies often don't understand why they are not fundable: they don't have a one-in-a-thousand or one-in-10,000 shot at being an outlier.
- Illustrative portfolio math of ten investments: six go to zero, the seventh and eighth return about half their money, the ninth returns two to three times, and with luck the 10th, 20th or 30th returns more than 30x. He calls this a unique kind of gambling that even insiders struggle with psychologically.

chunks.heading: How Jason sources deals and why brand matters
chunks.text:
- He meets founders largely through his podcasts. Among founders he's as known as a celebrity; outside the industry he's a nobody.
- He says tech investing is "really a popularity contest amongst investors". Investors have brands, and founders want to be affiliated with them, like a talent agency (CAA, William Morris) or record label. Affiliation validates a startup and gives others permission to engage with it.
- Podcasts, events and books are one thing: a way to meet people in the industry and let them share knowledge, so founders remember his name. The second thing is investing in their companies. He says everything his team does falls into those two buckets.
- Example: he met the founder of Cal.com on the podcast and invested because of it. He calls the podcast a tool and tactic that is in his wheelhouse as the company's leader.
- His firm Launch has a stated goal: be the best investors in the world. The plan he describes works backwards from that: support founders early, invest in 80 to 100 companies a year, reach 1,000 investments in ten years, and invest about ten times as much in winners as in failures.
- Funnel: roughly 10,000+ pitches a year, 2,000 to 4,000 meetings, about 100 investments.

chunks.heading: Expecting failure and making many bets
chunks.text:
- Most startups fail: he cites two out of three or three out of four. So a founder needs only three, four or five tries to get a likely success. He tells founders whose first company failed that Travis Kalanick's third company was Uber and Elon Musk's third and fourth were SpaceX and Tesla; the third or fourth attempt is often the sweet spot.
- First-time home runs (Gates, Bezos, Zuckerberg) are rare but memorable, which makes them seem common. He calls that confirmation bias, and also cites survivorship bias (the WWII planes: bullet holes only appeared on planes that made it back).
- Nobody knows which companies will win. He did not expect Cal.com to become the second-best company in his portfolio. He expected Uber to be a billion or two billion dollar company, not $60 billion, so he was off by 30 to 60x. He didn't think Robinhood's first idea would work, thought the second or third would, and was "delighted to be wrong".
- He doesn't think he's a great picker: "I think I have a great network and I have great relationships." One Uber hit doesn't prove skill, so he warns against concluding that.
- Because outcomes are unpredictable, he treats every portfolio company as amazing and supports them as much as possible. His summary: find the best people you can, invest in them, support the heck out of them. If it fails and they did a good job, pat them on the back; they can do another one.
- Even internally, if 12 team members each picked two companies he doubts the majority would pick the winner.

chunks.heading: Where an investor's time goes: the failing companies
chunks.text:
- About 90% of his time goes to the companies that fail or struggle. Winners hit their numbers and get high-fives; there's no point "screwing up your formula". Scaling winners still needs hiring, watching competitors and building infrastructure.
- With over 200 investments, he says one recent week was chaos at four companies (about 2% of the portfolio).
- Typical crises: running out of money, Google making your product free, a well-funded competitor selling "hundred dollar bills for 50 bucks" (as Uber did and had done to it), and hardware or shipping disruptions with only six to twelve months of runway.
- He uses a rocket metaphor: many startups have no finished rocket, no jet fuel, or no astronauts, and have to fix that before orbit.

chunks.heading: Leading a founder through chaos: goal, plan, people
chunks.text:
- He sees his job, and any leader's, as convincing everyone that there is a plan and that sticking together and executing gives better odds. He likes the lighthouse-in-waves image for this.
- His framework with a founder: what does success look like (goal), what is the plan to get there, who do we need on the team to execute? Then tackle tactical issues (lawsuits, leases, competitors) without losing focus. He says many founders have neither a goal nor a plan.
- He uses calm-under-pressure metaphors: firefighters and ambulance crews triaging, samurai and Jedi (Qui-Gon meditating and conserving energy), Gladiator's "fight together as one", and Black Hawk Down. The lesson: block out the non-essential, work together, and focus.
- Background: he grew up in 1970s and 80s Brooklyn in his dad's bar, did martial arts and marathons, and worked on an ambulance, which he credits for his discipline and fighter mentality.

chunks.heading: Fight or fold: how he handles struggling companies
chunks.text:
- He admits his weakness is a never-say-die attitude and that it probably hurts returns. Many VCs calmly stop funding, give up the board seat and move on, which he calls more efficient and rational; he can't do it easily.
- He's seen founders figure something out at month 18 or month 30 and go "supernova", so he keeps fighting. Sometimes, though, the idea or the market is wrong: "you can't swim your way out of a tsunami".
- His approach: ask the founder what they want. "Do you want to keep fighting or do you want to close this chapter?" If they want to fight, he fights with them. If they want to shut down or sell for parts to Google or Facebook, take a salary for two or three years, rest, and then come back, he'll back them again.
- Focus matters: founders can't run three or four companies or projects at once and still produce an outlier.

chunks.heading: Founder traits, superpowers and filling gaps
chunks.text:
- He says no single founder archetype wins. Introvert or extrovert, sales, marketing, engineering or visionary, none is a common factor. What the successful ones share is that they are self-possessed, focused, care about the idea and don't give up.
- He asks founders to know their superpower and lean into it, because the rest can be hired. Examples he gives: Elon is an engineer and material scientist; Steve Jobs was a packager, brand builder and experience designer. His own superpower is talking.
- Check for introvert or extrovert energy: after an interview, do you have more or less energy? He comes out with more.
- Immigrant founders over-index: he cites the many Indian Americans running big companies and sees the work ethic and risk-taking of immigrant families as a driver. He thinks restricting immigration is "bonkers".

chunks.heading: Markets he wants founders to attack
chunks.text:
- Look at big broken markets where technology has had little impact and ask which hard problem you hope a founder takes on.
- Robotics outside factories, especially replacing manual labor. Cafe X (robotic coffee) is his example, seen as the first frontier because it was the only robotics company he found that ran fully without human intervention; he expects robot arms to add steps each year (a cold foam, a donut) and eventually move to pizza or burgers.
- Housing and robotics building houses, including modular housing (his investment Blokable).
- Self-paced or small-group online education, in a US system where students take on huge debt. Examples: income share agreements, Steezy (dance) and Brilliant (math), vertical sites that teach one thing very well.
- On public tech stocks: he's not a stock picker, but notes mega-caps got more resilient by acquiring new business lines (Facebook with WhatsApp, Instagram and Oculus; Google with Android and YouTube; Disney with Pixar, Marvel and Star Wars) and that companies now stay private longer, until years 10 to 13.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Calacanis talks with Anthony Pompliano about ICO-era fundraising, why too much early capital hurts startups, and how he evaluates founders today. He stresses constraint, real customer traction, smart investors over high valuations, and a power-law portfolio approach.

chunks.heading: Angel investing: picking founders, constraint, and portfolio math
chunks.text:
- Jason says founders who raise huge pre-product rounds lose their edge: "the whole team gets off their game, entitlement goes off the charts."
- His analogy: it is like putting a chef in a Costco, or giving an artist a mural-sized canvas and truckloads of paint. "Constraint makes great art."
- Money distances the core team from the customer. They end up arguing over chairs, the receptionist's desk, or laptop RAM instead of shipping.
- A founder who needs $100K-$250K to build something that can now be built in a weekend has "signaled to the market that you are a permission asker."
- Jason invests after a product exists and he can play with it. His examples are Superhuman (Raul had done a company before, so a decent seed of several million, under $10M) and serial founders like Mark Pincus.
- Serial founders tend to raise about $10M for 10%, a 5-10x premium over the average for good reason.
