- He tells founders to treat investors as "somewhere between a checkbook or ATM and a coach or a close friend who can give you candid feedback."
- Y Combinator requires a technologist on the team. Jason's view is that if you can't build, "what's your goddamn excuse?" Free resources exist (freeCodeCamp, Lambda School with income-share agreements).

chunks.heading: Vetting founders in a world where everyone knows the playbook
chunks.text:
- Jason has done a thousand-plus episodes, so founders now pitch him exactly what he has said he wants. Some fabricate personal-itch origin stories.
- One pitch cited a dog killed by a car as the reason for the startup.
- Since stories can be faked, he leans on traction: "The secret weapon is to just talk to the customers." Customers are hard to fake, and he knows the techniques people use to fake them.
- He sees friction reduction (incorporation, cap tables, terms sheets, we-work space in a day for about $1,000) as a net positive. It also means authenticity is what separates founders.
- He compares this to NBA vs golf/tennis/skiing: accessible sports (a ball and a hoop) become the world's sport.

chunks.heading: Smart money vs dumb money, and why VCs get the best deals
chunks.text:
- Jason says some advisors tell founders to avoid sophisticated investors in the first round, take "dumb money" (dentists, naive investors) at the highest price with no governance, and roll over later. He has seen this as a deliberate strategy.
- He says founders wind up regretting it. You want the smartest people on your team, and the incremental 20% valuation is not worth it.
- Skin in the game matters: a dentist with $50K in will shrug when it goes badly. An investor like Aileen Lee with $500K in "is going to go to war with you."
- Examples of sophisticated seed investors he names: Aileen Lee (Cowboy Ventures), and Hunter and Satya at Homebrew.
- On non-accredited and crypto raises, he proposes that regulators let projects register and raise capped amounts from retail (for example, a $1,000 cap per non-accredited investor). His logic is that losing $1,000 is not the "risk of ruin."
- His existing SPV constraints: 250 investors, up to $10M, accredited only, with the syndicate lead on the hook.

chunks.heading: ICOs, crypto, and why he calls them out
chunks.text:
- Jason says he was never against crypto, only the ICO scams. He stayed cautious because he had something to lose and did not want to go to jail.
- He says that if ICOs became legitimate and legal, "the syndicate comm will be an ICO token and we will go all in."
- He notes the pattern in ICO-funded companies: no product, no hundreds of employees, despite $10M-$250M raised. He cites a pitch where investors simply sent crypto to a wallet and filled in a spreadsheet, with no KYC.
- He gives credit to Ethereum as a real outcome, and thinks Huobi is real.
- On Bitcoin, his view has shifted over time because it has not been hacked or shut down. He previously gave it a "majority chance" of going to zero or being replaced by better tech.
- He now says he would consider putting about 1% of his net worth in Bitcoin as a hedge. He lost an early ten-Bitcoin stash to an exchange hack; his wife bought a batch at $300-$800.

chunks.heading: Platforms, antitrust, and competition
chunks.text:
- On Amazon Basics: Jason says the problem is not making a competing product. It becomes a problem when Amazon gives its own product preferential search placement or cuts the third-party seller's traffic.
- Using Amazon's public data to pick products is fine if the same data is available to everyone (reviews, search terms).
- On Google: he says Google claimed organic results didn't change while moving the first organic result down about 400 pixels beneath its own boxes (shopping, travel, stocks, local). "90 percent of the clicks are above the fold."
- On lower prices: he argues rampant competition is good for society, because $4 Amazon Basics cables beat $30 Apple ones and Airbnb stays in Kyoto at $50.
- On the Apple App Store: he calls 30% reasonable compared with retail, where the store took half. It drops to 15% in year two for subscriptions.
- His advice to startups: "pay the Vig to Apple." Playing nice may get you promoted or featured, and subscriptions through the store put you on paid ranking lists.
- He thinks the principle should be equal treatment: if Netflix and Spotify get a different deal, that is where it gets murky.
- Zuckerberg vs Bezos: he calls Zuckerberg more cutthroat, citing "just copy Snapchat" and says Bezos tends to think "day zero" from first principles.

chunks.heading: Positioning, enemies, and audience
chunks.text:
- Jason cites Basecamp/DHH's Hey launch as a textbook case of picking an enemy. He quotes the Rework chapter: "Having an enemy gives you a great story to tell customers... people get stoked by conflict."
- He praises Hey's screener feature (approve or reject first-time senders) as a killer feature, and says he told Superhuman it should have it.
- On media: he argues "he who holds the audience has all the power." Elon Musk can't be cancelled because he has a bigger audience than any media corporation.
- Companies increasingly build the audience first, then the products (Instagram moving into shopping and ads).
- Barstool: he wrote a March 2017 blog post saying it would be a billion-dollar company, after Chernin bought about 50%. He expected it to expand beyond sports.
- Dave Portnoy "is the best in the world" at entertaining and "understands who he is as a character."
- On Robinhood: he was an early investor. When the founders pitched him, he objected that millennials are commitment-phobic and retail investors had been wiped out twice, but liked "free" as the answer to how they would make money.
- He views retail speculation as a silver lining because young people learn finance and wallets instead of betting on sports.

chunks.heading: Portfolio construction, ownership, and confidence
chunks.text:
- Jason's advice to new angels: reach about 30 investments, invest only 5-10% of net worth, and expect that "the top two or three deals" make about 90% of the returns.
- He tells syndicate members he is "swinging for the fences, not singles and doubles." Most people need 50-100 investments to hit an outlier.
- His ownership has evolved:
  - Sequoia scout, ten years ago: $25K-$50K checks, well under 1%.
  - Fund one, about seven years ago: 1-3%.
  - Superhuman: about 2%.
  - Uber (via syndicate): he put in $378K and owned about 5% at the time.
  - Accelerator: takes 6%, with a target of 10-20% in winners and a board seat where possible.
- Example: Fitbod, a subscription app doing over $10M a year, where he would follow on from the syndicate and fund. He says such companies might get 10x-20x revenue multiples (anywhere from 5x to 30x).
- Uber: he sold some shares at $50-60B valuations and still holds. Calls the dip to $15-16 during the pandemic a "gut check" but he did not sell.
- Confidence: he says he is "at peace with never hitting an Uber again" because he can make a career from hits like Robinhood, Wealthfront, Trello, Thumbtack. "You don't need to be Michael Jordan, you could be Kobe or Shaq."
- Sequoia's edge, in his view: "they show up for [work]" and meet founders every day.

chunks.heading: Remote work and content as deal flow
chunks.text:
- Jason treats his podcast as deal flow. He originally insisted on in-person guests but moved remote.
- He says the quality of guests improved and the loss in conversation is maybe 5-10%.
- Remote tech check: This Week in Startups sends guests a mic and headset, and an ethernet dongle (about $100 and a producer's hour). They run a speed test and a screen share. Accelerator founders must use a wired Ethernet connection and a proper headset, with no AirPods.
- He says this lets them avoid most technical issues, with failures roughly one in 50 presentations.
- On dream deals: he said he would love to buy the Knicks.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason explains how he invests (high-volume small checks, "what if it works"), how Launch and Founder University filter thousands of applicants, and how he approaches new media formats and interviewing. He also covers the Uber/Robinhood bets, Elon's work ethic, the Twitter overstaffing lesson and AI-driven job displacement.

chunks.heading: Interviewing: listen, then double-click on the last answer
chunks.text:
Jason studied Mike Wallace (60 Minutes), Oprah, Howard Stern and Charlie Rose as interviewers. His main rule: "the next best question is embedded in the previous answer."

- Many interviewers are slaves to a question list. They get nervous as an answer ends and queue the next question instead of listening.
- His fix: take a breath, listen, then double-click on something in the answer. This keeps the interviewer in sync with the audience, who don't have the question list.
- He thinks about the audience throughout. He asks "can you unpack that?" and re-explains acronyms such as GDP. He argues slowing down can speed things up because it takes people back to first principles.
- A period is sometimes the right end to an answer. Not every answer needs a follow-up.
- On Charlie Rose: his rambling, multi-angle questions gave the guest several directions to go and time to think.
- On Oprah: she used silence and empathy to draw out emotion.

chunks.heading: Media and content playbook: treat every new medium as a sandbox
chunks.text:
Jason has started roughly seven media companies over three decades. His approach: "what if it works?"

- When a new medium appears, he assumes it will work and goes in early. If it fails, he says nobody remembers the failure.
- He started Silicon Valley Reporter in 1995 as a photocopied zine. He made photocopies at a copy shop and handed them out at a party. The back page said "Subscribe for 100 bucks to 10 issues a year", and hundreds of people tore it off and mailed him $100. That was tens of thousands of dollars in subscriptions, enough to quit working for others. It grew into a 300-page glossy that hit $12 million in revenue in its top year, built off his credit card.
- Weblog Inc.'s Engadget became the number one blog in the world. He credits Peter Rojas, Ryan Block and Brian Alvey.
- Mahalo used a wiki to build search-result pages ("SERPs") with images, answers and content. It reached $10 million in revenue. Google then de-indexed it, even though Google was its ad partner, and revenue fell to about $500k. He says this is what Perplexity does today.
- He says content creators are being hurt by AI. The New York Times, the music industry and Reddit need to hold the line and insist on being paid to be indexed.

chunks.heading: Where he sees media opportunity now
chunks.text:
- Video is the current currency. Short-form video that pulls viewers into long-form is one opportunity. He says he doesn't see anyone doing it well yet.
- Vertical micro-dramas (mini soap operas for phones) are big in Asia, mostly aimed at middle-aged and older women. Great content often starts as genre, so he expects "a Tarantino of vertical short storytelling" and an award-winning version.
- He expects new IP (a Star Wars-style franchise) to come from VR or AR rather than books or film.
- He cites KPop Demon Hunters. Singalong screenings drew people into theaters.
- He points to Dasha and Anna's Red Scare podcast, Brett Easton Ellis and Pete Pachal's Stay Tuned as successful paid or fringe podcasts. He pays for these. His point is that authentic creators who aren't "trying to do a podcast" resonate.
- He thinks the podcasting space is saturated, and he finds podcasters interviewing podcasters self-referential.
- He expects "isolation vs. experience" to be a big theme. Examples: live music, vinyl bars, and young people carrying flip phones or point-and-shoot cameras to be more present. He stacks phones at dinner.

chunks.heading: How All-In started and runs
chunks.text:
- Chamath called him during COVID, after leaving CNBC, and wanted a podcast. They added Sacks and Freeberg, who joined for the COVID discussion.
- The format is modeled on The McLaughlin Group. The moderator is "full contact", pushes guests to answer, and breaks chops, which Jason ties to his Brooklyn roots and the poker game.
- His mental model for guests is a four-quadrant grid:
  - Axis one is knowledge and lived experience.
  - Axis two is whether the person cares about others' opinions.
  - Low-knowledge people don't belong on a podcast. Knowledgeable people who are scared to speak aren't useful either. The show is built on knowledgeable truth-tellers with "FU money".
- Topic selection: each week every cast member submits URLs to a producer, Lisa. Topics are ranked by how many cast members want them. The top news story of the week goes first.
- He says the audience is millions a week and includes heads of state and CEOs. The show stays high-level and doesn't dumb things down.
- He doesn't think the pod got Trump elected. He cites two reasons for the loss. One was Biden's cognitive decline. The other was replacing him with a "DEI candidate" picked without a primary. He says Democrats should have run a six-week primary and that Harris avoided unscripted podcasts.
- His rules for following Trump: wait 72 hours before reacting, since many statements aren't repeated. When something is unpopular he course-corrects, so the 2025 tariff crash led to a walk-back.
- He doesn't think founders should copy Trump's marketing. His advice for startups is to talk about customers, celebrate wins, show and explain the product, make launch videos, and appear on podcasts.

chunks.heading: Angel investing and the Sequoia scout program
chunks.text:
- He began by advising friends on fundraising after selling Mahalo to AOL and raising from Sequoia. He introduced Sequoia to deals for Tesla, Zynga and Twitter, and Sequoia didn't do the early rounds.
- Roelof Botha asked him to be the first Sequoia scout. The program is the first of its kind. The terms:
  - Scouts invest their own deal flow with $25-50k checks.
  - Carry is split 50/50.
  - The goal was expanding Sequoia's surface area after missing Facebook and Twitter.
- Other early scouts included Brian Sugar, Seth Sternberg and Sam Altman. Altman invested in Stripe. Jason invested in Uber, DataStax and Thumbtack. He says it was Sequoia's highest-multiple fund, not the highest in dollars.
- His view of venture:
  - The middle stages (Series A to C) are overcrowded and overvalued, which makes those portfolios hard to run.
  - Opportunity sits in early stage, which needs many bets, and in late stage.
  - About 80% of seed companies go to zero, and he cites about 60% pulling through to a next round.
  - Many companies stall out at $500 million to $2 billion because later rounds overvalue them, and that is the time to take chips off the table.
  - Decacorns are very rare and most VCs never hit one.
- His two big wins: Uber and Robinhood, both invested pre-launch.
  - Uber was about $5 million pre / $4.5 million post, pitched at an angel forum he hosted.
  - Robinhood was about $15 million.
  - Both were two of his first 100 investments.
  - He now invests in about 100 companies a year and expects about 150 a year at Fund 5.
- "Third or fourth" in Uber: he told Travis he wanted to be first, Travis said he was third or fourth, and it became a meme (via VC Brags). He doesn't know the true order.
- Why he invested in Uber and Robinhood: he asks "what if it works?" at the idea stage.
  - Uber: one VC told him to sell software to cab companies. He says the cab companies were the problem and Uber took the economics from them.
  - Robinhood: the objection was millennials have no money. He said that if it works they will have 401(k)s, 529s and Roths.
  - Airbnb and Canva: both were laughed at and both "manifested a TAM".
- Angel forums: he hosted free, invite-only dinners with about 10 angels taking five pitches each, and he said people could commit on the spot. He started them to destroy the "Keiretsu Forum", which charged founders $5,000 to pitch. His rule is "don't pay to pitch your startup to investors."
- Tesla: he was friends with Elon, whose cash was nearly out. Jason wired nothing but handwritten checks for two Model S cars at $50k each. He got reservation #1 after noting "you're the first person to buy it". He also owns Roadster #16.

chunks.heading: Launch and Founder University
chunks.text:
- The funnel: about 20,000 applications a year, or 400-500 a week. The team (22 people, 12 on investing) meets the top 100. They invest in roughly 1 in 150-200.
- Half the applicants were pre-incorporation, so they started Founder University.
  - It is a 12-week course with a speaker plus a pod of 20 companies.
  - About 350 teams were in the latest cohort and about 30 get funded.
  - Terms: $25k at a $1 million valuation, plus the right to follow on with $100-250k in the next two rounds.
  - He says about 40-50% mainly want the $25k to incorporate, and about 150 checks have been written.
- Results: about 60% of companies raise a further round at a higher valuation within a year. He doesn't want that rate above 50-60%, because the aim is to bet on crazy ideas.
- Fund economics: $25k checks are an experimental budget. A loss of $2.5-5 million across 100-200 deals, in a roughly $45 million fund, is fine. Winners are built up to about 7-10% ownership.
- Competing programs: apply to YC, Techstars, Antler, Neo and Launch together. Acceptance rates are under 1%. He thinks the top 10% are all roughly equal and the selection at 1% is imperfect. Some A16Z Speedrun companies came through Launch first.
- Founder feedback loop: he asks every applicant to rate the process. He reads every score of 6 or below.
  - The most common complaint was "you didn't understand what we pitched."
  - His fix is for callers to repeat back the founder's vision before moving on. Ratings improved.
- Advice for founders: fundraising is a volume game. You need two or three yeses from about 100 meetings, so talk to low hundreds before a Series A. Don't give up after 20.
  - Traction matters. A team with $300k in revenue beats three teams with none.
  - Don't set a sky-high valuation. Someone with a million in revenue growing 50% a year can win the investor over.
- VCs are "terrified human beings" making bets on incomplete information, "like poker".

chunks.heading: AI and jobs
chunks.text:
- He thinks AI could reduce headcount at the large tech companies by 2030 while earnings grow.
- Twitter after Elon: about 85% of staff were removed and the product shipped faster. He called the old setup "the greatest heist in the history of business". He gave an example of lunches costing $400 each.
- He sees a 90% chance this displacement is faster than past ones, over 4-10 years rather than 40.
- His advice to young people: "nobody's coming for you. Help is not on the way." Find two or three talented friends, learn all the skills and start a company.
- He is an investor in Athena (assistants). He pays about $3,000 a month per assistant, or $72k a year for two, with 80 hours of weekly coverage. He argues outsourcing beats hiring one assistant who leaves within 6-18 months.

chunks.heading: Elon Musk and personal habits
chunks.text:
- Elon's underrated strengths: he is a real engineer, and he is one of perhaps three or four people who understand factories as well as he does.
- His work ethic: at Twitter he took meetings until 1:30 or 2am with an NFL meeting at 10am the next day. Jason calls it "preternatural".
- GLP-1s: he gained two pounds a year for 20 years. He went from 213 lbs to 170 lbs at 5'8½". He says he wasn't open about it at first because it was experimental. Side effects he had: indigestion, and vomiting if he ate a lot of pizza or sushi after a dose. A benefit: less "food noise". He is now a paid spokesperson for Ro, with no discount code.
- "Comparison is the thief of joy." He says to stop comparing yourself to others, since there is always someone richer or more successful.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Calacanis and the Launch team walk through building a startup team: who to hire first, in-house versus outsourced work, hiring outreach, org structure, firing, and compensation. Jason's main points: keep engineering in-house, hire missionaries, explain the why behind goals, fire kindly but firmly, and let candidates choose cash or equity.

chunks.heading: Hiring a founding team: co-founders, vesting and first hires
chunks.text:
- Jason says a founding team should have complementary skills. At least one co-founder should be technical, since "being an engineer is not a skill you can just learn overnight". Another should cover sales, marketing or operations.
- Founders almost never all stay through an IPO, and often not even through seed and Series A. So he has founders vest their equity, typically a one or two year cliff with a four year vest.
- Example: three co-founders hold 20% each, 10% is in the option pool and 30% is with investors. If one leaves after a year, they keep only 25% of their 20% (5%). The unvested 15% is retired, and everyone else's share rises proportionally. A board can also steer some of it back to the founders who stepped up.
- Typical founding teams are two founders, sometimes up to five. Splits are common but not always equal. Someone who joins in year two may get a smaller share. A founder who puts in $500K of seed money may hold 20% as a founder plus about 10% as an investor, usually as preferred shares.
- Jason's rule of thumb: until about 10 employees, hire generalists. One person does five jobs, then five people do five jobs, then five people each do one job, and that is a department. Early staff must be hardworking, tenacious and need little management.
- After roughly 10 employees, hire where you personally spend 30-50% of your time and can hand it off. There is no fixed formula for who is hire 11.
- Experience level by stage: around Series A, 2-5 years; around Series B, 8-10 years. Senior people often wait for product-market fit and escape velocity (roughly 2 years of runway and $2M+ in revenue, with a known investor) before joining.
- Jason wants "missionaries not mercenaries".

chunks.heading: Remote vs office, and in-house vs outsourced
chunks.text:
- Remote suits solitary work such as writing and coding, if people can manage their time. Meeting-heavy work (investing, product conception, sales culture) works better in one room.
- Pick one model, all remote or all in the office. A few remote people on an in-office team become second-class citizens.
- Remote developers should do quarterly off-sites, about one week every quarter, in person.
- Geography limits the talent pool, and Jason notes many people no longer want to live in San Francisco.
- He tells founders to keep long-term vision, strategy and customer feedback in-house, especially before product-market fit. Enterprise sales and client success should stay in-house.
- Outsource repeatable, administrative work: accounting and taxes, payroll, HR (via a PEO), office space (WeWork). He notes four of the classic first ten hires (office manager, accountant, HR, receptionist/sysadmin) no longer exist as internal roles.
- He advises against dev shops. "You don't accrue the knowledge into the company", and shops want "the least amount of work possible for the highest amount of pay". In-house developers give a much faster cadence.
- A remote developer team on your payroll, where you are their only customer, is different from a shop. Prefer SaaS services over single contractors for redundancy.
- Tools named: Zendesk, Rippling, Gusto, Zenefits, TriNet, LinkedIn Talent Solutions, Breezy HR (run hiring like a sales pipeline), Comparably (salary benchmarks).

chunks.heading: Running a hiring process
chunks.text:
- Keep a hiring plan about six months ahead, because it takes about six months for a hire to settle into a role.
- Keep the team at about 80% capacity, not 100-110%, so people don't burn out and there is room for special projects. He compares people to CPUs.
- Be proactive: reach out to about five candidates a day instead of posting a job and forgetting it.
- Candidates should hear back within a day or two. Not replying is "bad karma" and bad for the brand. Keep the job board current.
- Founders should write job descriptions themselves, with personality and a mission. He also blogs and posts on social media about what he is looking for.
- Be opportunistic: if talent shows up, create a role. That is how launch hired Sam.
- Ask your network "do you know anyone?" when reaching out. It doubles as a soft pitch to the person.
- Start hiring for diversity and inclusion early, and be intentional about it.

chunks.heading: Structure, ownership and explaining the "why"
chunks.text:
- Give each early employee 3-5 things they own and report on. Each employee reports to exactly one person. With multiple founders, split the reporting lines to avoid "permission shopping" (asking another founder for a different answer).
- Draw an org chart and update it as structure changes. Example: a portfolio company moved to "sales pods" of an SDR, an account executive and a customer success person.
- Always explain the outcome and the reason behind it. Example: he wants 50 companies in the accelerator's final interviews, to accept only 7. That way, he says, "investors coming get addicted to our deal flow", and the batch has no duds.
- He argues younger employees want to know why. Managers must "take the time to explain why this is important" or lose purpose-driven Millennial and Gen Z talent.
- He says more people want part-time or freelance work, and part-time job postings attract more applicants than full-time ones.
- He prefers a small team (about 15 people) because you can know everyone, and he notes that founders will copy the seriousness you set.

chunks.heading: Performance, firing and communication
chunks.text:
- Firing should never be a surprise. Sequence: written note about slipping performance, then a verbal conversation, then a performance improvement plan (PIP). Jason says about 80% of PIPs don't work out, so a PIP is effectively a final warning.
- Judge the work, not the person. High performers can bend rules a bit (for example arriving late), but low performance plus lateness means the person is out.
- Document everything. Follow up verbal talks by email. This protects the company on unemployment claims and legal issues.
- Trust your gut and fire fast. "If there is any doubt, there is no doubt." Founders are good at picking people but cowards at cutting them.
- Be kind, firm and unemotional. Jason suggests giving 1-2 weeks of severance even without a formal policy, because "enemies accumulate" and Glassdoor will punish a bad exit. He once laid off 50 people at once.
- Use plain language ("you are being fired", not "let go"). No debate, and you don't have to give a reason in an at-will state, though he says to take legal advice when it's sticky.
- Defer an exit interview if they push back. The manager does the firing, and the team is told afterward directly, without gossip.
- Example of firing immediately: a sales hire was moonlighting for a customer and emailing the company's list from his work email.
- He is cautious about references and offers to be a positive reference for people who didn't work out.

chunks.heading: Compensation and equity
chunks.text:
- Make comp "transparent, fair and generous" where possible, without endless negotiation. Underpaying makes people keep a foot out the door.
- Startups shouldn't hire people seeking maximum compensation. Those people should go to Facebook or Google. Startup equity has a "70-80% chance of zero".
- Promise a pay review at the next round. Example: seed-stage $5,000/month draws can move to about $100K after a $3M seed, around a 10% raise when the next round closes.
- Salaries vary hugely by city. Miami salaries can be a third to half of San Francisco's, and Toronto about 25% less. Yelp moved support jobs out of the East Bay for this reason.
- Non-cash perks: remote days, team lunches, a company retreat (launch's is the Whitsundays, about 1% of annual budget), birthdays off, and mission alignment.
- Offer an either-or menu such as $80K + 1% vs $90K + 0.5% vs $100K + 0.2% so people choose their own cash-equity mix.
- ESOPs are typically 10-16%. A 409A valuation comes first. Common is worth less than preferred. Standard vesting is a one year cliff with a four year vest.
- Jason would prefer back-weighted vesting over 5 years, with about half in the first three years and half in the last two.
- He wants longer exercise windows (30, 60 or 90 days is too short). His idea: after three years, a 10-year window, or window length equal to double the years worked. He recalls employees at Mahalo spending real money to exercise and says he feels guilty about it.

chunks.heading: Culture and boundaries
chunks.text:
- Don't hire only people you'd have a drink with, and keep professional distance from reports because you may have to fire them.
- He says workplace dating is no longer the norm; people have dating apps. Know the chain-of-command rules, and report and separate reporting lines if a relationship exists.
- He says serious founders model the seriousness they want. Company parties and trips to Vegas "do not end well", and are a bad look in 2019.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Calacanis, with Launch's Jason Demant and Ashley Whitehurst, walks through whether to fundraise at all, angels vs VCs vs syndicates, diligence pitfalls, and the metrics investors want. He frames VC money as jet fuel for rare, venture-scale businesses, and fundraising as a full-time sales funnel.

chunks.heading: Whether to raise money at all
chunks.text:
- Jason's co-hosts and he open by saying most companies should not raise venture money. Most businesses are self-funded "lifestyle" businesses, and that is fine.
- The test is whether the company is venture-scale. Example given: a $5M-revenue business at 20% margin ($1M/year) growing 10% a year reaches maybe $12-15M revenue in 10 years. That is a $20-30M company, which would return a VC about 3x. VCs want 20, 30, 40 or 50x; angels want 100x.
- Jason's definition of venture-scale in 2019: roughly $100M in revenue with strong margins (30-50% gross margin, software often 80-90%), reached in about 5 to 7 years. Funds run about 10 years, so exits are expected in 5 to 8 years, 10 to 12 at the outside.
- He warns against founder projections like $300K in 2019 growing to $5M in 2024. That is 10x and still not what VCs need.

chunks.heading: Friends and family rounds
chunks.text:
- Raising from friends and family can work (examples he cites: Zuckerberg's parents, Gates's parents), but founders must be blunt that the money will probably be lost. Jason says to tell them they will most likely lose it, because he and co-hosts see roughly 7 or 8 of 10 early investments lose everything.
- He argues founders should still ask. If you skip them and build a giant company, they will be angry you never offered the chance.
- Paper everything. Use a SAFE (simple agreement for future equity): the money later converts to shares when a priced round happens. A convertible note is similar but is debt with interest and can run 15-20 pages, too heavy for a first-time founder or a relative to read.
- Have legal documents ready before approaching angels or an accelerator (Launch, Techstars, Y Combinator). Messy paperwork gives investors an easy reason to pass.

chunks.heading: What diligence catches (and how to avoid it)
chunks.text:
Items checked: cap table, bank statements, customer references, org structure.
- Founders with no vesting on their own shares.
- Early investors undocumented: who, when, note or SAFE, valuation cap, interest.
- Personal expenses mixed into company accounts (e.g., rent on an apartment used as an office with no allocation).
- A P&L with no cost of goods sold, or expenses swinging from $100K one month to $3K for the next three, or payroll booked as non-payroll expense.
- A $100K bank deposit with no paperwork is a red flag, since the person could later claim 20% equity while the founder says it was a loan.
- Jason's rule: if you are going to do something, do it properly. Learn the accounting software and spend an hour or two in it.

chunks.heading: Angels vs VCs vs seed funds vs syndicates
chunks.text:
- By size: under about $1M tends to be angels; above $1M is institutional capital.
- Angels decide faster (no team), but usually have full-time jobs and less time to help. VCs are usually more helpful.
- Minimum check sizes exist to keep the cap table manageable and avoid chasing many signatures later. Common minimums are $25K to $50K, higher for bigger rounds.
- Seed funds ($10M-$100M) usually have 2 to 3 partners and can move faster, but in practice diligence and decision time look much like VCs. Hunter and Satya at Homebrew are cited as a fast two-partner example.
- Syndicate (Jason's, run with Ashley): 250 accredited investors, median about 80 participating per deal, checks roughly $100K to $2.4M. The founder gets one cap table line and needs one signature, from the syndicate lead. Founders send a deal memo with a webinar link; interested investors can contact the founder directly. After closing, the founder should email all members a welcome note and ask for help (hiring, intros).
- Jason's surprise: syndicate members who put in $25K or $50K sometimes lead the next round. His first syndicate deal was Calm.com about five years earlier at a $5M valuation, now reported at a $1B valuation. He tells accredited investors a small syndicate check can be followed by add-ons of "a zero or two" later.

chunks.heading: Choosing target investors
chunks.text:
- Read the portfolio. Check for competitors, and flip it: if they funded you first and then a rival asked to invest, would you be comfortable? If not, exclude them.
- Related-category investors are good targets (e.g., fitness investments for a meditation app).
- You will be partnered for years, so you should like the person.

chunks.heading: Accelerators
chunks.text:
- Value: fundraising help and a peer network. By week 12 founders become close friends and go through the founder rollercoaster together.
- Skeptical cases: serial founders may not need one. Doing three or four accelerators can signal you could not raise a real round. He compares it to a 40-year-old with four graduate degrees.
- Check who runs it, their track record and their alumni.
- To evaluate a program, ask alumni three or four different ways what they got and whether they would do it again, to get past confirmation bias. He uses the owner who insists their Fisker beats a Tesla as the analogy.
- Jason's claim: accelerator companies get about two meetings out of every three intros pursued, because of intro quality. Without that, expect 5-10% intro-to-meeting conversion. If you convert under 10%, you need better intros.

chunks.heading: Metrics VCs look at
chunks.text:
- Revenue growth first. Typical target is 10-20% month over month, nearer 20% being strong. Example: $10K in January, $12K in February, then 20% on $12K ($2,400) for $14.4K in March.
- Marketplaces: both sides, e.g. Airbnb adding about 20 hosts a month, plus how demand was acquired. Liquidity matters.
- Consumer apps: DAU, retention, cohort analysis (January signups still using the product in March).
- SaaS: churn and negative churn. Example of 20% monthly churn: you must replace the base roughly every 5 months. Negative churn means existing customers spend more (e.g., a sales tool team of 10 adds a team of 5).
- Credit to Eric Ries (making startups a science) and SaaStr's Jason Lemkin (SaaS metrics as a science).
- Vanity metrics he does not value: social followers, blog readers, press (Forbes lists), site traffic, unless tied to revenue.
- Do not misrepresent. Putting a former employer's logo (such as Apple) on the team slide when you were retail staff, or calling TEDx Albuquerque "TED", loses credibility. It is "not fraud but twisting the truth," and a slippery slope.
- Pre-revenue companies (deep tech, AI) are judged on the founder: domain expertise, repeat founders help, big-name investors help, and the ability to explain it at a fifth-grade reading level.
- Pre-revenue consumer benchmarks as Jason sees them in 2019: about 10M monthly active users for a Series A; 10-20% of that for a seed round, i.e. about 1M MAU or roughly 100K daily users.

chunks.heading: Venture capital reality
chunks.text:
- Venture money is "jet fuel," not coal. Taking it means you are signing up for unnatural, inorganic growth for about 10 years.
- Ashley's cautions he agrees with: VCs pick their target ownership percentage (10-20%) and that determines valuation, and they may eventually push to replace the CEO.
- Jason: they give you millions to build, not to earn interest. He recalls once putting $10M+ into bonds and earning about $600K in interest, which covered about a third of monthly expenses, and calls that unusual.
- Math to know before negotiating: if investors take 20% and you want a $10-20M valuation, you can quickly work out the raise ($2-4M). Terms should be standard.
- Geography: this is Silicon Valley advice; he guesses valuations outside run roughly one-half to two-thirds, China possibly higher with personal guarantees, Europe about half.

chunks.heading: Running the process
chunks.text:
- Meetings: say yes selectively. They can distract you if you are not raising, and a VC may only be gathering data on your category (e.g., looking at Skimm and Axios when they email Inside). Sharing metrics is a choice. Buffer is an example of a company that publishes everything, but Jason generally protects metrics because a VC may fund your competitor. He answers with public information, says some things are the "secret sauce," or gives vague counter-answers. He also ignores requests from reporters or junior analysts, and sometimes uses a copy-paste reply such as "I don't speak on behalf of my companies."
- Typical funnel: about 150 qualified targets (not a Crunchbase dump), about 100-125 intros, about 75 meetings, about 10 diligence processes, and typically 3 investors in the round. That is roughly 1-2% of targets. Raising is a full-time job; delegate the day-to-day.
- Start with top-tier firms (Silicon Valley or leading hubs) and aim for the top 10%. Lower tiers can be less professional and overpromise.
- Raise enough for at least 18 months so you do not have to raise again, and have plan B and plan C.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason answers Reddit/Quora founder questions with his CMO. He covers low-cost offline marketing (meetups, street teams, podcasts), why unique ideas matter less than execution, keeping early momentum by studying feature usage data, and testing willingness to pay before burning five years on a startup.

chunks.heading: Low-cost marketing beyond social media and Google Ads
chunks.text:
- Jason's core point: social and search ads get very expensive in some verticals. Around the 2015 to 2017 app boom, app installs cost $50 or more, or $1 to $10 per click.
- Real-world meetups and events are a cheaper way to acquire users. His example is a dating app: have the whole team invite single people to a cocktail hour, buy each a free drink (about $3), and ask them to install the app and give feedback. That works out to roughly $3 per install, or less.
- Other offline tactics he lists:
  - Door-hanger flyers, as for a Nextdoor-style app.
  - Yelp Elite style meetups.
  - Direct mail postcards, with the CMO citing a service called Postie.
  - Vehicle wraps. He is an investor in Wrapify, which went through his accelerator, and says it is hard to scale but worth testing.
  - Local sponsorships. He cites Squarespace on the Knicks, and notes you can test it by comparing New York signups to markets where you didn't advertise.
  - Small podcast sponsorships, which he says you can negotiate hard on.
- Content marketing as a lead channel: if you sell a $5,000-per-year product, a podcast at $500 per episode only needs one client per ten episodes to pay off, even with 1,000 listeners, "if it's the right thousand people."
- Street teams: take a five-person team to a busy spot like Fisherman's Wharf and ask people to install the app and give feedback for a $5 Starbucks card. This gives installs plus product feedback. He notes that founders are often scared to get feedback, and he likes forcing it.
- He favors high-engagement tactics that create "super fans," because each super fan tends to bring one or two more users.
- Rule: test, test, test, then run another set of tests.
- Platform mastery: his CMO says basic proficiency on a platform like Instagram or LinkedIn takes a couple of weeks and expert level takes about a month and a half to two months. Jason's hiring advice is to stop spending 3 to 6 months searching for a social media expert. Find someone with aptitude and attitude and train them for about six weeks.

chunks.heading: Protecting a startup idea
chunks.text:
- Jason's main protection is silence: don't tell people about the idea before you execute. He calls broadcasting it a "rookie mistake."
- He pays close attention to the question's wording: it asks how to protect the idea, not the business.
- VCs stealing ideas: he knows of roughly two accusations in venture history, Cosmo vs. UrbanFetch being one. He argues VCs "do not want to work hard" and won't run with your idea.
- The real risk is on the margins. If a VC has a competing portfolio company, they may forward public information such as a page on your site, so don't expect public information to stay protected.
- He says to avoid meeting a VC who already backs a competitor, since you may hand them a roadmap for their company.
- Patents are "kind of meaningless in our industry except on the edges." Copyright, trademark and service marks exist but are secondary.
- Analogy: you don't go on Letterman to talk about an album coming in six months. Talk about what you have done, not what you plan to do.
- Credibility: he says investors split people into talkers and doers, and he wants founders to be in the second group. "Put your head down, shut up, get some goddamn skills, build the product."
- If you tweet or blog your idea and someone else builds it, "you really don't have a basis to complain."

chunks.heading: Where the next Google comes from, and accelerators
chunks.text:
- Peter Thiel is a contrarian who likes the unpopular side, and Jason treats the "next Google won't come from Silicon Valley" line as provocation meant to make you think.
- His view: $100 billion companies have only come from the US and China. He expects Airbnb, Lyft, Uber and Palantir to become $100B "super unicorns" and says future ones will likely come from China and the US because of market size.
- China argument: its growing middle class (he puts it in the low hundreds of millions, on track to exceed the US population) gives native-language companies a shot at trillion-dollar valuations. He says Google is number one in search in every country except China, Taiwan, Russia and Korea.
- Accelerators: Y Combinator started in 2005, and unicorns from accelerators take about 10 years to emerge, citing Dropbox, Reddit, Airbnb, and SendGrid from Techstars.
- Rarity framing: a unicorn needs about $100M in revenue and a "decacorn" over $1B in revenue. Netflix has over 100 million paying customers, so millions of paying customers is possible but not easy.
- Serial entrepreneurs like Evan Williams generally skip accelerators because they can self-fund.

chunks.heading: Keeping momentum for a niche social app
chunks.text:
- A niche gives you a natural audience, and the narrower the niche the easier it is to identify and reach the people in it.
- His examples: a women-only professional network (Sophia Amoroso's Girlboss network), and a network for women in finance on Wall Street, where there might be 100,000 people who mostly know each other and are on LinkedIn.
- Expand in stages, like Facebook (Harvard, then the Ivy League, then other colleges, then everyone).
- Use data, not opinion: plot features on two axes, how often each is used (daily, weekly, monthly, yearly) vs. what percentage of users use it. Put about 90% of attention on the top one or two features.
- Instagram example: the posting experience and the feed get most of the polish. He notes his birthday post got about 600 likes vs. 100 to 200 for a typical brisket post, which hints at why birthday content might be prioritized in an algorithmic feed.
- Re-engagement: emails and notifications that pull people back, such as missed tweets on Twitter, YouTube recommendations, or product update emails like those from Superhuman's CEO.
- Expand beyond the niche, but "don't do that too quick."

chunks.heading: Non-technical founders and focus
chunks.text:
- He says you don't need tech skills to found a tech company, but you do need tech knowledge and an understanding of what the technology can do. He points to Airbnb's designer founder, and says Gates and Jobs didn't write their core code themselves.
- Still, a technical co-founder is strongly preferred. Without one, you run out of runway: if you pay a dev team $10K to $15K a month, work stops when the money does. A technical co-founder "will never have to stop writing code."
- His example: at Weblogs Inc., Brian Alvey built the platform while Jason landed Peter Rojas and Mark Cuban. Jason sketched a 4x4 grid of 16 blogs at the bottom of every page as an SEO hack, Brian shipped it in 48 hours, and it gave a 15% traffic advantage.
- Founder's job: collect ideas from the team, prioritize them, and put the rest on a "not right now" list to avoid shiny object syndrome.
- Rule: understand what value users get from your product and "double down on that until it stops working."
- Focus: when a founder gets 300 people who love the product, they often start a podcast, event or book instead of growing 300 to 3,000 to 30,000.
- Compounding: small daily progress beats silver bullets. 1% a day compounds, and 3 to 7% weekly or 30% monthly is huge.
- Improve many things a bit instead of one thing 2x. Five parts of the show each made 25% better double the overall result.

chunks.heading: Transparency about funding, and getting fired
chunks.text:
- A question about being fired after 5 weeks for asking about funding: Jason notes the person was an employee, not a founder.
- He thinks founders should share the basics of funding with the team, because it gives employees certainty. He runs the business with 18 months of runway in the bank and tells people so.
- A reasonable middle path when fundraising is ongoing: "we're opportunistically looking at different funding scenarios," which avoids distracting staff or signaling weakness.
- He uses funding as a recruiting advantage, since rivals will tell candidates a startup is running out of cash. If the business is shaky and you brush off questions, staff will start questioning things.
- Personal lesson: he was fired from a computer store (Wolf Computers) for being late once or twice, despite selling many printers. The company went out of business six weeks later. His takeaway: don't give an easy excuse, and overperform so a single mistake isn't decisive.

chunks.heading: What entrepreneurs miss, and unique ideas
chunks.text:
- Entrepreneur mistakes he cites:
  - Overestimating the downside: you can go back to a job if it fails, so just start.
  - Lack of focus.
  - Underestimating small daily gains.
- Market creation: great companies often induce new demand rather than just competing. Airbnb brought in people who couldn't afford $150-a-night Paris hotels at about $50 a night, and Uber and Lyft got people to go out who would have stayed home.
- For his Jason syndicate project, he says the opportunity is the roughly 14 million of ~15 million US accredited investors who have never made an angel investment, not the 1 million who already have.
- You don't need a unique idea. YouTube was reportedly the 500th video site, but it differed in execution: free hosting, ad revenue share, plus falling bandwidth and storage costs. Facebook copied Friendster's look but kept its servers up, and Instagram Stories copied Snapchat.
- Ask "why now": reputation systems (Yelp, Amazon reviews) made Airbnb possible, and a pre-smartphone text-based taxi service never took off.
- Ways to find a new angle: new technology (GPS, phone cameras, AR/VR) and new business models (SaaS subscriptions like Slack versus $50K-a-server enterprise software; a $50/year meditation app vs. a $5,000 transcendental meditation course).

chunks.heading: Raising kids as entrepreneurs, and when to quit
chunks.text:
- Kids: he talks to his 8-year-old daughter about business using real terms (inventory, margin, rent) and takes her to his incubator. His own training: working every job in his dad's bar, including counting the money.
- Ideas for older kids: after-school jobs, entrepreneur clubs, and small projects like the laser-cut earrings idea. He also wants to buy a candy store or ice cream shop for kids to run, and recommends entrepreneurial movies such as The Founder and autobiographies.
- Reason: jobs change fast, and even big-company employees are expected to be entrepreneurial.
- Running out of money after 5 years: a day job or part-time work is fine to pay the bills. He says if it hasn't worked in five years it likely won't, unless you have data or intuition that year six is the breakout.
- Test the business: email your free users saying you plan to shut down or will charge $1,000 a year to keep it going, with options of yes, maybe or no. Anyone who isn't a "yes" tells you what you need to know. He also suggests asking users to vote on a maintenance window to see if anyone engages.
- Equity crowdfunding: unlikely to work, because investors will ask why a five-year-old product has no business model.
- Pricing: don't be afraid to charge. Creatives pay $100K a year for school, so a $25 a month app for them is reasonable, and early charging gives you data.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In this #AskJason call-in, Jason advises founders on which metrics investors care about, how to win enterprise customers bottom-up, and whether to raise venture money. His biggest lesson from 2018: after early traction, narrow focus and scale what works rather than adding new products.

chunks.heading: Choosing a metric when you're early: show you know the vanity metrics, then lead with raw growth
chunks.text:
- For an early consumer product, Jason says investors want to hear retention, viral coefficient and user personas, but only as proof the founder is competent.
- Viral coefficient: every customer who brings in 1 new customer is a coefficient of 1. Anything above that (his example: 1.5 to 1.7) compounds, because each new cohort brings in more people.
- Once you show you understand those metrics, savvy investors "check, check, check" and move straight to "the meat and potatoes": is it growing or not?
- He says that about ten years earlier, founders were obsessed with building the product. After Facebook, Uber and Airbnb grew into unicorns so quickly, the focus became "can you be a growth founder?"
- Investors assume you can build a great product and set up measurement tools. In 2019 he calls building a product "not a big deal" and says tracking metrics is not a big deal either, though it still separates you from half of founders.
- Investors want to know whether the founders are dogged and resourceful, whether they have customer acquisition channels, and whether they can grow the product.

chunks.heading: Pitching a new social network in its second decade
chunks.text:
- Jason says a founder entering social networking should expect investors to be burnt out on the space, to have lost money in it, or to think it is insurmountable to beat Facebook. He does not hold that view himself and thinks it is changing as Facebook runs into trouble.
- Investors will also ask how the network gets monetized. The easy answer is advertising, but that needs "tremendous scale".
- He warns against pitching a free, no-ads product that will make money from photo books. Photo books have been tried many times and tend to be a small opportunity, "low millions of dollars". He says that pitch may signal that you are "kind of delusional".
- He says it is "hard enough to build an at scale social network let alone trying to build a new business model". A new business model is "possible, it's just not probable".
- If you want to monetize in a new way, you need "a really compelling case" that either advertising works or that people will pay.
- He gives a similar example for the family-network space: Life360, whose killer feature is finding family members on a map.

chunks.heading: What to tell investors about acquisition when you don't have a growth channel yet
chunks.text:
- Pitch that you have no leaky bucket: people want the product, the target persona engages deeply, and you improve the product 2-3% every fortnight (maybe 5-10% a month).
- If the product doesn't churn, the next question is how to acquire customers, and that is where to focus your energy.
- Real-world options he lists: meetups, profitable content marketing, and a pitch to the local press.
- His script for investors: "we know we don't have a leaky bucket, we have a product people love. Here are the seven experiments we're running this quarter, next quarter we're going to run these seven experiments, and then we're going to take the learning from those 14 experiments, whichever three do the best we're going to triple down on them."
- Be honest that you don't yet know the growth technique. Have a list of the ten things everybody knows work, plus a handful of others to try.
- This shows you understand Lean Startup methodology, that there is no silver bullet, and that you are hard-working and humble. He says investors "love to engage" in that conversation.
- He also calls out personas as useful for customer acquisition and design: a stay-at-home parent, a single parent splitting custody days, and urban versus suburban versus rural families all need different targeting.

chunks.heading: Enterprise AI for franchises: sell to the end user first, not the chain
chunks.text:
- The case: a startup selling AI drive-through ordering to restaurant franchises, with two buyers. The chain's COO signs bigger contracts covering multiple regions or a whole country. Individual franchisees with 2-3 stores (or sometimes 25-50) close faster because they have autonomy.
- The caller had closed no chain-level deals yet. Jason's advice is to go after the short sales cycle and the more modest reward first.
- Why:
  - Easier sale, and a chain deal "might be a year" for a startup that doesn't have that time.
  - Feedback quality. Frontline operators are like "soldiers on the front lines" who hold the weapon. They will quickly tell you if the product is too expensive or too hard to use, and they will churn if it sucks. That feedback lets you refine the product.
  - Word of mouth. Franchisees talk to each other at conventions, on message boards and over dinner, so one operator tells another.
- His examples: Slack, Yammer and Asana did not try to win the CTO first. They won a group of developers or salespeople, who signed up on a corporate card at $10-25 per person per month and built consensus inside the company.
- When frontline staff tell the manager the tool is helping them win, the manager gives them what they want.
- He contrasts this with 25 years earlier, when a CTO or CEO would go golfing with a Lotus Notes or Oracle rep, cut a deal, and force the software on everyone, with implementations taking years. Now "they take out their credit card, they try it, if it sucks they unsubscribe".
- The goal in years 1-2 is to make the product so indispensable that when you double the price, customers say "I have no other choice". It should save people time or make them money.

chunks.heading: Raise venture money or stay bootstrapped: the tradeoffs Jason lays out
chunks.text:
- The case: a content-marketing marketplace that was profitable from day one. Roughly $25K of monthly recurring revenue, a partner, one full-time-equivalent and freelance writers, with investors interested.
- The model as described to Jason: customers pay a $500/month minimum for blog posts, up to $3,500 on a higher plan. The company pays writers $150-225 per post, for roughly 40% writer cost and 60% margin. Billing is automatic monthly retainers, so there are no invoices to chase.
- Jason's math on raising: pick an 18-month view, divide the raise by 18, and that is your monthly burn. A $450K raise is about $25K a month; $900K is about $50K a month. You work for about nine months, then look up to see how close you are to the next round's milestones. Months 10-12 become 3-4 months on the road raising, or you cut toward profitability if the market or the business turns.
- The cost: you add a third constituent. Today you manage your team and your customers; after raising, you also manage investors, which he estimates at about 20% of your time.
- Fast track warning: once you are on it, "it's very hard to get off". Investors want to return 25x, 50x, 100x their money. They do not want slow or methodical growth. They are "looking for their Uber, their Airbnb, their Google, their Facebook". If you take the money, you have to be willing to triple or quadruple revenue year over year for a couple of years until you reach $10M.
- His case for going for it: investors knocking is a signal the business could scale, like being recruited to the NBA (or at least the G League) instead of playing at the YMCA. "Nobody says at the end of their life 'I'm glad I stayed at the YMCA'."
- He compares the human-heavy model to early Uber and Airbnb, which many investors passed on because of drivers and hosts. The people-intensive work was arduous, but the reward was a billion-dollar business.
- The alternative: a lifestyle business throwing off $500K a year is a great business, and he would not judge anyone for choosing it. The worst case for the venture route is a blowup in two years, then you build the next lifestyle business.
- He tells the founder not to be precious about the business: he is young and will have more ideas.

chunks.heading: Pricing tiers: use a decoy "whale" plan
chunks.text:
- Jason liked a three-tier layout ("easy peasy" at $500, "fast and furious" at $3,500) and recommends adding a $10,000 enterprise tier.
- Reasoning: almost nobody takes the low tier, and people get steered to the middle. The top tier is a "whale" that may land a customer, and even if not, it makes the $3,500 plan look reasonable ("I don't need the ten, but I'll go 35").
- He adds that one $10K customer at 50% profit could pay for a freelance developer, so one whale could fund the hire the founder was worried about.
- He says the founder was effectively running business model experimentation, with a few customers on each tier.
- On the website: make it look great and tight, because investors and customers can quickly pass on a company that looks corny or not well thought out.

chunks.heading: Relentless focus: scale what works before adding new products
chunks.text:
- Jason's stated 2018 lesson: "focus and simplicity and what you don't do is as important as what you do do."
- His restaurant metaphor: if you make the best burger in town, don't start on lasagna. Make the burger more consistent, find more customers and more locations, and sell more burgers.
- At Inside.com he says they perfected the top 10 newsletter format. The plan: go from 30 newsletters to 60 in the next year, and triple from three world-class sales executives with two or three SDRs.
- At Launch he applies the same logic: go from two or three accelerator classes a year to seven, from 20 graduates to 50, and grow the podcast from two advertisers to three and from 100-150K downloads/views per episode to 300-500K.
- Founder types: 0-to-1 people are idea people; 1-to-a-million people are refiners and operators. ADD/ADHD-style founders find it boring to make the "ten thousandth" hamburger, "but that's where all the profit is."
- After product-market fit, "the key to success is scaling and it's a relentless focus". People often get something right, then stop seeing how far it can go.
- He said that even if a podcast or newsletter adjacency looks perfect, the right move is to stay focused until you get there: if 30 newsletters bring in $1M of revenue, 300 should be $10M or more.
- To get world-class investors' attention, you need to scale and set aggressive targets and try to hit them. He points to Zuckerberg's focus on getting users on the platform and keeping them there as his best quality, but warns not to let focus override basic human decency.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason explains why a product customers won't shut up about is the core growth engine, with marketing built on top of it. He also covers resourcefulness (RTFM, reaching 60-70% of any skill in weeks), selling early vs. taking secondary, and how new angels should deploy capital.

chunks.heading: Distribution comes from a product people won't shut up about
chunks.text:
Jason's core claim is that virality starts and ends with a great product. His examples: Slack, Uber, Tesla and Snapchat.
- Tesla owners tell friends to drive Teslas. Snapchat users annoy friends by showing them how to use it.
- Uber users hand a friend a referral code so each gets a free ride.
- He says "the great products people can't wait to tell their friends about them."
- His order of operations: build the product that delights customers, then build everything else (press, brand, marketing spend) around it.
- A great product also "buys you more time to make mistakes" on marketing and hiring. Companies that are good at press, raising money and culture but weak on product waste that effort.
- His example of that failure is Fab.com: great at fundraising and design, but the product was not essential, so it never got a strong business model or margins.

chunks.heading: Testing for virality with Net Promoter Score
chunks.text:
Jason uses NPS as the test for whether customers are truly engaged.
- Question: how likely are you to refer this product to a friend, on a scale of 1 to 10.
- 9 or 10 is an advocate (+1), 7 or 8 is indifferent (0), 6 or under is a detractor (-1).
- Products with the highest NPS are the ones people won't shut up about.
- A product stuck at 7 to 8 can still be a good business, but it lacks virality. It "better have margins or monopolies or something."
- At the early stage he doesn't need everything figured out. He wants a founder who studies the few 9s and 10s to learn why they love it.
- His hypothetical: a streaming startup finds its few superfans love documentaries, which are cheaper to license, so it uses documentaries as its beachhead against Netflix.
- He credits this lean-startup style: form a thesis, measure it, and "if you measure it you can manage it."

chunks.heading: Referral incentives and the half-life of marketing tactics
chunks.text:
- A "give $10, get $10" referral is a timeless channel because people feel good giving friends a discount.
- Economics: if acquiring a customer costs about $30 on Facebook, a $10 give plus $10 get can be cheaper. Without referrals Uber would pay more through radio or other expensive channels.
- Most marketing tactics have a half-life. Of 20 tips he could give, half would stop working in six months and the rest would work half as well.
- Infographics are his example: once everyone sent them to journalists, they became "the opposite of what journalists want to see."
- Marketing channels burn out, so the durable foundation is the product.

chunks.heading: Fund marketing from a profitable core, and pick the right press
chunks.text:
- Marketing spend is only available once the product or business makes money. Then you can afford to lose money on marketing.
- His own case: Launch events run at breakeven because the firm makes money by investing in companies. That let them spend on Instagram, Facebook and Twitter ads and give away about 1,500 free tickets for Launch Festival Sydney.
- Big brands buy bus and outdoor ads without proof it works. They spend 5%, 10% or 20% of profits on advertising to start a positive flywheel.
- Rule of thumb for experiments: if it works, double the spend; if not, cut it. A $100,000 radio test at $10M in revenue is 1% of yearly revenue.
- Match press to vertical. TechCrunch or Mashable may come by default from raising money, but you may need a trade publication for lawyers if you sell legal software.
- Ring needed local news in high-crime areas to move doors out the door fast.

chunks.heading: Spend frugally early, then deploy capital where it pays
chunks.text:
- Decide each purchase by ratio, not by principle.
- A $20,000 sales deck is a no-brainer if the company prints money and customers spend $250,000. It's a bad idea for a startup with $50,000 in the bank and two customers, where it is 40% of the capital.
- Early on, learn a basic deck, buy a template for about $50, and call it a day.
- He used to handle his own legal work, then outsourced the parts that needed a lawyer.
- Be frugal early so you can deploy capital correctly later, then loosen up once you have money.
- His "6 out of 10" logo rule: spend about 20 hours learning to make a decent logo, then hire a professional once you've raised.

chunks.heading: Resourcefulness and starting before you feel ready
chunks.text:
- He argues most people "overestimate what it takes" and set up their own roadblocks. His shorthand is "RTFM," read the manual.
- He looks for resourceful founders. Reaching about 60 to 70% of an expert's skill takes roughly 50 to 100 hours, so the skill to have is acquiring new skills quickly.
- Podcast gear is the example: roughly $150 microphones are fine, since only the top 10 to 15% of listeners notice a $3,000 mic. Content comes first, but bad audio will lose people.
- He fixed his tennis-ball machine and pool heater by looking up the parts online, so he knew the board cost about $300 before hiring a plumber.
- Podcast origin: he says he recorded for selfish reasons, to talk to people he wanted relationships with, and the audience was secondary. He did Calacanis Cast first, then This Week in Startups.
- Kevin Pollak started his chat show by simply being handed the studio keys on Sundays. The lesson: do the behavior and you are that thing.

chunks.heading: How Jason evaluates founders and finds deal flow
chunks.text:
- He backs the founder on objective evidence: what they built, how they built it, what customers think. Examples: a Google sales VP making sales tools, or a founder whose product spread across eight campuses.
- He asks short questions and listens to how well-considered the answers are, such as whether they interviewed incumbents' staff to learn the real margins.
- Common thread in winners (Uber, Thumbtack, Robinhood, Wealthfront, Desktop Metal, Datastax): passionate, resourceful founders who care about their market.
- Randomness still applies: timing, competitors, and whether technology is ready (YouTube before cheap bandwidth, ride services before GPS phones).
- He is a founder-focused investor, not industry-focused, because nobody can define the next big category on demand.
- Deal flow is a funnel from his podcast, events, Founder University, social media and book. Reputation for being helpful matters, so founders recommend him.
- He travels to cities (Miami, Orlando, Iowa, Sydney) and finds two or three good companies per trip.
- He says about 20 to 30 great companies emerge each year, and his "Goldilocks zone" is post-idea, pre-Series A: a small team, a minimum viable product, and a few customers, often with $1M to $2M raised.
- His first filter for investors reaching out is a built product, since ideas are cheap and "execution is far more important."

chunks.heading: Advice for new angel investors
chunks.text:
- Use bankroll management: decide a percentage of net worth to deploy (e.g. 10%) and don't blow past it with bridge rounds into a friend-of-a-friend's startup.
- Go where the deal flow is: Silicon Valley, New York, Seattle, Boston and other top hubs. Investing in your home town usually means weaker deals.
- Make small bets of $10K to $25K and learn the game, like entering a $20 poker tournament instead of the $100,000 buy-in table.
- Don't invest pre-product. Plenty of companies have finished products and are raising, and you can be the fifth or sixth investor and follow signals from better investors.
- Be wary of charismatic founders who take $250,000 and pay down debt, and never ship.
- His syndicate at Jason.syndicate.com has about 2,400 members who can join deals from $1,000 to $3,000 up to $20K to $40K, starting small and growing.
- Liquidity advice: sell secondary shares along the way instead of waiting for a single exit. He sold Web Logs Inc. to AOL after about 18 months for $30 million, having turned down a $20 million exit earlier in a prior company. He says the quick way to get "poor" is to sell too early, and founders should think in decades.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason walks through items 81-90 of his startup checklist: pitch rules, building a curated list of about 150 investors, a short cold email with a Loom, nailing the first meeting, following up, backdoor-referencing investors, and SEC basics. He treats fundraising as a sales funnel, a numbers game where careful targeting and practice matter most.

chunks.heading: Fundraising as a numbers game: building the investor target list and funnel
chunks.text:
- Jason says investors should be found by working backwards from adjacencies. If a startup is an on-demand pet grooming app, he looks at who invested in Uber, Instacart and other on-demand businesses, plus consumer technology and e-commerce.
- He tells founders to use Crunchbase, PitchBook and Google to build the list.
- Target the specific partner, not just the firm. Check each partner's profile and Twitter to see whether they talk about SaaS, consumer or commerce. Emailing the wrong partner can get the lead forwarded and ignored, "burning" it.
- Also check stage. Some partners do seed, some Series A, some growth, and scouts write the small checks.
- His launch accelerator suggests a curated list of 150 investors. He says generic emails to 1,500 investors are "the wrong way".
- Funnel as he describes it:
  - Roughly one in three or one in four targets gives a first meeting, depending on how hot the company and category are. Maybe 40 meetings from 150.
  - Maybe half of those convert to a second meeting.
  - Perhaps 10 go into diligence, about 5 into lunch, and a few produce one to four term sheets.
  - That is about one in 50 to one in 75 targets giving a term sheet. "Everything is a numbers game."
- He also says to check whether an investor can actually invest: ask how deployed their fund is, when they raise the next one, and what their follow-on strategy is. Some are between funds or only doing follow-ons.

chunks.heading: Jason's pitch rules: the five golden rules
chunks.text:
Jason says he built these from running pitch events since 1997 (Meet the Alley) and the Launch accelerator, after sitting through thousands of pitches.

1. **Get to the product in 15 seconds.** Show it fast so the audience's "neurons fire".
2. **Examples matter.** Use a specific user story with numbers. His Airbnb example: Susan has a $1,200 spring break budget. Paris hotels start at $179 a night, so 8 days blows the budget. A $60-a-night room makes it about $500 for the room, plus a $379 flight, and she can afford Paris.
3. **Synchronicity.** What you say must match what is on the screen. Reveal Susan's picture, then her budget, then the options in step with the story, not a slide of projections while you tell a story.
4. **One slide, one message.** A slide with four paragraphs of business model is a "deal memo". Give each business model its own slide, and keep slides moving and breathing.
5. **Show, don't tell.** Show the product, data and customers instead of vague descriptions.

Other pitch advice:
- The slide is a guide, not a script. Don't memorize the deck; the slide should trigger what you say.
- Practice deliberately: record yourself, get a transcript, highlight the "um"s, and redo it.
- Be able to explain the startup in one jargon-free sentence. Examples: Airbnb lets people rent rooms; Uber is everybody's personal driver.
- Keep three decks: a teaser deck of 10 slides or fewer to email (no confidential info), a 20-40 slide deep dive, and an appendix. A rule of thumb is about one minute per slide, and he says some people go 20-30 seconds a slide.

chunks.heading: The cold email and "loom, zoom, room" sequence
chunks.text:
- The cold email should be short and specific. His template: reference something the investor said (e.g. "we saw your interview on This Week in Startups where you talked about your investment in Robinhood"), say what you do ("something similar in Latin America for millennials, plus crypto"), give traction ("1,400 customers", "$25 a month for unlimited trades"), and link a demo or a Loom.
- He describes the email as a movie trailer: "The trailer is not the entire movie. The trailer is to get you to buy a ticket."
- Sequence: **Loom, then Zoom, then room**.
  - A custom Loom walkthrough of the deck, addressed to the person, plays on reciprocation: they took time for me.
  - Every Loom is also another rep at your pitch. He suggests 10 a day at 10 to 15 minutes each, and reading the replies for feedback (for example "you didn't talk about your customers").
  - Lead with whatever is strongest: product, traction or team, such as "three engineers from Facebook, Amazon and Google".
  - Then ask for a short Zoom, offering flexible availability and a calendar link for 30, 45 or 60 minutes. Offering 10 to 20 minutes shows you respect their time.
  - The in-person meeting comes after, if it fits.
- He says he likes emails from people who name a specific episode or tweet and give a traction number, such as $25,000 in monthly recurring revenue.

chunks.heading: Running the first meeting
chunks.text:
- Start with investors you care less about for about two weeks to get reps and feedback. Move to top targets in weeks two or three.
- Bring two decks: a 5 to 10 minute, 10-slide version and a 15 to 20 minute, 30-slide version, with an appendix. Ask the investor which they prefer. He says this shows you think about the other side of the table.
- When he is the investor, he asks the founder what format works best (10 minutes of pitch and 10 of questions, or a product demo).
- Be high energy and positive. Answer questions concisely, "like ping pong". An answer should take about as long as the question.
- His accelerator records founders answering questions and times them. Example: "tell me about your team" at 70 seconds may be too long, while "how many employees" should be about 7 seconds ("five full-time employees and three contractors").
- Close with clear next steps. Ask directly whether they want to invest, go to diligence, present to their partnership, meet customers, or meet the team. He says he likes founders who say "you're our dream investor, would you lead the round?" because it shows the confidence he wants in someone selling or hiring.
- Know the revenue answer cold, for example "$27,000 in recurring revenue", rather than hedging.

chunks.heading: Follow-up, urgency and investor updates
chunks.text:
- Don't be passive after the meeting. Follow up on anything unclear: for example send the Notion page with the hiring plan he asked about, or add an answer on a competitor. "Never lie, tell the truth."
- Create urgency honestly: "We have two term sheets, we plan to decide on Friday." Add fresh progress, such as closing two enterprise customers or an upfront payment of $40,000.
- Send concise monthly investor updates with a chart up top. Put non-investors who passed on a BCC list or mail merge too. If growth proves his concerns wrong (he gives "we grew 17% this month" as an example), he may invest later, perhaps at a higher price or in the next round.
- "People invest in lines, not dots." Many updates over time build the line and the founder's credibility.

chunks.heading: Diligence on investors and SEC rules
chunks.text:
- Founders should do "dark references": email founders the investor backed, without telling the investor, and ask about them. Jason says email about 100 and expect around 99 positive answers; a few clashes are normal.
- Know what kind of investor you want: hands-off check writers, or deeply involved ones. He cites a past episode where a founder described a nightmare VC experience, and notes there are two sides plus the reality.
- Rule 506(b), the most common route, means no public talk about the raise. With 506(c) you can raise publicly but must verify accreditation (W-2s or letters from lawyers or accountants). That costs more, and founders often use a service; he names AssureFund Management, in which he is an investor.
- Only take money from people who understand the risk and can afford to lose it. $50K from a friend with $50M is fine; a third of someone's retirement account is not. He says a small share, around 3 to 4 percent of a retirement account, may be fine if they really want to support you.
- Use a good law firm. He says he trusts Republic and SeedInvest as platforms and doesn't trust other ones. For private raises, he says lawyers will tell you to stay private if you can.

chunks.heading: How to get on his podcast (and why not to pay for it)
chunks.text:
- This Week in Startups doesn't take PR pitches. His team replies "we don't take pitches for the podcast" and he penalizes pitchers.
- His guest criteria: do something interesting, be successful, have a hot take, or write a great blog post. Strong performances on other podcasts also get noticed.
- He wants real answers, not media-trained ones, and says "don't give me the media trained answer."
- He says booking services claiming to place people on the show are lying, and he warned off one that implied an inside line.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason explains how he approaches early-stage investing: make many small bets, judge founders on performance and customer love rather than charisma, and pre-emptively fund winners to raise ownership. He also argues family offices should avoid passed-over seed deals or hire a dedicated investor, and covers remote work economics and consumerized enterprise software.

chunks.heading: Why Jason says this is the best moment to angel invest
chunks.text:
- Jason argues downturns are when great angel entry prices appear. He made his best bets in the Great Recession years.
- Uber, Calm and Thumbtack were valued at about $5M, $5M and $4M when he invested. He puts the combined entry at roughly $14-15M.
- In recent years, companies with less performance than those were asking for $12-20M valuations.
- His portfolio split in the crisis: some companies doubled usage and revenue, others fell to zero revenue.
- He was investing more going into the crisis than before it.
- He says creative energy peaks in a crisis and many great companies are founded then.

chunks.heading: Valuation discipline and shots on goal
chunks.text:
- Jason tells founders and new investors to "be valuation conscious". Entry point matters even if you later hit a $10B outlier.
- The reasoning: a fixed pool of capital buys a fixed number of swings. $1M for 1% of one company could instead be ten $100K checks for the same total ownership.
- Cheaper entry means more shots on goal for the same money.
