- He also argues that a team which breaks even on its bets still wins. Staying in the game gives a chance at an outlier, and the market intelligence is valuable.

chunks.heading: Portfolio construction and pro rata
chunks.text:
- Jason describes early startup investing as roughly 80% of bets going to zero.
- He describes three of four companies failing and about one in 30 or 40 becoming an outlier.
- The edge he lists: proprietary deal flow, many bets, spotting which ones break out, then putting 10x more capital behind them.
- His book's rules, as recapped on the show: make 30+ investments, invest only in startups with product in market and revenue, start with very small bets, then go 10x on winners. Spread the 30+ over about three years so you learn along the way.
- He now insists on pro rata rights or he doesn't invest. In his early $25-50K check days he never thought about them.
- A team member tracks the quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year performance of about 150 active portfolio companies.
- When a company is about to raise, Jason makes a preemptive offer. Example: $250K or $1M at a $15M cap.
- Companies sometimes say no and go to market, but he says they win the deal about 80% of the time.
- This moves his ownership from about 6% to 12-20% in winners.
- Ownership history he gives: under 1% in Uber, about 2% in Superhuman, 5-6% in Calm, now 9-15% in newer winners such as Fitbod and Steezy.

chunks.heading: Advice for family offices
chunks.text:
- Jason says family offices usually see deals only after Silicon Valley has passed on them. His poker analogy: the best hands get played by others and the rest get passed down.
- Founders see family office money as not valuation sensitive. He says to them: "So what you're saying is you want an investor who is not smart."
- Before buying a deal, he says to check it wasn't passed on by everyone else. He doesn't want you "splitting the arrow".
- Better routes for family offices:
  - Back fund managers who know what they're doing, then try to get their pro rata allocation downstream.
  - Invest in companies that already have $10-50M in revenue. You then check in every 6-12 months instead of monthly or weekly, and you avoid the 80% mortality.
- A family office with real appetite could hire a young Jason-type, paying salary plus bonus, and put about 1% of the fund to work per year.
  - Example: a $100M office deploying $5M over five years.
  - The intelligence gained is worth it even at break-even. A person bringing one strong deal a week would make the whole organization smarter about the future.
- His view is that he sees the future about 10 years before everyone else.
- He keeps his public-market money in a low-fee Wealthfront account. His reason: he has no edge competing with high-frequency traders.

chunks.heading: How he evaluates a startup
chunks.text:
- Core idea: judge potential through performance. The question is whether the company can reach $50-100M in revenue.
- Capital is a zero-sum competition. Funding one company means another doesn't get the check.
- Founders are highly charismatic, so he separates charisma from performance.
- Talk to customers:
  - Ask what they'd do if the product went away.
  - "I'd be upset" is one level of product-market fit.
  - "Can I buy a license for $10,000, this is mission critical" is a stronger level.
- Check craftsmanship in the product. He cites the iPhone, Tesla, Wacom and Uber. If he can see detail in the product, customers can too.
- He asks founders: "is there some other idea you have that's better than this one?" Some answer yes, and he moves on.
- He reads whether founders hold firm on their business model or ask whether he'd invest if they changed it.

chunks.heading: Where venture capital fits
chunks.text:
- He defends the VC model. He says VCs forgive losses by calling investments "experiments", and the system works when you can make 100-300 bets.
- Venture backs rocket-ship outcomes, not steady growth. A pizzeria or dry cleaner growing 10% a year (doubling in about 7.2 years) is a "lifestyle business".
- He says that term isn't an insult. The owner keeps 100% of the profits and the shares.
- Accelerators, seed funds and platforms have taken over the "picking apples" stage that VCs moved downstream from.

chunks.heading: Building a syndicate and an angel brand
chunks.text:
- His first AngelList investment was Calm, a $378K syndicate check.
  - The company went from $5M to $1.4B.
  - His syndicate sold about 10% of shares at a $250M valuation in a secondary, booking roughly a 3x cash-on-cash return in under five years while keeping 90%.
- He left AngelList after about 40-50 investments and created his own syndicate site, to control the experience and have a direct relationship with investors.
  - About 4,000 members, around 2,000 active.
  - The top 250 are in a Slack workspace helping with projects.
- Goal: 10,000 active members, so 250 people at $40K each fund a $10M round.
- Distribution engine:
  - His podcast, running 11-12 years with 1,000+ episodes and 6-7 full-time staff, is "top of the funnel" for deal flow.
  - Listeners email him and strangers pitch him in the street.
- He teaches Angel University, three hours for a $100 charity donation. Cohorts of 150-250 people raised about $50-60K.
- He ran Open Angel Forum, now remote demo day, where about seven startups pitch investors.
- Uber came through being helpful: he introduced Travis Kalanick to investors. He had known Travis from interviewing him as a journalist.
- On his own record he says: "I got lucky 12 times."

chunks.heading: Work from home and the economics of talent
chunks.text:
- Jason sees remote work as an efficiency shift that will help pull the economy out of recession.
- Bay Area workers carry a $20-50K salary premium; he expects pay to reset by location. He cites Zuckerberg's policy of cutting pay for people who move.
- Facilities spend is often the number two or three line item, so shedding offices can make companies 20%+ more profitable.
- Remote work exposes low performers through daily stand-ups and end-of-day reports.
- He doesn't believe a $50-500B company can be built fully remote. Culture and in-person collaboration matter for those.
- He expects commercial real estate to fall at least 50%.
- He expects employees to value flexibility, so employers that refuse will struggle to hire.

chunks.heading: Skills over degrees and the education shift
chunks.text:
- He expects a homeschooling and subscription boom of $10-500 a month, naming Brilliant and Khan Academy. Rich parents may hire a teacher for a small pod of kids.
- He expects second- and third-tier colleges to struggle and gap years to rise.
- Hiring is shifting to skills. His test: rate yourself 1-10 at a specific skill.
  - A 6 is unneeded, an 8 is tolerated, 9-10 is "employable forever".
  - "Business degree" is not a skill.
- He thinks Harvard "picks" smart people rather than making them smarter, and he sees his own role as picking, not making founders 10x better.
- He passed on investing in MasterClass and calls that a mistake.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Calacanis explains why he moved from "I only invest in myself" to angel investing, and walks through the playbook in his book Angel. Bet on the founder rather than the idea, start with small checks across many deals, and be psychotically helpful. Insist on monthly updates, and wait for a launched product before writing a check.

chunks.heading: Why Jason started angel investing
chunks.text:
- Jason first refused to invest in friends' companies because he trusted only his own judgment, and he got burned. He passed on Zynga after telling Mark Pincus that virtual poker chips make no sense ("a $25 million mistake").
- He gave Elon Musk advice on Tesla when it traded around a dollar a share, but he wasn't angel investing then.
- He turned down Twitter when Evan Williams showed it to him, predicting "a cacophony of idiots." He calls that a $50 million mistake.
- The fix was to decouple his opinion of an idea from his ability to pick great people. He now invests in friends and smart people, not in ideas he personally likes.
- His first 15 to 20 investments were made with Sequoia's money. He had introduced Sequoia to companies, they gave him a small pool, and the returns were split 50/50. That pool outperformed Sequoia's own parallel fund.
- Sam Altman's Stripe position and Jason's Uber and Thumbtack positions (about $200 million) drove those returns. He then raised his own fund and has done about 150 investments.
- He wrote the book because he's one of very few people with more than 100 investments and several unicorns (he says six). He believes it can change people's economic mobility.

chunks.heading: Why he thinks getting on a cap table beats the old wealth playbook
chunks.text:
- The old advice was banker, lawyer or cop, marry someone with a good job, buy a home, and leverage it. That broke when houses went from roughly 1 to 1.5x household income to 10x or more, and graduates carry about $100,000 in debt.
- He lists four ways onto the cap table of high-growth startups:
  - **Founder:** one big bet, but you might get three or four tries in a lifetime. Most people quit after one.
  - **Employee:** small equity that rarely pays off.
  - **Adviser or consultant:** work for half cash and half stock, vesting monthly. He suggests young people advise about five startups a year with a skill like design or development.
  - **Angel investor:** increasingly accessible through syndicates and Reg CF/Reg A style rules for non-accredited investors.
- Pay attention to where the value gets created. Outside the Valley, a $10 billion or $100 billion company is very rare. New York has had billion-dollar companies like Tumblr, Etsy, Kickstarter, DoubleClick and iVillage.

chunks.heading: How a beginner should start (low-cost, high-learning)
chunks.text:
- Make many small bets. Put about $1,000 into each of the first ~10 deals through syndicates (AngelList, Seed Invest, Republic, his own Jason Syndicate) and act as if you had put in $10,000 or $100,000.
- Treat it as an education and networking cost:
  - A founder sees you as a helpful, engaged investor regardless of check size.
  - You can see who else co-invested, build a spreadsheet or list of those co-investors, and email them for coffee when you travel.
- Plan for 20 to 30 startups over 2 to 4 years, diversified, with small bets first and bigger bets later. Double down on the winners.
- Never put much of your net worth into one deal; he suggests a fraction of 1% per investment.
- Total downside is small. Risking 5% to 10% of net worth across a portfolio is survivable, and a lost 5% is outweighed by the network and education. "Most people overestimate the downside risk" (a line he attributes to Elon).
- Year two is the worst. Maybe 7 of your first 10 are running out of money while you're making your next 10. People who bet too big too early quit right before winners pay off. If 1 to 3 of 10 survive, something special is going on, and the payoff should be far more than 5x.
- Know your own psychology. From watching poker players, he saw some love to lose and rage-quit, while winners step away, eat a sandwich and come back disciplined.
- Alternatively, find the top 10 angels by track record and put $1,000 into their syndicates. He frames this as having their experience work for you.

chunks.heading: How he evaluates startups and founders
chunks.text:
- He invests in the arc of a founder's career, not a single idea. He expects the first investment may return zero, the second 2x and the third 100x. He tries to be the first call and first check for repeat founders.
- He now writes down the reasons something will fail, then often tears up the page and lists only the one or two reasons it could work. Examples: Airbnb sounded like it was "for serial killers and meth heads"; Google was roughly the 11th search engine; YouTube was about the 50th video site; Uber and Lyft weren't the first to try hailing cabs by phone (Vindo texted for cabs).
- "What if it works?" is the core question. If success is obvious, the price is probably wrong; the upside lives in ideas that seem crazy.
- Separate your limited ability to judge the idea from your ability to read the founder's passion. Check whether five crazy early customers could become the 90% who use it. Founders in true billion-dollar opportunities will know more and care more than you do.
- Look for craftsmanship and obsessive attention to detail, like Barry Diller's staff stripping labels off a Fantastik bottle so it looked clean. Great founders can seem stubborn, annoying or even jerks because they believe the world must change. Thumbtack's Marco Zappacosta impressed him with rich, passionate, detailed answers.
- He sometimes seeks out the founder a VC finds "uncomfortable," because the discomfort may come from strong conviction.
- Don't judge a company by disgruntled ex-employees. He compares the New York Times piece on Amazon to asking people who washed out of Navy SEAL training about the SEALs.
- Run due diligence. The first 50 deals he skipped it. In the next ~100 deals he caught two founders in outright lies and wrote about them in the book.

chunks.heading: Timing: when to invest (his 2017 view)
chunks.text:
- He doesn't recommend investing before a product has launched and has a few customers. Many teams can build an MVP with friends-and-family money and sweat equity, so waiting eliminates about 97% of failures.
- Of launched products, perhaps two thirds die within two or three years, but you get that time to see whether anyone actually uses it. Even a few customers show the founders aren't "tourists or [bullshitters]."
- After a hit like Instagram, a me-too app has to be about 5x better, not 10% to 20% better, to get people to switch. After "The Social Network" came out, a wave of tourists arrived.
- He stays at the very early stage (5 people, 6-month-old companies) and turned down offers to do later-stage $25 million to $50 million checks, because that's the most exciting point.

chunks.heading: How to be valuable to founders (and build your network)
chunks.text:
- Be of service without expecting return. He built goodwill at Silicon Alley Reporter by delivering magazines himself on a luggage cart, putting people on the cover, and inviting them to parties, then tapped that goodwill later.
- Advice for founders or would-be investors: study the deal flow, then offer help (for a salesperson, rewrite a job description for a company that's hiring). "Be of service" is his main networking tactic.
- Treat angel investing as an arms race of who adds the most value. He tries to give the same value to failed startups and to companies he passed on.
- Passing on a round isn't the end. Ask to be on the monthly update list and reply helpfully. He gets about 100 updates a month from companies he passed on, but only about 75 of the 150 companies he did invest in send updates.
- For companies that come back for a bridge, he adds a side letter requiring monthly updates. No updates usually means a 99% chance of failure; even Uber sends quarterly updates.
- Tell founders up front that most startups fail and that if it happens, shut down gracefully and call him first for the next idea. Once, a founder who sold his company early agreed on the phone to make Jason the first investor in the next one, and similar promises have paid off two or three times.
- He tells founders to call him when the news is too scary to tell their team (they'd quit) or other investors (they won't fund again). Once a founder called after throwing up in the shower. Jason told him he could shut down, take a big-company job for two years, and he'd be the first check back.
- Communicate candidly. He prefers "candid" to "honest" (an idea from Ed Catmull's "Creativity, Inc."), because asking for honesty implies you weren't being honest before.

chunks.heading: Syndicates and cap table leverage
chunks.text:
- About half of the companies he invests in agree to syndicate their rounds. He moved from AngelList to his own Jason Syndicate, with about 1,300 people.
- Founders benefit because syndicate members can open doors. Members work at places like Google and Disney, and include authors and athletes. For Cafe X (robotic coffee), the question "does anyone know anybody at Google?" gets answers.
- Backers invest as little as $1,000 per deal, and the whole group sits in one LLC with paperwork handled.
- He says it breaks the idea that angel investing needs $100,000 checks. A recent syndicate for a company he works with raised over a million dollars and broke the platform's record.

chunks.heading: Motivation, goals and marketing tactics
chunks.text:
- He's driven by an addictive, competitive personality and sets audacious public goals. Next goal: 300 total investments and being the best angel ever.
- The chip came from growing up in Brooklyn, feeling "bridge and tunnel," and wanting to be the person who decides who goes on the magazine cover.
- Silicon Alley Reporter's Top 100 list was a growth hack:
  - The first year only 60 people could be found, so he asked each person to name others (accountants, headhunters, lawyers) to reach 100.
  - He ranked by tiers (most important, least important, middle).
  - He deliberately ranked a loud player (DoubleClick) at number 2 and Esther Dyson at number 1 to provoke controversy. After the list, the invites to Knicks games and parties poured in.
- Book promotion tactic: a raffle ticket in the book to win dinner with him and James. Winners tend to be entrepreneurs, and he said he'd probably invest in one at dinner.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Episode 5 of the Launch scaling series covers early sales. Founders run the first calls themselves, then hire a line account executive instead of a senior VP. Pay is roughly half base and half commission, paid when cash arrives. Other topics include outsourced SDRs, email sequences, BANT, and upselling.

chunks.heading: Hiring the first sales people: founders sell first
chunks.text:
- Jason says sales solves everything. He cites Mark Cuban from the Weblogs Inc. days: "sell solves everything", because with great sales you have resources to fix every other problem.
- Founders should be on the first sales calls themselves. They are always selling anyway: to investors, partners, press, customers and new hires.
- Hiring a super senior sales leader too early is dangerous:
  - They expect big event and marketing budgets, an assistant, a designer and SDRs.
  - They often are no longer active sellers and won't get on the phone.
  - They become resource consumers, and the founder sets them up for failure.
- His preferred first hire is a line Account Executive working in parallel with the founder, not a VP.
- The founder and AE should aim for ten phone calls a week. After five to seven weeks they learn the objections, who picks up and takes the call, and which title to target.
- He wants those decision-maker details made transparent in the organization, not opaque.
- He notes that senior hires tend to have wild comp expectations of hundreds of thousands of dollars.

chunks.heading: Sales compensation structure and rules of thumb
chunks.text:
- Early salespeople are inefficient. Contacts don't know you, there are no marketing materials, and they reach the wrong person first and navigate the org through several calls.
- Jason tells founders to count half of an early salesperson's comp as R&D or market research. Example: a $100K package ($50K base, $50K commission) is $50K of market research and $50K of sales.
- Selling something new is harder. His example is Balloonr (ideation software), where there is no "VP of ideation" to target, unlike customer support for Zendesk.
- Commission-only is legally risky in California. Labor boards default to the employee's position, so someone who works 50 hours a week and sells nothing can claim pay.
  - Contractor deals (1099, e.g. paid per closed deals) can work.
  - Ad reps and real estate brokers are paid this way. At Silicon Alley Reporter, a Chicago rep got 30% of ad sales, so a $10K back cover paid $3,000.
- His preferred model is base salary plus commission.
  - Paying a draw or advance against commission works to cover ramp-up. Example: $1,000 a month for the first six months against a $50K commission plan.
  - Pay commission when the money comes in the door. If a customer pays twice, the rep earns twice. Cancellations and refunds mean no commission on that money.
  - Some cash-rich businesses pay on signing and claw back later.
- Typical split is 50/50 base to commission. If they crush it, two-thirds can come from commission.
- Red flag: a candidate who wants less than a third of their comp from commission. "That's not a good sales executive."
- "Base pays your rent."
- Examples he gives:
  - Yelp reps in Arizona, per what other salespeople told his team for Inside.com: about $30-35K base, about $20K more at target, so roughly $55-60K total.
  - Silicon Valley SaaS reps: $100-150K base plus about $100K on target.
- Founders should expect salespeople to out-earn them. He wants the founder to be around the sixth or seventh highest paid, and calls three reps making $200K while the founder takes $100K "success". Founders hold 10-30% equity while sales hires hold a fraction of a percent.
- He warns that salespeople can be the worst to deal with internally, and the better they sell, the worse they can be. Build a clear culture with proper incentives.

chunks.heading: Outsourcing and structuring prospecting (SDRs)
chunks.text:
- Prospecting is the research and data gathering of leads. Founders do it first, then hire SDRs, and ideally outsource it.
- Define target demographics first: industry, company size, roles.
- Why outsource SDR work: people hate the job and burn out, with turnover around every six months. Many SDRs become account executives or leave.
- Outsourced SDR firm test at Inside.com: $3,000 a month for two SDRs (offshore).
  - They expect to find about 2,000 leads, roughly $1.50 per lead.
  - They expect 10-20 calls a week, about 50 a month, so around $60 per phone call.
  - He compares it to a roughly $35K a year employee at about $15 an hour.
- At Launch, an in-house Toronto team spends about one hour a day finding leads for the two Silicon Valley account executives. That is roughly 10 hours a week, 50 companies a week with about four contacts each, or 150-200 names. They enjoy the work, which is why it stays in-house.
- Jason is open to up-work style offshore help. He notes a Serbian designer at $15/hour versus a $100/hour San Francisco quote.
- Build an "autonomous sales machine":
  - Set an SDR weekly goal, such as 200 contacts.
  - SDRs load leads into a CRM as cold leads, and CRM flags duplicates and existing clients.
  - Spot check and assign leads, then reps send outreach.
- CRMs and tools named: Zendesk Sell, Pipedrive, Salesforce, HubSpot, Outreach.io, Mixmax, LeadIQ.
- Decide which skills your AEs need from SDRs. Some reps want leads queued up for calls and others want to write their own outreach.
- At Launch, SDRs only load leads. Salespeople assigned leads randomly do the outreach with templated sequences and customize the first line.

chunks.heading: Email sequences and outreach tactics
chunks.text:
- A sequence is a series of automated actions, typically three to five emails, with follow-ups spaced about three days apart. Newer tools also add Twitter follows, LinkedIn connects and voicemails.
- Jason's team approach: new reps write a couple of sequences and test them, so they learn themselves and might find something new. Proven templates are introduced later.
- Another approach at Launch: three emails within two weeks, then move interested contacts (those who opened more than once or clicked) into a slow-drip sequence of one email every month or two across a year, with reminders to connect on LinkedIn or Twitter. Don't put non-openers in it.
- Jason dislikes sequences with five, six or seven follow-ups.
- Best practices from the discussion:
  - Keep cold emails short and valuable, and make it easy to say yes.
  - Offer specific windows of time.
  - A/B test subject lines, body, day of week and time of day.
  - Mix very short "did you see my last email" notes with informative emails or demos.
  - A chart, screenshot or looped video of the software works; goofy gifs don't.
- He finds the "hey, can I ask you a question?" opener annoying: say what you want upfront.
- Scheduling links (Calendly, Mixmax, Google Calendar) let prospects pick a slot. He doesn't think cold calling happens as much, and says he doesn't answer unknown phone calls (Pixel call screening).
- Track and compare reps' open rates, calls per week and close rates to find what works.

chunks.heading: Closing: the BANT framework
chunks.text:
- Launch uses IBM's BANT: Budget, Authority, Need, Timeframe.
- Budget: try to get an exact number. Knowing how frugal or flush a company is changes how you pitch. Think of ways to evolve your product to capture open budget.
- Authority: identify a champion and the decision-maker, who may differ, especially in larger companies. Accounts Payable may also need to approve. Tailor the pitch (ROI, fit in budget) to each.
- Need: find the prospect's pain points during nurturing and show how you make their life easier or beat competitors.
- Timeframe: use urgency, such as budget that must be spent this quarter or a holiday deadline. Move quickly on your side.
- Jason notes personal motivation matters. Advertisers on his show buy for different reasons: fandom, leads, closed sales, or the quality of the read.

chunks.heading: Upselling, renewals and client success
chunks.text:
- Separate sales (closing) from client success (renewals and upsells) once you have the money to do so.
- Pay attention to what the product does for customers and add features or tiers that capture more of their open budget. Example: a $99 per month product adding offers worth $100-200 more per month.
- Double down on "whales", your largest customers. Founders should handle them at first, then pass them to account managers. Get their feedback, build rapport, and thank them with experiences such as a dinner or a Warriors game.
- Renewing and upselling is much easier than booking new clients. Keeping customers from quitting matters as much as or more than winning new ones.
- Create monthly recurring revenue on top of one-off services or products. Founders often take off when they learn to turn this on.
- Jason's own example: on This Week in Startups, he and the team improve content and guests to keep advertisers. In 2019 they had ten unicorn founders on the show.

chunks.heading: Bribes, gifts and ethics in sales
chunks.text:
- Jason was offered $100 for taking an expense software demo, another $100 if he got his boss to close that day, and $50 more for requested info. He calls it a bribe and "dirty", even though he says it was the best product he'd seen.
- His test: would you be comfortable if your boss, or the New York Times or TechCrunch, saw it?
- Gifts and coffee are fine. Above about $25 you should tell your boss immediately.
- Corporate bribery can bring jail time, and US companies are held to the American standard abroad. He cites Walmart's bribery in Mexico and Sony sales junkets (Cabo, business class) as examples.
- Thanking a customer with an experience after they've spent money is different from a bribe to win a decision. His example: a bank taking 25 VCs and 25 founders to Turks and Caicos for kitesurfing.

chunks.heading: Sales tools and getting the team to adopt them
chunks.text:
- Tools named: Mixmax and Outreach for sequences, Zendesk Sell and Pipedrive for pipeline visibility, LeadIQ for lead data.
- Use the same tool for each function so reporting stays in one place. Switching costs are high (about $100 and team training when Launch changed CRM).
- Use free trials and ask for extensions. Negotiate hard in competitive tool markets.
- Budget roughly $300-400 a month per sales executive in tools, about $5,000 a year. A $10K sale pays for it.
- Getting adoption:
  - Let people opt in and have early adopters report results at team meetings, so others see the wins.
  - He argues email sequences let you invite 100 investors to an accelerator with one push of a button.
  - Jason's rule: if a lead isn't contacted in the CRM within 60 days, it opens to anyone (some companies use 30).
  - For old-school reps who refuse to use the CRM, he gives about a year of amnesty, but by the third or fourth salesperson they must adopt it.
  - "The people who don't adopt these new tools are no longer competitive."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason hosts Doug Leone and Gili Raanan on Wiz, hiring, product-market fit and VC cycles. Most of the substance comes from the guests; Jason mainly asks questions and adds a few reactions about repeat founders, founder-led selling and tying equity to performance.

chunks.heading: Founder equity splits should reflect performance, not an equal cut
chunks.text:
- Jason points out that Steph Curry doesn't make the same as the five players on the Warriors bench. Everyone is paid differently based on performance.
- He calls the equity split a hard conversation because people "lean socialist". Three founders means 33% each, four means 25% each, and that sours things when one partner stops showing up.
- He wants splits tied to performance and to what the team gets if it performs well. In his view, an even split is "just a math equation" and not a value-based one.
- This is his reason for treating the split as the foundation of the company, to be discussed openly at the start.

chunks.heading: Integrating outside hires into a close founding team
chunks.text:
- Jason notes that senior hires from outside, who weren't part of founding the company, still need to feel like part of the core team.
- His example is Kevin Durant joining the Warriors. Durant never quite felt like part of the core team, which is the failure to avoid when an outsider joins a tight group.

chunks.heading: Founders are often the best early salespeople
chunks.text:
- Jason says there is "honesty" and a transfer of enthusiasm when founders explain in the room why they built something. The buyer feels it across the table, or in his words today, directly through to the customer.
- The buyer's reaction he describes is "I want to be part of this."
- The hard part is getting later salespeople to carry the same conviction.

chunks.heading: Reputation compounds: how helping Travis Kalanick led to Uber
chunks.text:
- Jason says someone at a party told him he was "lucky" to invest in Uber, and he agreed. Travis Kalanick, standing next to him, corrected the story.
- Travis said Jason had helped him with his first two companies, Scour and Red Swoosh. Whenever Travis needed help, Jason picked up the phone, had dinner with him and talked through the business.
- Travis's point was that this is why Jason got the investment. It wasn't luck.
- The tactic is to help founders early and for free, long before they are an investment.

chunks.heading: Repeat founders: take the call
chunks.text:
- Jason's working rule is that second- and third-time founders who still have the energy are people you simply take the call from.
- His open question is how to tell whether a repeat founder is still hungry or just going through the motions.

chunks.heading: Small teams and revenue per employee in the AI era
chunks.text:
- Jason argues that AI is letting companies earn huge revenue with very few people. His example is coding assistants like Cursor, which he says have reached revenue above $1M per employee.
- He cites Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke's stance on headcount: don't justify new hiring unless it can't be done with AI.
- He expects this to show up first in consumer businesses.

chunks.heading: Venture is crowded and moving earlier
chunks.text:
- Jason invests through four funds and says investors everywhere are moving toward early stage.
- In his view the market is more crowded, Series B is "hot", and Series A is crowded too. Investors want to take the entire round, so everyone is pushing earlier.
- He treats the podcast as a learning tool and not just a place to talk.
- He is interested in programs like Sequoia's ARC as a way into early stage.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Calacanis explains his angel investing approach from his book "Angel": bet on founders rather than ideas, invest in the "Goldilocks zone" before Series A, and build networks through syndicates and monthly updates. He also shares advice for founders on engagement over investor-hacking and where false-start technologies may now work.

chunks.heading: Angel investing's "Goldilocks zone" and why Jason bets on founders, not ideas
chunks.text:
- **Where angels fit.** VCs have moved downstream. Jason says they now want enterprise companies with $50,000-$100,000 a month in revenue, or consumer products with 10,000-50,000 daily users and months of traffic. They often wait for around 10 million monthly users before a series A. That leaves what he calls the "Goldilocks zone": after the product has launched, before VCs "with their sharp elbows" take board seats.
- **Why that window is attractive.** Nine out of 10 products can reach market for sweat equity or $100,000 or less. Investing after launch screens out the 99% of founders who never ship. He puts the window at roughly three years.
- **Many small rounds.** Startups now raise pre-seed, seed, angel, pre-series A and extension rounds, usually as convertible notes that convert at the series A. Angels can wait and build a relationship over six months instead of panicking to get in.
- **Scale.** Ten years ago there were one or two dozen angels of note. He now estimates 500 to 1,000 people in Silicon Valley doing it as a primary activity.

chunks.heading: Jason's law: back the person, not the idea
chunks.text:
- His rule: "I don't need to know if your idea is going to succeed. I just need to know if you're going to succeed."
- His biggest misses were Tesla, Twitter and Zynga. At the time he wasn't an angel, but friends were founding them, and he estimates about $50 million each at his later check sizes. He passed on Twitter because he thought it would be "a cacophony of idiots" and a worse Blogger. He later realized "big things in the world generate tons of wealth" regardless of his taste.
- He passed on Airbnb because he overthought the risks (strangers on a couch, meth parties). He later saw that hotels have the same problems.
- Traits he screens for:
  - passion
  - skill
  - the ability to build a product and a team
  - "they won't give up"
- He says a rational person who understands how hard the job is will quit unless they truly care. Founders must be able to blow up rockets and "still go to work the next day", as he says Elon Musk did.
- Quick diagnostic questions:
  - What are you working on?
  - Why will this work now?
  - Why does this one feature matter?
- He credits YouTube's early team with a clear "why now": syndication plus cheap cloud computing, so embedded videos gave free marketing.
- His list of reasons a startup will fail is long, so he writes it out and rips it up. He asks "what could go right?" and takes a 1-in-50 or 1-in-100 shot if the payoff is larger.

chunks.heading: Risk, portfolio math and sizing
chunks.text:
- Dead money: he says people hold too much in bonds, real estate and balanced portfolios returning 4-7% a year. He suggests putting 5-10% of net worth into something highly risky with a shot at 100x or 1,000x.
- Losing six or seven in a row is normal. As a high-stakes poker player, he compares it to losing hands you were favored to win. When he introduced Uber to about 20-25 investors, only three said yes, and some of the greatest investors said no two or three times. Those three hold nine-figure positions.
- Human instinct is conservative (the alligator or lion). "There is no crocodile that's going to eat you if you lose your $10,000." People overestimate the downside.
- Even losing half of a 5-10% allocation is only about 2.5% of net worth, and he argues the network and knowledge gained cover that.
- Track record: six unicorns in his first 100 investments. At book time he had three. The book title promises turning $100,000 into $100 million.
- Fund: just closed a $10 million angel fund of friends' and his own money. He expects roughly 150 more investments to reach about 300. He says angel investing is very hard to scale.
- First-timers vs. serial founders: roughly 50/50 for big outcomes, so he doesn't filter on experience. "All you have to do is hit one."

chunks.heading: How to break into angel investing cheaply
chunks.text:
1. Join syndicates (AngelList, SeedInvest, Funders Club, his own "Jason Syndicate") and watch deal flow go by.
2. Start with a fantasy portfolio:
   - Read deal memos.
   - Score conviction from 1 to 10.
   - Pretend to invest $5,000.
   - Log it in a Google Sheet and check valuations every six months.
3. Then use real money. He says money on the table changes your judgment, "like playing poker for $1, $2" instead of fake chips.
4. Put in $1,000 to $3,000 across about 20 deals, roughly $50,000-$60,000 total. That's the price of one angel check, with 20-30 companies' monthly updates to learn from.
5. Treat a $1,000 check like a $100,000 one:
   - Email the founder.
   - Follow them on Twitter and retweet them.
   - Check their job board.
   - Ask every 60 days how you can help.
6. Network via co-investors:
   - Find co-investors on Crunchbase or Mattermark.
   - Put them in a Google Sheet.
   - Send a mail merge, e.g. "We're co-investors in Acme. Any interesting companies you're looking at? I'm breaking into angel investing."
   - About half respond, and some reply repeatedly.
7. Why it works: a round needs 30-50 investors before the series A. Earlier investors have more open slots to fill, and co-investors share deals because "that makes you like family members."

chunks.heading: Democratizing access and accreditation
chunks.text:
- He calls the accredited-investor rule (roughly $200,000 a year income, or $1-2 million in assets) unfair. About 95% of Americans are non-accredited yet can bet on sports or buy public stock, but can't buy private startups, where outsized returns are made.
- Europe lets everyone invest as they like. In the US, equity crowdfunding sites (SeedInvest, Republic) let non-accredited people invest around $500.
- Example: early Etsy sellers, eBay sellers, AdSense partners, LinkedIn recruiters and YouTube creators all knew those platforms would be big but couldn't invest.
- Traction: 25 days after the book launched, his syndicate had 1,200 members and 700 more joined. He was seeing about 30 applications a day and accepting about half.
- Cafe X (a robot coffee machine) raised over a million dollars from syndicate investors at $10,000 each.
- He sees crowdfunded deals as so far mostly the ones that didn't clear the market with VCs or angels.
- He thinks investing is bigger than money: angels back the "crazy kids" behind Google and YouTube.

chunks.heading: Advice to founders: stop hacking investors, show engagement
chunks.text:
- Rookie mistake: spending 90 of 100 units of effort on hacking investors. He says to spend those on tripling customer engagement, then use the last 10 to tell that story.
- What investors want: someone who can build a team that builds a product users love. Credibility builds over five to seven meetings and email updates, not one pitch.
- Monthly updates:
  - He now requires them in his legal docs.
  - They lead with metrics: months of runway, cash in bank, when the next raise is, revenue and engagement.
  - He tells prospects: put me on your monthly update for three months and I'll decide when it's in my zone.
- Known cost of silence: one company sent him legal docs after 18 months with no contact.
- Know each investor's timing:
  - some invest pre-product (product-driven people)
  - he invests after about six weeks of data
  - VCs want two years of data
- He's happy for investors to lose money "as long as they tried hard."
- He re-backs founders: Raul (Rapportive, sold to LinkedIn, then Superhuman) called him first for the next round, and he put in $1 million. He says this has happened about three times.

chunks.heading: Geography and "pivot"
chunks.text:
- New York, LA and SF can all produce great companies. Outside the Valley there is less competition for talent, lower costs (about a third less) and talent stays longer, but fewer unicorns come from there. Amazon and Microsoft are the exceptions.
- Tactic he describes: keep a small HQ or WeWork in the Valley for investors, and put the team elsewhere (Arizona, LA, San Diego, Waterloo).
- To be a great investor, he says you need Silicon Valley access. He did it by flying up two or three days a month and booking all meetings, and hit four of six unicorns that way.
- SF is "the worst-run great city in America", but investors are increasingly tired of SF living costs and open to LA.
- Pivot: he says it means keeping one foot planted and changing direction slightly, not dropping the idea. Example: Uber added ride sharing on top of black cars. Stewart Butterfield pivoted from failed games to Flickr and Slack.
- Side hustles: he generally prefers a clean break and a full-time founder.

chunks.heading: Where he sees opportunity: revisit false starts
chunks.text:
- Rule: look at categories where people tried and failed. Investors wrongly reason "it hasn't worked before." Google was the 11th or 12th search engine, just 20x better.
- Examples of timing changes:
  - YouTube: cloud computing made free video hosting viable; earlier, going viral meant a $5,000 bandwidth bill.
  - WebVan to Instacart, UberEats, PostMates and Google Shopping Express: GPS, logistics and unit economics improved.
  - Gaming repeatedly reinvents in waves (casual web, Facebook social, apps).
- AI: past false start, now real. He cites AI for HR, support and legal (contracts, accounting). He expects many white-collar tasks at risk over 10-20 years and expects entrepreneurs to rebuild each vertical as AI-enabled.
- Robotics: past false starts (Roomba, Segway). Now:
  - Cafe X: coffee in under 60 seconds, at about a third less cost.
  - Blockable: robot-built modular housing. He says the real savings is 6-12 months of build time, with the cost possibly 10-30% lower.
- VR: he calls it a possible false start, 4-5 years from mass use, with early VR startups running out of money. AR looks closer, perhaps 10 million daily users in two years.
- ICOs (2017): he calls the first wave scary, like the dotcom bubble. He sees $30-100 million raised on unbuilt products from "dark money" and expects most to go to zero. He thinks tokenized fund LP interests are inevitable within two to three years.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason hosts a VC roundtable on secondaries, backlogged unicorns, and the shift from growth-at-all-costs to profitability. His own contributions: scaling a portfolio via buckets and pods, selling some shares along the way, and a closing point that automating a job function beats the pain of recruiting.

chunks.heading: Why Jason sees the post-ZIRP unicorn backlog as a portfolio-management problem
chunks.text:
- Jason frames the startup market as three eras: peak ZIRP ("money's cheap, go for the growth"), the post-ZIRP collapse, and the AI era. He says the "game on the field" changes roughly every 3 years, so founders get conflicting advice at once.
- He points to a chart showing roughly half of unicorns growing 0-20% or declining. He calls this "that backlog": companies valued on "performance yet to come" that did not deliver.
- On the Rule of 40 (growth plus profit margin), he notes few unicorns clear it. He cites Palantir's CEO talking about a "rule of 80".
- He uses Uber as the example of the shift. Under Travis, it was growth at any cost ("we can lose $3 per ride. Who cares?"). Later it posted large profits and announced a $20 billion buyback, about 12% of the company.
- He notes the same shift in public markets, where capital allocation is now questioned (for example, Apple's $700 billion in buybacks).

chunks.heading: Seed investors: the 1-2-3 portfolio buckets and "pods"
chunks.text:
- Jason built an investing system for very large portfolios, with the basic numbers: roughly 50-70% of seed companies fail, and only a small share become huge.
- At his fund, 11 investment professionals plus analysts, researchers and associates (young people hired out of school and trained) are organized into "pods" of about 30 companies.
- The pods meet monthly. About 10 of the 30 show up, so founders solve each other's problems.
- Companies are put into three buckets:
  1. **Clear breakouts** (examples he gives: Robinhood, Superhuman). They need little help. Senior people manage the board relationships, and the team "pops champagne."
  2. **Figuring it out.** They have traction, customers and investor interest. These are the ones the pods help most, for example with churn, product-market fit or wrong pricing.
  3. **Struggling.** They cannot get customers, are not raising, team size is flat, and runway is under 12 months. Jason calls this "hospice care": help the founder decide whether to shut down, sell, pivot or start over, and invite them back to the accelerator with their next idea.
- The three signals he looks for in a company: getting customers, investor interest, and traction.
- Hard conversations with founders about wrapping up should start with a plan question: "what's your plan?"

chunks.heading: Selling secondaries: the evolution of Jason's philosophy
chunks.text:
- Jason describes four chapters in his own thinking:
  1. Never sell a share.
  2. Didn't sell, and regretted it after offers were declined and companies later went to zero or lost value.
  3. Sold roughly 10-20% in secondary transactions. He never felt like an idiot for selling (for example, some Uber at $30 a share, which he used to buy a house that doubled in value, while Uber later traded around $90).
  4. Proactively pushes founders to sell. When a company he invested in at roughly $10-15 million reached about $500 million, he asked the founder about a secondary plan.
- Chapter 4 tactic: he proposed a $20 million secondary in an oversubscribed round, with the founder selling roughly $5-7 million of stock (1-2% of shares) and the fund selling about 10% of its holding pro rata.
- The structure he describes is an auction-style tender: everyone says how much they want to sell, and everyone gets their share. A 10% holder would get about $2 million of a $20 million sale, and a 40% holder about $8 million.
- He says he wishes he had sold 20-40% in some past cases, especially around 2021. He tells founders to take money off the table after years of work.
- He regrets that he wasn't sold enough in some cases, and he regards educating founder-partners about secondaries as part of his role.
- He agrees that fund managers should manage end-of-life portfolios through partial secondary sales or by helping portfolio companies reach M&A.

chunks.heading: The state of M&A, IPOs and exit timing
chunks.text:
- Jason thinks a big part of the logjam was the four-year freeze on small and mid-size acquisitions (roughly $50 million to $500 million). He says companies like Meta and Amazon had small acquisitions scrutinized or blocked.
- His example is that the freeze affected even small deals, not just high-end ones such as Figma.
- He shows a chart of startups buying startups: 46% of VC-backed M&A deals had a VC-backed buyer on a full-year extrapolation. He reads this as consolidation and a way to wrap up old funds.
- On IPO thresholds, the number he hears is that a company needs roughly a billion in revenue growing 20-30% a year, though he adds he is not sure it is true. He also mentions half a billion to a billion in revenue as another version of the bar. Figma, which he cites, was around $700 million growing 45-46%.
- He notes 70% of unicorns may not actually be unicorns, and are growing under 50%.

chunks.heading: Advice for a stuck, slow-growing, profitable-ish company
chunks.text:
- Jason lays out the options and trade-offs for a company with revenue but low growth:
  - Sell to private equity. EV-to-revenue multiples are around 2-4x for classic software.
  - Reposition as an AI company if the company has the balance sheet and wherewithal.
  - Run it for profit, possibly with debt.
- On the debt idea, he argues a company doing about $100-200 million in revenue with 10-20% growth and profitability "might be a great company to borrow 20, 30, 40 million at 10% and run the business." He also says: sell to PE later, maybe after doubling the business's value.
- He raises the conflict of interest in this decision: venture investors targeting 100x have to sign off on a loan sitting ahead of their preference. His summary of the question to ask them: "do you want zero dollars or do you want 50 cents on the dollar?"
- He notes a PE sale can be good for founders who own 40-60% of the cap table, and for employees.
- On shutting down a company, he frames it as an experiment ("failed experiment") and asks whether the founder has "another experiment you want to try with a clean cap table." He notes that cap tables get convoluted when a company struggles.
- He points out a company with $30 million of capital in it will probably not return that on a small exit, while one with $2 million could.

chunks.heading: Capital efficiency, AI-first teams and recruiting
chunks.text:
- Jason's observation from his accelerator: founders come with little or no capital raised (or a $125,000 raise) and are quickly at a $500,000 a year run rate. He says AI tools make startups cheaper to run and sell.
- He argues that capital-constrained teams look for "the cheapest, fastest, best way to do something," which is increasingly AI.
- What he sees in startups: people who are not AI-first are being cut and replaced with AI-first people. An AI-first executive who knows Zapier and large language models has leverage of 2-4x the person sitting next to them.
- He also points to using international employees at a fraction of the cost.
- His example product is Athena, an AI/virtual personal assistant service he invests in.
- Key quote on hiring: "Recruiting people is painful. You wind up hiring the wrong person half the time. It takes three to six months." His conclusion is that talented people who can automate a job function beat adding more headcount: "I don't need to solve every problem by adding a body."
- He compares this to when startups stopped having to stand up their own servers: abstracting a function away rather than staffing it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason is interviewed about raising Launch Fund One from his conference, his friends and a big list. He covers pairing the fund with an AngelList syndicate, charging fees, ownership concentration and scaling a team. His mistakes and fixes are as useful as the wins.

chunks.heading: How the LAUNCH Fund Started
chunks.text: Jason's first fund came out of the LAUNCH Festival, his free startup conference. At the 2013 festival, David Sacks suggested Jason pick the top five conference startups each year and said he'd put in $50K each, a mini fund of about $250K. Jason says he had already been forwarding founders to investors for free, and he first doubted angel investing. His thesis was that entrepreneurs in their prime should put all their money into their own company and stay focused. Roelof Botha and Alfred Lin then showed him Sequoia's Scouts program, which gave $25K to $50K checks. At that time, $50K into a $5M company bought about 1%.

chunks.heading: Raising LAUNCH Fund One
chunks.text:
- The plan: raise $10M, make roughly 100 investments of $100K to $250K, and take a 20% carry.
- He ran it as a side hustle while running other companies.
- He first collected $50K checks from friends, including poker friends.
- A mutual billionaire friend then allocated $5M, half the fund. Jason calls this the big moment: "you don't know where your luck's gonna happen."
- He closed the $10M quickly and deployed it over about three years. He then ran LAUNCH Fund II and says Fund III was wrapping up.
- He announced it on September 24, 2013 by email to his big list, saying he would invest in 100 to 200 startups over five years.
- His advice is to say yes to things. A few a year lead nowhere, but the good things in his life came from taking that leap.

chunks.heading: Syndicate rules and economics
chunks.text:
- Naval taught him how SPVs and syndicates work. In Calm, he put $50K from the fund, shared it with about 150 syndicate members, and $328K came in.
- That was about 6.5x extra capital on a $50K check, so he describes it as a $10M fund plus a $60M fund. It didn't happen on every deal.
- The rules of the road:
  - The fund gets 100% of deals. No deal is syndicated unless the fund is in it.
  - LPs are the highest class and have access to every deal.
  - Once the fund hits its target check, any leftover allocation is offered to the founder to syndicate.
  - Founders choose; about 50% of them syndicate, so syndicate members see about half of all deals.
- Founders decline for these reasons:
  - Their round is oversubscribed.
  - They don't want the 4 to 6 week process, which requires a deal memo and a webinar to the syndicate (then about 300 members, later about 9,500).
  - They already have other funding sources.
- Founders who do it get these benefits:
  - In Calm, Jason went from owning 1% to 5% through the syndicate.
  - About 150 people at roughly $6K to $7K each are voting with their dollars. They become advocates who reply to asks like needing a CFO, an intro to Disney or a patent attorney.
  - It adds 150 investors as one cap table line (the SPV), a way to turn a company's supporters into loyal advocates.
- By 2022 his biggest syndicate deal was $6M. Early deals averaged $200K to $300K, so one deal now equals about 20 early deals.
- He says people claimed syndicates, equity crowdfunding and micro funds would never work, and "innovation in venture capital, everybody's like this can't work and then it inevitably does."

chunks.heading: Mistakes and fixes
chunks.text:
- He charged no management fee, only legal and accounting costs, and the media company paid for everything else. He now calls that "a dumb decision."
  - A 2.5% fee is about $250K a year, enough for a couple of support staff.
  - Fees come out of the returns: on a $10M fund returning $20M, carry is $4M, and four years of $250K fees would be netted out to $3M.
- He believes a16z hired rich partners so they needn't take big salaries, which let the firm fund marketing and HR departments.
- LAUNCH was first to add a fee to every syndicate deal: $5K on small deals, $10K up to $1M, and 1% over $1M. It is taken out of the money invested, so it doesn't affect the founder.
- The fee pays for support staff who answer the phone about K-1s, updates and trust name changes. He says many syndicates failed because they had no support and no fee, and compares it to a hotel with no front desk.

chunks.heading: Events, deal flow and the accelerator
chunks.text:
- He split from his former partner in the TechWrench 50 conference, which he calls "the greatest thing ever." Once he controlled the event, he made it free, even the demo pit tables. The largest SF one hit 15,000 attendees, and he ran two years in Australia.
- Lesson: if you pick a cynical, dark partner, things trend dark.
- Format: 50 companies, 3 minutes each, with pitch coaching and an invitation to invest.
- Many founders couldn't close with investors, so he started the LAUNCH Accelerator, first called an incubator. He says incubating means hatching an idea, while accelerating means an MVP plus a couple customers, then adding customers and capital. He has run 24 classes and says it is a better product than YC's for founders.
- He doesn't want to scale it far: going from 7 to 14 to 21 companies per class "is not fun for me, it's not magical."
- Deal flow was his early edge. Now it is a burden: about 200 qualified contacts per week and 50 meetings a week as a firm.
- He sends founders to the team first, with the goal that your conversation with him is already a fit and starts with your business.

chunks.heading: When he knew it worked, and non-consensus bets
chunks.text:
- Signals: people asked to buy his positions in Uber, Thumbtack and Robinhood. Up rounds followed.
- Calm was the best example. He watched revenue and cash balances grow, especially after Apple moved apps from a one-time $10 charge to subscriptions. The company later converted at about $250M and offered him a chance to sell some shares, locking in 50x.
- The Calm team had met 40 investors, all said no, and LAUNCH was the only yes. They said they would shut down without it. He says non-consensus bets that work are what make you an investor.
- He says Travis Kalanick credited him on Uber, noting he supported founders for 10 years and brought three of the first five investors.
- He knew he'd be good at it from day one because friends he referred to VCs built multi-billion dollar companies, and journalism gave him a sense for people who are bullshitting or media-trained.
- Advice to new investors: watch 100 pitches and see the pattern. Compare revenue, valuation, headcount, and customer types (pilot, Kickstarter, real) and business models (SaaS or one-time hardware). Founders self-select for charisma, so ask for margins, customers and the books.

chunks.heading: Fund manager commandments
chunks.text:
- Build a wide LP base so you aren't dependent on one LP. His first LP was 50% of the fund.
- Make capital calls less annoying. Funds like Sequoia call money when needed, because IRR starts when the money is drawn. Twelve calls of $4K each annoy LPs, so he now tells LPs to expect larger calls like 25% at a time.
- Take your time, and concentrate. Top LPs told him he was an idiot for not following on, and that you need 5 to 15% of a big winner rather than 50 basis points.
  - His targets and examples: 10% ownership, Calm about 5%, Superhuman 2%, Grin 12%, and 6% in another.
- Get a board seat or observer seat. Without one you miss the next round, which closes before you hear about it.
  - On boards he tells founders to skip the funding tour: "last round was 10 million, I think the company's worth 20, would you like us to put a million dollars in at 20."
- Have a multi-fund strategy and find your "Goldilocks zone" in stage, founder type, sector or geography, then press that advantage. YC doubles its accelerator rather than adding a Series A fund.

chunks.heading: Scaling the team
chunks.text:
- He no longer takes most first meetings. Most founders are too early, so they are routed to Founder University (a 12-week or 2-day program) or the Accelerator.
- He delegated legal, accounting and similar work because his superpower is communication, not spreadsheets.
- He is moving to where the team makes accelerator and Founder University acceptances, and he meets companies once they are in.
- He compares it to sports: stars need a team in the playoffs. Breakout success comes with a team, and he enjoys training people to do the job.
- He is the pioneer of the journalist-plus-investor model and expects more.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2011 Startup Grind fireside where Jason explains how he undercut pay-to-pitch conferences, why resilience and product focus matter most, and when to ignore advice. He also argues founders should take big exit offers and ignore the press, drawing on his own $20M mistake.

chunks.heading: Early ventures and the path from IT to publishing
chunks.text:
- Jason grew up in Brooklyn, the child of a bartender and a nurse. He describes the family as "barely middle class and scraping by month to month."
- His parents couldn't afford college. He studied at night at Fordham for five years (about $10,000 a year) while working days fixing laser printers, then moved into IT, setting up Novell networks.
- At Sony in the early 1990s he built "Jason's News," a Lotus Notes app that pulled news from LexisNexis. He emailed it to senior executives, and it ended up being read daily by the Sony leadership.
- He cold-searched a Sony director's press history, sent him the file, and got invited to lunch. That relationship led to the Sony jet and an exec-level internet advisory role at age 23.
- He started Silicon Alley Reporter at 25. It peaked at 70 employees and $11.6 million in revenue, built on credit cards.
- After the bust it shrank to 10 employees and $600,000 in revenue. He says: "I learned more on the way down than on the way up."
- He later started the blog company (Weblogs Inc.) from an idea on the night of Patrick Ewing's retirement ceremony. He proposed 10 or 20 vertical blogs, his developer partner said it would need 100, and Jason replied "let's do it!"

chunks.heading: Perseverance, resilience and resourcefulness
chunks.text:
- He names perseverance, resilience and resourcefulness as the most important entrepreneur traits, with resilience probably first: staying positive while "getting your ass kicked."
- At Mahalo, "resourceful" and "resilient" are two of the 10 words in the culture document, and he uses them to hire. His test for resourceful: someone who can "get a dollar out of a nickel" or solve a problem nobody has solved in 10 years.
- If you're about to give up, he says you may not be cut out for it. If you persevere through two or three attempts and learn each time, "you will succeed."
- "You miss 100% of shots you don't take." Ask whether in 20 years you'd rather say you tried and failed than say "I had the same idea for Twitter, I just didn't do it."
- Even "the silliest entrepreneur on their worst day" is more impressive than someone punching a clock.
- He says entrepreneurship is typically a younger person's game. Someone with two kids working 40 hours a week on a startup has it harder than a founder who doesn't sleep.

chunks.heading: When to listen to advice and when to ignore it
chunks.text:
- Knowing when to listen and when to ignore is one of the hardest things for young entrepreneurs. "Consider the source."
- He now avoids ideas most people immediately understand: if the majority likes it, it has probably been tried, everyone has the idea, or it won't be big.
- He wants an idea where about 5% say it's brilliant, 10% say it could be interesting, and 85% don't get it.
- His Human Power Search (Mahalo 1.0) idea failed. Tell-tale sign: he wasn't using it himself. He realized that even if Google has 3-4 spammy results in 10, there are 6-7 good ones, and hitting back is low effort. "People just adapt to imperfect situations."
- He calls it his Newton: "too early," but some people were jazzed about it.
- Product check questions: Are people getting value? Do you use it yourself? Do your employees? Do people use it repeatedly? Are you part of someone's everyday life?
- "All of my success in life has come when I've focused on the product." He cites Silicon Alley Reporter, TechCrunch, Autoblog, Joystick and the Mahalo video pivot.

chunks.heading: Timing, iteration and small decisions
chunks.text:
- Success is "all timing and iteration." YouTube won after thousands of failed web-video attempts because bandwidth dropped, storage collapsed in cost, Flash made playback easy, and syndication made sharing possible. "3-4 things unlocked that magic."
- Facebook was not the first social network. It was the first with a good clean UI.
- Friendster had a similar UI but its servers weren't kept up. MySpace could have won with reliable servers and a more professional look. LinkedIn might have won with public profiles and messaging. If Twitter hosted images, Facebook might be smaller.
- His point: "little decisions along the way can make a big difference."

chunks.heading: Search, switching costs and not playing games you can't win
chunks.text:
- Beating an incumbent search engine requires being 2-3 times better. "The mental cost of switch is high, people think it's low." Nobody switches for something 10-20% better.
- Swap the logos on search results and testers can't tell the difference. Put the logos back and they say the brand they know is better. He calls that a lesson in brand.
- Google's relevancy relied on domain age, inbound links and page count. Demand Media bought an 11-year-old domain, added millions of pages and built links. J.C. Penney bought links at scale. The "emperor has no clothes" exposure makes it easier to game.
- He predicted Google would move to social signals, time on page and browser data, turning the index upside down. A year earlier he pivoted Mahalo out of the content-farm race for that reason.
- On partners: "the worst thing you can do to a partner is make them look stupid." eHow boasting that its algorithm outsmarts Google invites retaliation.
- "You never get high on your own supply." Know the game you're playing: "Me vs. anybody at Google in poker, I'm rich; I will win." He would not play chess or write an algorithm against Google.
- When he can't win, he changes the rules. He would publicly show a $1,000 page next to the three pages ranking above it and campaign publicly for the problem to be fixed.

chunks.heading: Content economics: why depth loses in SEO and how Mahalo pivoted to video
chunks.text:
- Ad-supported content has a perverse incentive: the better your page solves a problem, the less people click ads. Spending $10 on 100 thin pages beat spending $1,000 on one deep video series.
- Jason spent $500-$3,000 on a series of videos with an expert in HD, with Q&A and articles, and still got beaten by thin pages. He described the 100-page strategy as roughly 300-to-1 odds against a single deep page.
- His Mahalo pivot was expert-led educational video, in the style of Khan Academy (one teacher, 3,000 lessons) and Lynda.com. Targets: music, food and video games, then language, math and science.
- Claimed numbers at the time:
  - 26,000 videos produced
  - 30 million views the previous month, 12 million site visitors
  - 105 staff, planning 100 more video editors
  - 800-900 videos a week, planning about 2,500 a week with more studios
  - A target of 500,000 videos in 2 years
- His video unit economics: a guitar video ("How to Play Hotel California") cost about $100 and got 500,000 views in 6 months. At a $3 CPM that is about $3,000 a year and $10,000 over 3 years. Related songs cross-link and compound.
- About 95% of views came from YouTube. Even with TubeMogul distribution, "YouTube is where it's at." His rule: when something is working, focus on the platform that matters rather than building for five.
- Casting: he picks teacher credentials over presentation skills when forced to choose.
- Evergreen topics (a quadratic equation is the same tomorrow) and translation make each video reusable. He expected US internet companies to make two-thirds of revenue outside the US.
- His vision: one brand that teaches everything, with video, articles and expert Q&A together. Lesson plans and exercises come next.
- He says design matters less than assumed: eBay, Craigslist and Huffington Post are ugly. "Community and content trumps the look and feel."

chunks.heading: Running Launch as a founder-first conference
chunks.text:
- His conference strategy was pricing as disruption. DEMO charged about $20,000 for a six-minute slot, TechCrunch50 charged startups nothing, and at Launch "I pay you."
- The Launch ticket tiers: $1,000 for non-bootstrap startups, about $400 for regular startups, with 10-25% off for people who follow him on Twitter and read his newsletter, and a "sob story" email route.
- Initially he expected to lose about $150,000 and was running at a loss or break-even, with any profit reinvested in the companies.
- He gave away roughly 10 free Demo Pit tables (a $1,000-$1,500 value each) via Hacker News and Quora, asking only that attendees "kick ass."
- He kept the focus on the 40 startups. He kept his own company's presence off the event and opposed staging fights between big names (the Disrupt direction), so the headline would be the startups' moment. "Everyone can win, it's not a zero sum game."
- Mandatory rehearsals: he scored each rehearsal and wouldn't let anyone onstage under an 8, but wouldn't let them drop out either. He compares himself to the man at the back of the run with a stick. "It's so awesome to watch companies go from having a great product but a terrible presentation to having both."
- He asked rehearsing companies for their number one need ("venture capital and angels"). He then invited the open angel forum members free and personally emailed whole VC firm teams a form letter ("Will no one come as my guest?"), which got replies. He then offered VIP party access.
- On conference pricing generally: SXSW grew from about 500 to 5,000 people by staying affordable ($450-$800). He now sends his best developers to conferences as a reward.
- He wants more builders (developers, product managers) rather than only CEOs, who he says give "bullshit press releases." "There's an inverse correlation of how much money you've made and how freely you speak."
- Origin: TechCrunch50 came out of a 2006 dinner where he told Mike Arrington to run an event that picks startups on merit instead of selling stage time.

chunks.heading: Fundraising, exits and financial realism
chunks.text:
- He took on consulting income while building businesses rather than going all-in: "fuck you I have to pay my rent!" A severance from his Venture Reporter sale (19 months remaining on his deal) funded a year of building Weblogs Inc.
- He says it's easy to say "it's not about money" once rich. Venture capital means "venture" plus "capital," and exits are the point. "Anyone who says this industry is not about money is lying."
- He sold Weblogs Inc. after 18 months with $10,000 left in the account and a $30 million offer: "what would you do? Take the money!"
- "If they offer you $100 million, take the money for God's sake!" He thinks young entrepreneurs get bad advice not to sell. Turning down a disproportionate offer is "in a way saying you'll never have another good idea."
- His first company got a $20 million offer that he declined; he later got under $1 million. That stung for a long time, because it was the money meant for his parents. He now plays long and aims for a top-25 site.
- Selling makes sense at the peak when the business can't get much bigger (his example: Huffington Post). Keep the chips on the table when growth is visible (Facebook, Groupon), where a big stack lets you "play some marginal hands." Know when to cash in.
- He saw angel rounds overpriced: valuations double or triple what they should be. Angel rounds should be $1-3 million, not $6-8 million. He was sitting those out unless he received an advisory stake.
- He argued 2011 was not a bubble: Groupon, LinkedIn and Facebook were profitable, scalable businesses. Mahalo's 105 staff were funded by revenue and he didn't need to raise more.

chunks.heading: Positioning, press and fighting as an underdog
chunks.text:
- He deliberately embraces the outsider and underdog role: "I like it better when I had to fight my way up." He picks fights on behalf of startups against entrenched players that prey on them (DEMO, pay-to-pitch forums).
- Angry emails and attempts to blackball him are a signal: "when people start trying to blackball you or get you fired or shut you down, that means you're on the right track." If people in power get concerned, you're disrupting something.
- Press advice for founders: ignore it. Whatever is written is "in the rearview mirror," writers often don't understand the business, and headlines are written separately from the story and optimized for clicks.
- He criticizes journalism for hating on everything and writing anti-success stories. His newsletter is deliberately a celebration of what's great.
- Location: he based Mahalo in LA because he met his wife there. LA lets him be the big fish in a small pond for hiring, since no one leaves Mahalo for a local rival. The big Valley companies pay about 50% more for the same people. He thinks New York funding may be easier than the Valley because many East Coast VCs won't take a long flight.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Calacanis says his 20-person firm moved about 20% of its tasks to OpenClaw agents ("replicants") in 20 days and expects not to hire another human for a year or two. He argues agents that act, not just advise, and improve through skills and memory are cheaper and faster than adding headcount.

chunks.heading: Replicants as the new default hire: OpenClaw at Jason's 20-person firm
chunks.text:
- Jason spent 20 days obsessed with OpenClaw, an open source platform that runs on a Mac, PC or in the cloud. He calls it "everything we were told Siri and Alexa would be."
- Its difference from ChatGPT-style LLMs: once you authenticate it with your online services, it "does things" as opposed to "tells you things."
- He sees LLMs as great researchers and archivists. They make middle managers "100% more effective, instantly" by summarizing meetings, creating action items and preparing plans for humans to execute.
- He says LLM makers don't let their products execute because the companies are "scared to death of the mistakes they would make."
- With OpenClaw, "you assume that responsibility." If it makes a mistake after you gave it your password, "that's on you."

chunks.heading: What an OpenClaw agent actually does
chunks.text:
- Podcast booking: it researches potential guests, finds their contact information, emails an invite, builds a CRM to manage those contacts, and schedules the appearance on the calendar.
- Errands: it can fill an Uber Eats cart and order lunch.
- Jason's 20-person venture and podcasting firm offloaded about 20% of its tasks to OpenClaw in 20 days.
- He says it keeps improving daily because of "skills" and memory.

chunks.heading: Skills and recursive self-improvement
chunks.text:
- Skills are built by you or third parties and "function like apps."
- His favorite is /last30days by Matt Van Horn. It lets you instruct an agent (he calls it a "replicant") to research best practices for any skill on the web and fold the learnings into its skill stack.
- Example: for thumbnails, the firm's Producer Replicant runs a deep research project every Saturday at noon. It finds people discussing how to make better thumbnails on Reddit and elsewhere on the open web.
- His framing: unlike humans, the replicant "doesn't take breaks and doesn't forget. It just relentlessly makes itself better. It's recursive."

chunks.heading: The hiring hiatus and the economics behind it
chunks.text:
- Jason doesn't expect to hire another human at his firm "for at least a year or two."
- He expects efficiency to rise at least 10% a month, which he equates to two new full-timers.
- His reasons: it's easier, faster and more cost-efficient to set up replicants.
- Cost: replicants burn about $1,000 in tokens a month and "never ask for a raise."
- Claimed performance: replicants "don't make mistakes," get 10% better at their jobs each week (which he says typically takes humans about a year), and "don't complain, they train."
- A new human hire becomes "a luxury spend for now," something you do because you can afford it and enjoy having another interesting person around.

chunks.heading: Team buy-in and the optimistic framing
chunks.text:
- He says everyone on the team buys in because "chores are not fun."
- Each time a replicant takes over repetitive chores, the team gets more time with other humans: founders, podcast guests and one another.
- He rejects the dystopian read: "This isn't dystopian. It's nirvana!" He compares it to Star Trek, where humans solve problems alongside "Computer."
- His headline: "AGI is here. It's just not implemented yet."

chunks.heading: Investing angle
chunks.text:
- Jason's firm (LAUNCH) is looking to invest in OpenClaw-related startups. Founders are asked to email what they're building, why, and a bit about themselves to openclaw@launch.co.
- His team has covered OpenClaw heavily on This Week in Startups and launched a new podcast, This Week in AI.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason Calacanis explains his angel investing playbook: invest in a Goldilocks stage window, build ownership via pro rata and super pro rata, and sell some on the way up. He argues down markets are the best time to invest and hire, and that startups come down to team, product velocity and customers.

chunks.heading: Down markets are the best time to invest, and "tourists" leave
chunks.text:
- Jason says "fortunes are made in the down market, they're collected in the up market." He calls the best time to invest a down market.
- In a downturn fewer people start companies and fewer people invest in them. That gives time to meet companies and make "a really thoughtful investment, not out of fear or FOMO, but out of really doing your research."
- The founders and investors who stay active in downturns tend to be the most resilient. He calls them "the crocodiles, the sharks, the cockroaches, the people who don't die."
- He describes the 2016-2022 boom as "tourist season in Silicon Valley and startup land for five, six years." People who are not committed or full-time go home when the market turns, and he says he has "seen this movie before."
- He first scouted for Sequoia around 2009, at the tail end of the Great Recession. He says he lived through two intense recessions as a professional.
- Recessions make everyone focus on what matters. He calls the 2022-era correction "a great flush": weak companies and weak projects get flushed out and the strong ones remain.
- He planned to invest more in startups over the next year or two than in the previous two years, after pausing on overpriced deals.

chunks.heading: Valuations reset: what overheated looked like and where prices went
chunks.text:
- He blames the overheated market on stimulus, low rates and cash piling up during COVID: PPP, extra unemployment and stimulus checks, with nowhere to spend it. Then came inflation, Ukraine and China lockdowns.
- Late-stage valuations were cut roughly in half. A billion-dollar valuation became about 500 million. SaaS multiples of 100x to 200x revenue fell to something like 30x to 50x revenue.
- In private markets, companies had been raising at 25 to 50 million valuations with no launched product. He calls that "over."
- A standard seed round used to be around 5 million, then went to 15 to 20 million, and he expected it to come back down to 6 to 12 million.
- He sat out deals he couldn't justify, like paying 50 million for a startup that hadn't launched, or 25 million for one with 500K in revenue.
- His rule: "Entry price does matter." Investors were crediting companies "for work not done" by valuing them as if they would execute perfectly for five years.
- He cited the Peloton example. At roughly $30,000 per subscriber of valuation, you had to bet on 10x more subscribers to make it back.
- He says everyone got entitled: employees, VCs, public-market investors, crypto investors and founders. "Everybody thought this was easy. It's never been easy."
- Hedge funds and public-market investors dipping into private markets, and investors who skipped diligence and copied what Sequoia or others did, were part of the overheating.

chunks.heading: Sell on the way up and lock in downside protection
chunks.text:
