- Jason says he is always selling on the way up as an angel. If he invested at 5 or 10 million and a secondary appears at 250 million, 500 million or a billion, he takes it or considers it deeply.
- His example schedule: sell 10% at 250 million, 10% at 500 million and 10% at a billion. He accepts that he may look stupid if it goes to 10 billion, because the proceeds get redeployed into more startups that could also go up.
- On his math: if you sold 20% of an investment before an asset fell 90%, you would not be down 90%. "You'd have that 20% as a floor." He says "a little downside protection never hurt anybody."
- He says many investors were locked up in Coinbase, Peloton and similar positions and "never realized it." You also have to be able to capitalize on a win, not just make it.
- Selling part of a position while keeping some ownership is a theme across his alternatives too. For example, he could sell half of his Tesla Roadster through Rally Road for 125K against a 150K cost and still own half.

chunks.heading: Portfolio construction: the Goldilocks window and milestone-based follow-ons
chunks.text:
- Jason invests in a "Goldilocks window, not too cold, not too hot."
  - Too cold: an idea, passion and a white paper.
  - Too hot: $20 million in revenue at a $200 million valuation, selling 1% of the company with only a quarter percent available to him. He can't build a position.
  - Just right: product launched, about 250K in annual revenue (for example 20K to 30K last month, times 12) at a reasonable valuation multiple, buying about 5%.
- He starts at roughly 3% to 6% ownership and aims to build a position of about 15%. For an exceptional founder he may go straight to 10%.
- Follow-on plan: if revenue triples and valuation triples, go to 10% ownership. If it doubles again, go to 15%.
- He has learned to love the milestone-based process in Silicon Valley: "You don't need to buy all the shares in the seed round. You just need to be a great partner to the founder."
- He discusses follow-on rights with founders up front: pro rata, and super pro rata if the company is growing. If it goes sideways he takes his pro rata at most. If it is going poorly, he does not do bridges.
- He tells founders it is their job to keep the company growing if they want more money from him.
- Deal sizing at his syndicate: the average investor puts in about $7,000, with roughly 100 to 150 investors per deal. He likes lots of small bets and doubling or tripling down where he has conviction.
- He has invested in well over 300 companies. His firm invests about $100 million a year in early-stage startups, and he runs a 21-person company with podcasts, conferences and an investment team.

chunks.heading: Process over prediction: write it down and review it
chunks.text:
- His core advice: "Process, have a process, write it down." You can't predict the market or the outcome, so you focus on what you control.
- Track the funnel: how many companies apply, how many he meets, how many second meetings, how many follow-ups, how many bets, how many double-downs, how many times he can liquidate.
- Write down why you said yes and why you said no, then go back and review. He recommends the book "Superforecasting," and compares it to poker players who review their decisions (outs, expected value).
- Review passes, too. His own example is passing on Indiegogo when he was only writing 25K checks and had no team, and passing on MasterClass at the first round because of valuation and because he discounted the founder's access to Dustin Hoffman. He says the lesson was that the access was itself a signal of ability.
- He spent two hours on two consecutive days with his investment team refining process: how many companies to meet, what to ask, when to say no versus "not yet," and how many days to wait before following up if a founder doesn't book a meeting. He says they debated day three through day six and concluded any would work.
- He follows up with almost every company he passes on to look for signals that he was wrong.
- "If you want to get good at something, you better be a [maniac], because you're competing against people who are [maniacs] like me."
- Book recommendations tied to this: "Thinking in Bets" (Annie Duke) and "The Checklist Manifesto" (checklists for discipline and process).

chunks.heading: How to spot a breakout company
chunks.text:
- He says you probably can't pick the unicorn at the earliest stage, and warns about survivorship and confirmation bias afterward. So make 20 to 30 bets, monitor them and watch for breakout signals.
- Signals he looks for: over 10% month-over-month growth (doubling about every 7.2 months), revenue tripling year over year, heavy hiring. Those signals are "undeniable," and he double-clicks to find out why.
- A company is "about three things": the team that builds the product, the product, and the customers who consume it. Get that flywheel going and it will "work out fine in all likelihood."
- Things that distract founders: total addressable market, competitors, culture. He focuses on the three core signals instead.
- Product velocity check: a software company should push a release about every two weeks. During diligence he asks, "When was the last update? Can you share the release notes?"
- Customers: you have to "delight" them, which takes a great product, which takes a good team.
- Red flag: founders who are better at raising money than building products, who convince investors to give them money at a higher rate than they convince customers to. He says it is not insurmountable but a major flag.
- He passed on crypto deals with no product because "I'm a product person." For crypto he only sees a team and a white paper, and cannot talk to customers.

chunks.heading: Serious founders: what he wants, and what he doesn't
chunks.text:
- He doesn't like "pre-seed" rounds where founders ask for 250K to quit their job, hire a dev shop and go to conferences or crypto parties. He sees it as entitlement.
- Preferred path: do consulting three days a week and work on the side project four days, work seven days a week, get the product launched or to 10K a month in revenue, then raise a proper seed round. That avoids dilution and shows commitment.
- Founders who skip steps, and investors who skipped diligence and customer calls, were both part of the problem.
- He says a downturn sorts founders. "If you're not serious about it, this isn't like a hobby, it's a vocation."
- The generation that found accelerator admission (Techstars, Y Combinator) the hardest step, with seed, Series A and Series B coming easily, now has to catch up. They have the valuation of a later stage but the traction of an earlier one, and need to "fill in all of that credit you got in advance."
- Equity crowdfunding: Inside.com raised about 700K from its users on Republic. He likes the discipline of having hundreds of $100 investors, because it makes him feel the responsibility more than a VC writing a check that is 1% of a big fund.

chunks.heading: Hiring in a downturn
chunks.text:
- In the boom, mediocre people held 10 offers and CEOs had to negotiate pay packages that didn't make sense.
- In a down market: "You're going to have a great person with two and a mediocre person with none." You can say the package doesn't make sense and offer one that does.
- After the dot-com bust and the Great Recession, people said "I have nothing else going on, sure, I'll work at your startup," and he says "great magic happens" when that occurs.
- Talent who can't get through hiring freezes at IBM, GE or Google will "take a flyer on a startup."

chunks.heading: The syndicate, the podcast and where he sees opportunity
chunks.text:
- His syndicate (thesyndicate.com) was the first on AngelList. It has done over 250 SPVs, run with SureFund management. Roughly 11,000 to 12,000 syndicate members.
- First deal: Calm.com, invested 376,000 at a 4 to 5 million valuation. The company is worth over 2 billion, a nine-figure position for them, and they have sold some shares for returns while keeping the majority.
- Writing a deal memo for thousands of accredited investors makes him sharper. He compares it to playing in the NBA finals: every turnover is remembered, so he is more careful than he would be "bawling in the street."
- Podcasts as a deal-flow and learning tool: over 1,300 episodes of This Week in Startups and about 80 of All-In. He has portfolio founders on as guests, which helps them and brings in more deal flow. He compares it to "getting an MBA every year."
- He says podcasting isn't required for every investor. Writing, conferences or one-on-one research can also work, whichever the person is best at.
- Sectors he likes: B2B SaaS (subscription pricing that is affordable and high-value), industrial companies (he cites Blockable, which builds homes and factories), and consumer subscriptions that are singularly focused. His subscription bets: Calm (meditation), FitBot (workouts), Steezy (dance), Musician (popular music), ToneBase (classical music) and Fluent Forever (languages).
- He expects the next big wave of companies to be business-to-business and industrial, citing Stripe and Flexport as likely next big IPOs, rather than consumer-facing like Google, Facebook, Uber, Airbnb and Tesla.
- He remains a large holder of Uber and calls it undervalued, pointing to network effects favoring the winner over Lyft.

chunks.heading: Alternative assets: what he owns and how he thinks about them
chunks.text:
- Focus: startups are his main asset class ("the greatest asset class available"). Elsewhere he makes many small bets to learn and goes deeper only where he has an edge.
- Crypto: he bought Bitcoin at about $100 and did well, but is not active. He stays "crypto curious" and has a handful of investments. He passed on token deals like Filecoin because there was no product to evaluate.
- Cars: he owns the 16th Tesla Roadster (a signature series, among the first 100) and the first Model S ever made (signature number one). He was offered 250K for the Roadster on Rally Road after paying 150K. He thinks both will be worth low millions in 10 years. He might keep the Model S until he is 70.
- Art: he owns a fractional piece of a Basquiat via Masterworks. He says he doesn't have an edge buying a whole painting and would be too concentrated in one investment. Platforms he uses and thinks curate well: Masterworks, Republic, SeedInvest and Rally Road, plus others he named like Rcrowd.
- Real estate: three properties (primary home, Tahoe ski house, one in the Bay Area), bought for use and as a hedge, not speculation. He tried Airbnb on a previous home and sold the house after a party caused $5-6K in damage and neighbor complaints.
- He likes fractional ownership of homes (for example, Picasso) and shared planes among friends, and notes the hard parts are cleaning, maintenance and scheduling.
- Yield: he doesn't need distributions from alternatives because he has lumpy angel exits plus steady media revenue from This Week in Startups.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Jason explains how profitable "dude businesses" doing about $1M a year can raise angel money to scale, what angels expect, and why founders should take more risk and run cheap experiments. He also covers why he moved Inside.com from apps to email and why podcast networks struggle.

chunks.heading: Why Jason wrote the angel investing book and how wealth is built
chunks.text:
- Jason's book *Angel* (2017) draws on 150 angel investments, six of which became unicorns. Desktop Metal, a metal 3D printer maker he backed in its first round, announced a raise of over $1 billion the day of this interview.
- His agent had pitched him "for Dummies" books for a decade. He argues books should come from subject-matter experts, not from inexperienced people who write them to become experts. He says he was a good entrepreneur, not an elite one, but has real credibility in angel investing.
- His core thesis: wealth in the 21st century comes from getting on the cap tables of high-growth companies, "specifically in Silicon Valley, because the hit rate there is so much better." He says the numbers there are "add a zero or two from any other market."
- He argues the 20th-century path (save, pay down a house, brown-bag lunch) has broken. His parents' Brooklyn brownstone cost about $45,000, under one year of their combined income. Today it is a $1M-$2M house against roughly $300,000 of household income, with student debt of up to about $150,000 on top.
- His hope: if 100,000 people buy the book and 5-10% start angel investing, maybe 100 get an incredible result. If the rest land within plus or minus 50% of their money, that is still a fine outcome.
- He says the book also works in reverse for founders. It shows how angels and VCs think, so founders can sync with them rather than "game" them.

chunks.heading: What angels and VCs expect, and the "add a zero" idea for small profitable businesses
chunks.text:
- Return expectations:
  - A regular angel wants 5-10x in about seven years.
  - Professional angels hope some companies hit 50-100x.
  - Jason himself looks for companies that can do 100x to 500x.
  - VCs invest millions and aim for about 10x, with an outside chance of 100-200x.
- Taking outside money is "lighting a fuse" or "hitting a starter pistol." Your life changes: you send updates, answer questions, and are now expected to scale.
- He frames what small, profitable "grinder" founders (e.g. a one-person plugin or template business at $1M a year) already have and lack. They have product sense and customer sense, but not yet scale sense.
- His method for adding a zero: study your customers. If the top 5-10% share a need, double or triple down. Example: three of 1,000 customers are financial companies asking for the same features, so tell them you are building that product and charge them $25,000 a month.
- Illustrative cap table math: $1M revenue, $5M valuation, 5M shares at $1. An investor puts in $500,000 for 10% and the company deploys it on five salespeople ($50,000 plus commission) and two developers.
- His advice: "just add a zero." He says this is what he tells founders, and when they do, he says "let's add one more and we're done."

chunks.heading: How to pitch angels: a profitable small business is an asset
chunks.text:
- Some investors read a bootstrapped $1M business as "thinks small." Savvy ones see a "dude business" (a founder-run $500K-$1M business) as a sign of smart, lean operators who learn a lot.
- Examples he gives:
  - Phil Kaplan (DistroKid) runs lean companies of himself plus freelancers up to millions in revenue.
  - MailChimp reached about $400M in revenue without outside money.
  - SurveyMonkey took investment after scaling off revenue.
  - Both paths can work.
- His pitch template for a profitable company: "We made a million dollars. We can grow 20% a year for 10 years and make $10 million. We want to build a billion-dollar company; here's the opportunity and why we need $1.5 million for 15%."
- If revenue has been flat for five years, you need a credible story for why it will accelerate. Example: you never had outbound sales, so add a team. Investors would want to test that theory and might give you $500K to do it.
- First-contact email: send about 10 angels fewer than five sentences. Say what the company is, how it makes money and for whom, include a revenue chart (weekly, monthly or quarterly) and a product demo link. He says angels click the links and then take the meeting.
- He criticizes the opposite approach: "Most people write their life story and what they plan on doing, the talkers, the tourists."
- Founders who reach $1M can reach $10M. He is unsure whether they can reach $100M, but a $10M business is worth 5-20x revenue, and investors can tell you which people you need to hit the next milestone.
- Recent example: his first cannabis investment, in a company making about $1M from advertising, cannabis tourism, magazines and festivals. He took the scrappy revenue base as a good starting point.

chunks.heading: Take more risk, and treat funding as a starter pistol
chunks.text:
- He argues most founders earning $500K-$1M "don't take enough risk" because they protect an affluent lifestyle. If you never risk it, there is no chance of outsized success.
- Failure is recoverable: if you fall climbing "the startup mountain" you have more credibility and start over at the bottom. "You put another quarter in the machine, you get to play the video game again."
- Having built a million-dollar business before, you can build another.
- On Shark Tank-style thinking: money is not the prize, it is "the starter pistol." Investors want a return on capital, and finishing matters.
- Why fear the downside when "it's not life or death"? Bringing in investors gives you several people working for your success with skills you lack.

chunks.heading: Investor updates and planning discipline
chunks.text:
- Jason asks for a monthly update from each founder. It takes about an hour to write and covers key metrics, challenges, wins, losses, and where investors can help.
- Writing it creates discipline, and sending it to about 10 investors and the management team opens up dialogue. Companies that do this "go a lot further."
- He believes in planning. Example: plan to go from $1M to $3M in year one, then $3M to $9M after. If you only hit $2M and $6M, you will likely still be further along than someone without a plan.
- Founders who resist giving updates signal to him that they are not serious about the business or the relationship with investors. He likes people "serious about the business" who "want to do the business right."
- How involved he is depends on the founder: involved if they want help, less if they do not.

chunks.heading: Own the direct relationship: email, paid tiers and ads (Inside.com)
chunks.text:
- Platform risk lesson: Google featured Weblogs, Inc in its first quarterly report as an ad partner (over $2,000 a day), then cut about 90% of the traffic after algorithm changes. Calls went unreturned, despite a 10-year relationship.
- He argues Google should have paid content partners a licensing fee (e.g. 10 cents CPM) for content shown in its answer box.
- Same pattern with YouTube: it changed the rules and cut ads for creators with under 10,000 views, so he left the platform.
- Facebook example: its API is allowed until you gain traction pulling people off Facebook, then it is shut off.
- His response: go direct with email. "Use any of these other platforms if it gets you customers, but own a direct, deep relationship."
  - "I can't tell you how many people I know who have apps and have no emails."
  - Email "is the big growth hack" (Twitter's "here's what you missed" emails). If you are not collecting emails everywhere and giving subscribers massive value, "you're doing it wrong."
  - He also began experimenting with SMS.
- Inside.com numbers:
  - 200,000 subscribers across 26 newsletters, targeting 50.
  - LAUNCH Ticker: of 27,000 subscribers, over 1,000 pay, about 4%.
  - If 4% of 200,000 pay, that is about 8,000 paying subscribers, roughly $1M a year, funding about 20 journalists working from home.
  - The paid tier launched about three to four weeks before the interview with 1-2% of free users as the target.
- Staffing: remote journalists with 3-5 years' experience for $40,000-$50,000 plus benefits is a strong offer outside New York and San Francisco.
- Ads versus paid: LAUNCH Ticker let about 1,000 paid users turn off ads by clicking a profile setting. Only 10-20 did, because people like targeted ads. He thinks about 20% of people will pay a few extra dollars (his Hulu example: $10 with ads versus $13 without), so a paid tier can still carry ads.
- Idea he floats for Netflix: sponsored free days (e.g. a Mercedes-sponsored free Saturday with an ad and survey) as onboarding.

chunks.heading: Run experiments like probes, and cut apps for email
chunks.text:
- Mental model: send 100 probes to 100 planets and see which return a signal. Crossing planets off the list produces data. Entrepreneurship is "triangulating around a signal," where revenue and engagement (such as open rates) are the signals.
- Test cheaply and quickly. Ask, "what's the least costly and quickest way to get the signal?"
- Inside.com example:
  - The news app had hundreds of thousands of downloads, but under 1% used it daily.
  - Emails get 30-50% opens, with two sent a day. He calls this a 50x improvement on an old technology.
  - The app team of about eight highly paid people could be redeployed to hire about a dozen journalists.
  - He says no news app has worked, including ones he invested in such as Circa.
- Daily Brief test: 40-50% opened it in the morning, but readers said the news was stale the next day. He sent an afternoon update to about 1,000 people, then told the whole list they were moving to twice a day, with unsubscribe as the option. Only a few complained.
- Listen to metrics over vocal customers: "Sometimes people listen too much to their customers." Use data and experiments, not "emotions, feelings, predictions, or who's in charge." The restaurant analogy: you can charge for bread; if someone does not like it, they can go elsewhere.
- Cart-before-horse lesson: his Inside Drones video series was paused because the audience engagement was not there yet. His fix is to work backwards and build engagement first.
- He recommends *The Lean Startup* (Eric Ries).

chunks.heading: Podcast networks versus independent shows
chunks.text:
- His experiment seven years earlier: he and friends put $100K each into a network of shows (This Week in Startups, Kevin Pollak's Chat Show, Mark Suster's venture show, a Mad Men recap, Pensado's Place). Only two shows broke out.
- Lesson: credible hosts succeed and emerging hosts rarely break out in 3-4 years. The credible ones do not need a network, since an episode costs about $500-$2,000 to produce.
- He argues great podcasters stay independent as $1M-$10M businesses (Leo Laporte, Joe Rogan, Sam Harris, Adam Carolla). Networks struggle because hosts leave for life events or bigger deals. He believes Rogan and Laporte are above $5M.
- His own podcast started as recordings of two lunch conversations and turned into nearly 800 episodes and about 150,000 downloads per episode. He calls it a networking tool and a way to find founders to invest in.
- Open-source and defensibility: pick where you make money and make that part defensible. Google open-sources everything except its search algorithm; Facebook open-sources hardware but not its ad network or social graph.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A Substack index page of Jason Calacanis's recent posts. The substantive content is his pitch for a zero-tuition VC training program (hiring for work ethic over pedigree) and his rationale for reviving LAUNCH Festival to give founders affordable access. The rest is event and podcast promotion.

chunks.heading: Content and events (Substack newsletter)
chunks.text:
**All In Summit 2026**
- Jason promotes the All In Summit, September 13-15, 2026, in Los Angeles. He passes along a limited number of discounted scholarship tickets "for those of you just starting your careers."
- He reuses his newsletter as a distribution channel for events, podcasts and hiring calls, with a direct "hit reply" or email CTA each time.

**This Week in AI (podcast launch, March and May 2026)**
- Jason launched a weekly round-table podcast, "This Week in AI", in March 2026. It is "100% AI" and features founders and builders in the space.
- He frames podcasts as "my way of committing to lifelong learning, networking with driven people, and sharing with like-minded folks."
- Distribution: he lists the show on Substack, YouTube, Spotify and Apple Podcasts, and re-announces it in May 2026 to drive subscribers.
- He asks for reply feedback on every announcement, so the audience becomes a feedback loop.

chunks.heading: Hiring: the VC training program (April 2026)
chunks.text:
- Jason offers four slots in a "world's best VC training program" for recent graduates or career changers. Tuition is $0, and pay is "what you would have spent on your MBA tuition."
- Workload: about 60 hours a week, or 10-12 hours a day, plus checking email on weekends.
- Path: researcher, then analyst, then associate. He says "1.5 in three" make it to associate.
- The four traits he screens for:
  1. Being a learning machine
  2. High executive function
  3. Being extremely focused and curious
  4. Being able to work 12 hours a day for the founders
- Selection: he accepts under 1% of applicants and doesn't care how fancy the degree is. He loves candidates from UT Austin and "folks with a chip on their shoulders."
- Application: a cover letter on why you want to be a venture capitalist, your current skills and examples of your work ethic, sent to researchers@launch.co.
- His edge thesis: "80% of VCs are lazy AF," so simply showing up and working 10-12 hours a day beats most of them.

chunks.heading: LAUNCH Festival 2026 (San Francisco, March 16-17)
chunks.text:
- Origin: Jason created TechCrunch50 / LAUNCH Festival about 20 years ago because networking events cost about $4,000 a ticket and demoing on stage cost about $20,000. He ran it for about 10 years, paused after COVID, and brought it back in 2026.
- Format:
  - 50 startups each demo for three minutes
  - Judges give feedback and pick favorites
  - 250 founders attend free
  - 100 investors and LPs with whom he co-invests attend as guests
  - 50 VIP seats for the public at $1,000 each, which "unwrite" the free founder tickets
- Theme: OpenClaw, AI and agents.
- Prizes: Jason invests $25,000 in the best OpenClaw startup and $25,000 in the best non-OpenClaw startup, on the terms of the winner's last round or a Note/SAFE for the next round.
- Lesson learned: previously, "some bad actors" claimed a $100M valuation to game the prize. He now asks winners to act in good faith because he wants to invest in real startups.
- He also invites others to match his investment through partners@launch.co and sponsors to buy breakfast or the post-event mixer. The top ten startups from his Founder University Tokyo program are included too.
- His stated motive: "to make the industry open to more people on the way up."
